title: Activation, password reset and invitations
text:
Five routes of the console answer without a session, because each of them is the destination of a
link somebody received by email:

| Route | Reached from | The link lives |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `/account-activation/:token` | The email sent after [registering](#registration-and-activation) | 24 hours |
| `/reset-password-request` | The **Forgot your password?** link under the login form | — (it is a form, not a link) |
| `/reset-password/:token` | The email sent by that form | 1 hour |
| `/project-invitation/:token` | The email sent by [inviting somebody to a project](../project-settings/users-and-roles.md#inviting-a-member) | 5 days |
| `/organization-invitation/:token` | The email sent by [inviting somebody to an organization](../organizations/managing-an-organization.md#inviting-a-member) | 5 days |

The token is the whole of the authentication: whoever holds the link is whoever the email was sent
to, so it is worth treating one like a password until it is used.

:::danger[Without SMTP an installation cannot do any of this]
Every one of those tokens is delivered by email and by no other means. There is no screen that
prints a link, no CLI that generates one, and no way to read one back out of the console. An
installation with no `EMAIL_SMTP_HOST` therefore **cannot activate an account, cannot reset a
password and cannot confirm an invitation** — and it does not tell you so during installation.

What it does instead differs per flow:

| Flow | On an installation with no SMTP |
| --- | --- |
| Registration | Silently skipped. No activation token is created, no email is attempted, and the new account is usable straight away — nothing gates it. |
| Invitations | Silently degraded. No token, no email: the address is added as an **already active member**, with nothing having proved the person owns it. |
| Password reset | **Refused.** The recovery form answers that the installation has no email server and that resetting the password is not available; nothing is written to the account. |

Configure SMTP before you let anybody else near the console. See
[`EMAIL_SMTP_HOST` and its siblings](../self-hosting/environment-variables.md).
:::

title: Activation, password reset and invitations — Registration and activation
text:
Registering at `/register` creates the account and sends an activation email carrying a link to
`/account-activation/:token`. The screen does its work as it mounts and leaves for the login as soon
as the API answers, so what a person actually reads is the moment in between:

![The Account Activation screen, with the activation in progress on the token from the emailed link](../assets/account-activation.png)

There is nothing to fill in and nothing to confirm. On success a toast says *"Account activated,
redirecting you to login"* and the console goes back to the login form; on a token that is unknown
or more than 24 hours old the card shows the error instead, and the account stays unactivated.

:::caution[Until the link is followed, the account cannot be used]
When the installation has SMTP, a newly registered account carries an activation token, and the API
refuses **every authenticated request** from an account that still has one. The login form itself
accepts the password — signing in succeeds — but every call the console makes after it is answered
with *401 "User not verified, please verify your email"*, so the person lands straight back on the
login form. Once the 24 hours have passed the message becomes *"User not verified and the invitation
is expired, please reset your password"*. The [MCP server](../build-with-ai/mcp-server.md) refuses
such an account in the same way.

What gates access is the activation token, not the account status: an account is stored as `ACTIVE`
from the moment it is created either way. Two kinds of account never carry a token, and are
therefore never gated:

- accounts registered on an installation **without SMTP** — there is nothing to deliver the link with;
- accounts **provisioned automatically** the first time somebody signs in through a federated
  provider such as Auth0 or Google.

Note too that `REGISTRATION_ALLOWED=false` is not a barrier either: it hides the *Register* link
without closing the route behind it, as [The first startup](../self-hosting/first-startup.md#the-endpoint-stays-open)
sets out. A self-hosted installation that must not accept accounts has to be closed off in front of
the console — a private network, an ingress rule, an authenticating proxy.
:::

Where SMTP is not configured the flow is shortened rather than broken: no activation token is
generated at all, no email is attempted, and the registration screen sends the person to the login
form with "log in to access your account" instead of "we have sent you an email".

### Locked out of an unactivated account

An activation link that expired unused is a dead end, and none of the obvious ways out works:

- following the link answers *"Activation token expired"*, and there is **no way to request a new
  activation email** — the console has no screen for it and the API no endpoint;
- [resetting the password](#recovering-a-password) changes the password but leaves the activation
  token in place, so the account is refused exactly as before — despite what the error message
  suggests;
- registering again with the same address fails, because the account already exists.

The only recovery is on the database: an operator removes `activateEmailToken` and
`activateEmailExpires` from the user's document, after which the account signs in normally. Tell
people who register to follow the link within the day.

title: Activation, password reset and invitations — Recovering a password
text:
**Forgot your password?** under the login form leads to `/reset-password-request`, which asks for one
thing:

![The Recover Password form, asking for an email address](../assets/reset-password-request.png)

Submitting it ends in one of three ways:

| What happened | What the screen shows |
| --- | --- |
| The address belongs to an account, and the email was sent | *"If an account exists with this email, you will receive a password reset link"*, and back to the login form |
| The address belongs to no account | An error toast — *"The password reset link could not be sent. Please try again."* — and the form stays where it is |
| The installation has no SMTP | *"This installation has no email server configured: resetting the password is not available. Contact an administrator."* Nothing is written to the account. |

The confirmation is shown only once the API has answered with success.

:::note[The screen reveals whether an account exists]
Despite the wording of the confirmation, the form is not non-committal: an address the API has
never seen is answered with an error, and the console shows that error rather than the
confirmation. Anybody who can reach the form can therefore test whether an address has an account
on the installation — worth knowing if you expose the console publicly, put it behind a WAF or read
its access logs.
:::

The email carries a link to `/reset-password/:token`, good for **one hour** and for one use — the
token is cleared from the account the moment a password is set through it.

![The Reset Password form, with the new password and its confirmation](../assets/reset-password.png)

The new password must be at least 8 characters and the second field must match the first. Both rules
are checked in the browser; the confirmation field exists only there, and the API is sent the
password alone.

title: Activation, password reset and invitations — Accepting an invitation
text:
Both invitation links land on the same shape of screen, one naming a project and one naming an
organization, each stating the role that was chosen:

![The project invitation screen, naming the project and the role, asking for a password](../assets/project-invitation.png)

![The organization invitation screen, naming the organization and the role](../assets/organization-invitation.png)

The two password fields are **conditional**: they appear only when the invitee has no password yet,
which is the case for somebody the invitation itself created. Somebody who already had an account on
this installation sees the same card with nothing but **Accept invitation** on it.

Accepting does three things at once: it sets the password when one was asked for, it marks the
account active, and it signs the person in — the response carries an access token, so they land in
the console already authenticated rather than at the login form.

An invitation link is good for **five days**. The date is shown to whoever sent it, under
**Expires on** in the [pending invitations](../project-settings/users-and-roles.md#managing-invitations)
table.

### When the link does not work

A token that matches no invitation — because it was already accepted, or revoked, or mistyped — gets
a screen that says so and offers the way back:

![The invitation screen for a link that matches no invitation](../assets/invitation-not-found.png)

:::caution[An expired invitation does not say "expired"]
The screen above is shown when the API answers *not found*. An invitation that exists but is past
its five days answers with a different status, and the console has no case for it: it falls back to
**"Something went wrong — We couldn't load the invitation. Please try again in a moment."**

Trying again in a moment will never help, and the person has no way to tell an expired link from a
console having a bad minute. If somebody reports that message, check the invitation's **Expires on**
date and [resend](../project-settings/users-and-roles.md#managing-invitations) it.

Both cases also raise a toast carrying the raw HTTP message — *"Request failed with status code
404"* — which is not addressed to the person reading it. Ignore it; the card underneath is the real
answer.
:::

### The route that needs no email

Somebody who is already registered and signed in does not need the emailed link at all. Invitations
addressed to them are listed inside the console, and can be accepted or declined from there — which
is also the only way an invitation can be answered on an installation where email does not leave the
building. See [Switching organization](../organizations/managing-an-organization.md#switching-organization).

title: Activation, password reset and invitations — What the platform sends, and when
text:
Four emails exist in the product. There is no fifth, no digest, and nothing periodic:

| Email | Sent when | Subject | Link expires |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Account activation | An account registers, and SMTP is configured | 🎉 Activate Your Account | 24 hours |
| Password reset | The recovery form is submitted for an existing account, and SMTP is configured | 🔑 Reset Your Password | 1 hour |
| Project invitation | Somebody is invited to a project, or the invitation is resent | 🎉 You're invited to join *project* | 5 days |
| Organization invitation | Somebody is invited to an organization, or the invitation is resent | 🎉 You're invited to join *organization* | 5 days |

The origin of every link in them comes from `FRONTEND_URL` on the backend, not from the host the
browser used: set it to the address people actually reach the console at, or the links will point
somewhere they cannot follow.

Nothing here is marketing. The platform records a
[marketing consent](./profile.md#marketing-communications) where an operator turns that on, and never
sends a commercial email of its own.

title: Your profile
text:
The profile page is about the person signed in rather than about a project. Open it from the
**account button at the bottom of the sidebar** — the one carrying your name — and then **Profile**.

![The profile page, with the profile picture and personal data cards](../assets/profile.png)

Three cards, and the third is conditional: **Marketing communications** exists only on an
installation that [collects a consent](#marketing-communications). The page lives inside the console
layout, so it needs a project selected to be reachable at all — a brand new account is asked to
create one first.

title: Your profile — Profile picture
text:
![The profile picture card, with the upload button and the accepted formats](../assets/profile-avatar.png)

**Upload picture** opens the file dialog; **Remove** appears next to it once a picture is stored.
Until then the circle shows your initials, taken from the name and surname on the card below, or a
generic person icon when neither is set.

The rules are not on the screen in full, so here they are:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| Accepted formats | PNG, JPEG, WebP and GIF — those four, as a list and not "any image" |
| Maximum size | 1 MiB (1 048 576 bytes) |
| Where it is stored | In the database of your own installation, in a collection of its own, one picture per user |
| How it reaches the browser | Inline, as a `data:` URI on an authenticated response — there is no public URL for it |

Both limits are checked twice: once in the browser, so an upload that would be refused is not sent,
and once on the server, which is the check that actually decides. The server measures the **bytes it
received**, not the length the upload claimed in its headers, so a client that lies about the size
gains nothing.

:::note[Why a list of four formats and not "any image"]
The picture is served back into the origin of the console, and `image/svg+xml` is a document that can
carry script. Accepting anything beginning with `image/` would make a profile picture a way to run
code in the console of everybody who looks at it. The four formats above are the ones that are only
ever pixels.
:::

Removing a picture asks for a confirmation and is immediate — there is no version of it kept.

:::info[The picture in the sidebar is not always this one]
This card is the only place your **uploaded** picture comes from, and the only picture it will ever
show. The small avatar in the sidebar falls back through several sources when you have not uploaded
one: the picture from your Auth0 or Google login if you signed in that way, and failing that
**Gravatar**, addressed by a hash of your email.

That last fallback means a console with no picture uploaded makes a request to `gravatar.com` from
the browser, carrying a hash of the signed-in address. Uploading a picture here stops it: the
uploaded one wins over every other source.
:::

title: Your profile — Personal data
text:
The name and surname shown wherever the platform names you — the sidebar, the members list of a
project, an invitation email. Both are optional, both are capped at 100 characters, and **Save**
stays disabled until something actually changes.

The email is displayed and cannot be edited, by design rather than by omission: it is the identity
the account is looked up by, and the address every
[emailed link](./email-flows.md) is sent to. There is no
change-of-address flow — an account is created with the address it keeps.

title: Your profile — Marketing communications
text:
![The marketing communications card, with the consent granted and the date it was given](../assets/profile-marketing-consent.png)

This card appears only where the operator of the installation turned the consent on with
`MARKETING_OPT_IN_ENABLED`. Where they did not, the section is absent from the page and the endpoint
behind it refuses the change — there is nothing to consent to.

It behaves unlike the rest of the page in one deliberate way: **there is no Save button**. Ticking
the box is the act, and it is stored the moment you tick it. A consent sitting unsaved in a form is
neither given nor withheld, so the form does not offer that state.

What gets recorded when you grant it is three things: that you granted it, the moment you did, and
the **version of the text you agreed to** — the last one is what keeps an old consent attributable to
the wording it was given for. The date is printed under the box, as in the shot above. Withdrawing
clears all three: a date left next to a withdrawn consent would read as though the consent were still
the one given that day.

Only the consent currently in force is kept. The page shows no history of the times it was granted and
withdrawn, and none is stored.

:::info[The platform records the consent and never sends a marketing email]
This is worth stating plainly, because a consent checkbox usually implies a mailing list behind it.
Flightroom sends exactly four emails — account activation, password reset, project invitation,
organization invitation — and all four are transactional. There is no newsletter, no product-update
mail, no announcement, and no code anywhere in the product that reads this field to decide who to
mail.

The consent is a **record**, kept so that whoever runs a mailing list elsewhere has a lawful and
dated basis for the addresses on it. On a self-hosted installation that list is yours; on an
installation where nobody runs one, turning `MARKETING_OPT_IN_ENABLED` on collects a consent that
nothing will ever act on.
:::

The registration form carries the same checkbox, under the same condition, and it starts unticked —
a box that arrives already ticked is not a consent. Whichever of the two you use, the record is the
same.

title: Architecture
text:
Flightroom is a **control plane**. It never runs your apps itself: the AI writes their code into
your Git repositories, a deploy is a commit to your GitOps repositories, and your Argo CD runs them
on your Kubernetes. For frontends served by Flightroom, it also stores which versions belong
to which environment and where their files live — then answers, at runtime, the single question
the host application asks: *what should I load?*

This page draws that out. If you have not read [Core concepts](./core-concepts.md) yet, start
there: the boxes below are the objects described on that page.

title: Architecture — The system at a glance
text:
The orchestrator ships as **one container**, listening on port 80. Inside it there are two processes: nginx serves the console as static files and proxies `/api/` to a Node process on localhost:3000, which is the authenticated management API and the public serve API together. All of it therefore arrives on one port, from one image. State lives in MongoDB — Redis is optional and holds only short-lived caches and locks, see below. Artifacts — the actual frontend bundles — live outside the database, either on the orchestrator's own storage or in a cloud bucket you own. ```mermaid flowchart TB subgraph clients["Who talks to it"] direction LR people["Console users"] ci["CI/CD pipeline
GitHub Actions · GitLab CI · Azure Pipelines
authenticated with an API key"] browser["Host application in the browser
Module Federation shell + remotes"] end subgraph orch["Flightroom — one container"] direction LR console["Console
React SPA"] mgmt["Management API
authenticated"] serve["Serve API
public, unauthenticated"] storage["Storage layer
resolves a version to bytes"] end subgraph state["State, and one optional cache"] direction LR mongo[("MongoDB
projects · environments · frontends
deployments · storages · members · API keys")] redis[("Redis · optional
token and API-key caches · repository locks
pending assistant actions")] end subgraph artifacts["Where the bundles are stored"] direction LR internal["Internal storage
MICROFRONTEND_HOST_FOLDER
default /upload-microfrontends"] s3["Amazon S3"] blob["Azure Blob Storage"] gcs["Google Cloud Storage"] end subgraph optional["External services · optional"] direction LR idp["Identity providers
Auth0 · Entra ID · Google
or local login"] smtp["SMTP
activation, invitations, password reset"] end ext["Your CDN or static host
hosting type: Custom URL"] people --> console console --> mgmt ci -->|"upload dist.zip + version"| mgmt browser -->|"GET /serve/all/:projectId/:envSlug"| serve browser -->|"GET .../remoteEntry.js"| serve mgmt --> storage serve --> storage mgmt --> mongo mgmt -.->|"when REDIS_URL is set"| redis serve --> mongo console -.-> idp mgmt -.-> idp mgmt -.-> smtp storage <-->|"write on upload
read on request"| internal storage <-->|"your credentials
bucket stays private"| s3 storage <--> blob storage <--> gcs browser -.->|"fetched directly: the platform only hands out the URL"| ext ``` A few things worth reading off the diagram: - **The browser never talks to your bucket.** For internal storage and for [Custom Source](./frontends/hosting-options.md#custom-source-your-own-bucket) buckets, the serve API reads the bytes server-side with your credentials and streams them back. Your bucket stays private and needs no CORS configuration. [Custom URL](./frontends/hosting-options.md#custom-url) is the exception *in the manifest*: the platform returns the URL and the browser fetches it itself — though `/serve/mfe/files/...`, called directly for a Custom URL frontend, proxies those bytes server-side like any other. - **The serve API is public and unauthenticated** by design — it is called from browsers. The management API is the authenticated surface, used by the console and by CI with an [API key](./ci-cd/api-keys.md). - **Artifacts are not in the database.** MongoDB holds configuration and deployment snapshots; bundles live on disk or in object storage. - **Redis is optional, and has four consumers.** Without `REDIS_URL` the plugin logs a warning and returns, and the platform runs without it. What uses it when it is there: | Consumer | What it keeps | For how long | Without Redis | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Token cache | The answer of Auth0 `/userinfo`, keyed by a SHA-256 of the token, and of Google `tokeninfo`, keyed by the token | Auth0: one hour, never past the token's own expiry. Google: one hour | Every request asks the provider again | | MCP API-key cache | Which API keys were just found valid by the [MCP server](./build-with-ai/mcp-server.md), keyed by a SHA-256 of the key | 60 seconds, never past the key's expiry | Kept in memory, per process | | Repository locks | One lock per working copy, so two [AI changes](./build-with-ai/ai-changes.md) never share a checkout | 60 seconds, renewed while the change runs | Kept in memory, per process | | Pending assistant actions | The destructive actions the [console assistant](./build-with-ai/console-assistant.md#confirming-actions) is waiting for you to confirm | 15 minutes | Kept in memory, per process | Local and Entra ID logins never touch it, the rate limiter keeps its counters in memory, and nothing on the serve path reads it at all. With a **single replica** Redis only saves calls to the identity provider. With **more than one** it matters: the in-memory fallbacks are per process, so without Redis two replicas can run AI changes on the same checkout at once, a confirmation can land on a replica that never saw the action it confirms, and an API key revoked on one replica can keep working on another for up to a minute. - **Git providers are reached from the management API**, not shown above to keep the picture readable: with a [repository](./repositories/connect/github.md) connected, the platform scaffolds a repo from a template, injects a build pipeline and creates the deploy secret that pipeline needs.

title: Architecture — From a request to a running app
text:
Building with AI and deploying to Kubernetes add three outside systems to the picture: the AI model your organization chose, your Git provider, and your Argo CD. The orchestrator talks to each of them over HTTPS, with credentials stored in MongoDB — encrypted when `SECRETS_ENCRYPTION_KEY` is set. ```mermaid flowchart LR member["Project member
console, assistant or MCP client"] subgraph orch["Flightroom"] direction TB agent["AI change agent
works on a clone
REPOSITORIES_FOLDER"] deploy["Deploy"] end model["Your AI model
Claude · GPT · Gemini"] subgraph git["Your Git provider"] direction TB code["App repositories
ai/… branches, pull requests"] gitops["GitOps repositories
configuration + applications"] end ci["Your CI
tests each branch; on a tag,
pushes the image"] argo["Your Argo CD"] subgraph k8s["Your Kubernetes"] direction TB ns["One namespace per environment"] route["Gateway API · HTTPRoute
TLS from cert-manager"] end member --> agent agent <-->|"prompts and file edits"| model agent -->|"push to an ai/… branch"| code code --> ci ci -->|"register the version"| deploy member --> deploy deploy -->|"commit manifests and Helm values"| gitops deploy -.->|"Argo CD API: set up AppProject,
ApplicationSets"| argo argo -->|"pull, read-only token"| gitops argo -->|"sync, prune, self-heal"| ns ns --- route ``` - **The agent never runs code.** It reads and writes files on a clone and pushes a branch. Your CI tests that branch like any other; on a tag, the template pipeline builds and pushes the image and registers the version with Flightroom, ready to deploy. See [Guardrails](./build-with-ai/guardrails.md). - **The console holds no cluster credentials.** It calls the Argo CD API to set up the project, and commits to Git to deploy. Argo CD pulls the commit and applies it to its own cluster. See [Argo CD](./kubernetes/argo-cd.md). - **No commit, no deploy.** Flightroom commits before it records a deployment; if the commit fails, nothing is deployed. The history of an environment is the history of its repositories. See [GitOps](./kubernetes/gitops.md).

title: Architecture — Deployments across environments
text:
A project's configuration is mutable — versions, variables and storage settings are drafts. A **deployment** freezes them into an immutable snapshot for **one environment**, and exactly one snapshot is active per environment at any moment. That is what lets `prod` keep serving `1.2.0` while you stage `1.4.0` in `uat` from the same project. ```mermaid flowchart TB cfg["Project configuration — mutable drafts
frontends with their selected version and hosting config
environment variables, per environment · storage configuration"] subgraph prod["Environment: prod · isProduction"] direction TB prodA["Deployment 3 · ACTIVE
catalog 1.2.0 · checkout 0.8.4"] prodH["Deployments 2, 1 · history
redeployable"] end subgraph uat["Environment: uat"] direction TB uatA["Deployment 5 · ACTIVE
catalog 1.4.0 · checkout 0.9.0"] uatH["Deployments 4, 3, … · history
redeployable"] end subgraph dev["Environment: dev"] direction TB devA["Deployment 12 · ACTIVE
catalog 1.5.0 · checkout 0.9.1"] devH["Deployments 11, 10, … · history
redeployable"] end cfg -->|"Deploy dev"| dev cfg -->|"Deploy uat"| uat cfg -->|"Deploy prod"| prod devA -->|"answers every serve call for dev"| serveDev["dev.example.com"] uatA -->|"answers every serve call for uat"| serveUat["staging.example.com"] prodA -->|"answers every serve call for prod"| serveProd["app.example.com"] ``` The snapshot is a **copy**, not a set of references — editing a frontend afterwards does not reach back into it. Two consequences: - **Rollback is activation, not rebuild.** Redeploying `#2` in `prod` re-activates an older snapshot; the artifacts it points at were never deleted. - **Promotion is just a deployment.** Select the version live in `uat`, deploy `prod`. The bundle is not rebuilt or copied — both environments point at the same stored files, and what differs is the [environment variables](./environments/environment-variables.md) each snapshot carries. Which environment a request belongs to can be given explicitly, or resolved from the browser's `Referer` against the environment's [allowed domains](./environments/domains.md) — the arrows on the right of the diagram. That is what lets one build run unchanged in every environment. See [Deployments](./deployments/overview.md) for the full behaviour.

title: Architecture — How a request for a bundle is answered
text:
The hosting type of each frontend decides where the bytes come from. The host application's
URL does not change between the three cases — only what the orchestrator does behind it.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant B as Browser (host app)
    participant S as Serve API
    participant DB as MongoDB
    participant F as Internal storage
    participant C as Your cloud bucket
    participant X as Your CDN

    B->>S: GET /serve/all/{projectId}/{envSlug}
    S->>DB: active deployment of this environment
    DB-->>S: frontends + versions + variables
    S-->>B: URLs, versions, globalVariables

    B->>S: GET /serve/mfe/files/.../assets/remoteEntry.js
    S->>DB: resolve version + hosting type from the snapshot

    alt Hosting type: Flightroom Hub
        S->>F: read {folder}/{projectSlug}-{projectId}/{mfeSlug}/{version}/...
        F-->>S: bytes
    else Hosting type: Custom Source (your bucket)
        S->>C: read with your credentials, bucket stays private
        C-->>S: bytes
    end

    S-->>B: bytes · entry point sent no-store, other assets cacheable

    opt Hosting type: Custom URL
        S-->>B: URL with $version substituted
        B->>X: GET the file directly
        X-->>B: bytes
    end
```

The entry point is always served with `Cache-Control: no-cache, no-store, must-revalidate`, while
the hashed assets around it stay cacheable — which is why a deployment takes effect immediately
without stale chunks. All served files carry `Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy: cross-origin` so a
host on a different origin can load them.

Details: [Serve API reference](./integration/serve-api.md),
[Hosting options](./frontends/hosting-options.md), [Buckets](./buckets/overview.md).

### Artifact path layout

Both internal storage and your own bucket use the same deterministic layout, with the project id
in the prefix so several projects — and several installations — can share one bucket:

```
<root>/<projectSlug>-<projectId>/<frontendSlug>/<version>/…
```

Versions sit side by side and nothing is overwritten on release. That is what makes rollback
instant, and why you may want a lifecycle rule on old objects — see
[Housekeeping](./buckets/overview.md#housekeeping).

title: Architecture — Running the orchestrator itself
text:
The same control plane runs either as the hosted console or on your own infrastructure. Only the API base URL differs. Self-hosted, the reference `docker-compose.yaml` is the container plus MongoDB, a persistent volume and an optional Redis: ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph host["Your infrastructure — the reference Docker Compose topology"] direction TB app["flightroom
container port 80"] mongo[("mongodb
NOSQL_DATABASE_URL
volume: mongodb_data")] redis[("redis · optional
REDIS_URL
volume: redis_data")] vol["Persistent volume
MICROFRONTEND_HOST_FOLDER
volume: upload_microfrontends"] app --> mongo app -.->|"optional"| redis app --> vol end users["Browsers · CI · console users"] -->|"FRONTEND_URL"| app app -.->|"optional"| cloud["Your S3 / Azure Blob / GCS bucket"] app -.->|"optional"| idp["Auth0 · Entra ID · Google"] app -.->|"optional"| smtp["SMTP"] ``` :::caution[Mount the artifact folder] `MICROFRONTEND_HOST_FOLDER` must sit on a persistent volume. Without it, every container restart loses the builds uploaded to the internal storage — in the reference `docker-compose.yaml` that is the `upload_microfrontends` volume. ::: That diagram is the Compose topology. The Helm chart is deliberately thinner: it ships the deployment, a service, an ingress, a persistent volume claim and the environment variables, and no database of its own — `NOSQL_DATABASE_URL` has to point at a MongoDB you run, and `REDIS_URL` defaults to empty, which is the supported way to run without Redis at all. MongoDB can be replaced by a managed service, and so can Redis where you run one; the identity providers, SMTP and cloud buckets are all optional. See [Docker Compose](./self-hosting/docker-compose.md), [Terraform](./self-hosting/terraform.md), [Use external resources](./self-hosting/use-external-resources.md) and the full [environment variable reference](./self-hosting/environment-variables.md).

title: Store builds on Amazon S3
text: This page walks through connecting an S3 bucket to Flightroom.

title: Store builds on Amazon S3 — Prerequisites
text:
- An AWS account
- Permission to create S3 buckets and IAM users/policies

title: Store builds on Amazon S3 — Step 1: Create the bucket
text:
In the AWS console, open **S3 → Create bucket**:

- **Bucket name** — globally unique, e.g. `acme-frontends`
- **Region** — pick one close to your users; note it, you will need it
- **Block Public Access** — leave **enabled**

:::tip[Keep the bucket private]
Flightroom reads objects server-side with your credentials and streams them to browsers
itself. The bucket never needs to be public, and no CORS configuration is required.
:::

Versioning is optional. Flightroom already stores each release under its own version prefix,
so S3 versioning adds protection against accidental overwrites rather than release history.

title: Store builds on Amazon S3 — Step 2: Create an IAM policy
text:
Create a policy granting only what the platform needs. Replace `acme-frontends` with your
bucket name, and `mfe/` with your intended path prefix (or drop the prefix to allow the whole
bucket):

```json
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Sid": "ObjectAccess",
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": [
        "s3:GetObject",
        "s3:PutObject"
      ],
      "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::acme-frontends/mfe/*"
    },
    {
      "Sid": "ListBucket",
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": "s3:ListBucket",
      "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::acme-frontends",
      "Condition": {
        "StringLike": {
          "s3:prefix": "mfe/*"
        }
      }
    }
  ]
}
```

`s3:GetObject` and `s3:PutObject` are what the platform needs. The `s3:ListBucket` statement is
optional: Flightroom never lists the bucket. Keep it if you want a missing file to come back from S3
as *NoSuchKey* rather than *AccessDenied*, which makes a wrong entry point easier to tell from a
permission problem.

Note there is no `s3:DeleteObject`: Flightroom never deletes artifacts. Leaving it out means a
compromised key cannot destroy your release history. The only thing the platform tries to delete is
the probe file **Test connection** writes, `.flightroom-connection-test`; without the permission it
is simply left in the bucket. Add it only if you plan to use the same
credentials for housekeeping — better still, use a
[lifecycle rule](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/object-lifecycle-mgmt.html),
which needs no credentials at all.

title: Store builds on Amazon S3 — Step 3: Create an IAM user and access key
text:
1. **IAM → Users → Create user**, e.g. `flightroom`.
2. Do **not** grant console access — this identity is only used programmatically.
3. Attach the policy from step 2.
4. Open the user, go to **Security credentials → Create access key**, and choose
   *Application running outside AWS*.
5. Copy the **Access key ID** and **Secret access key**. The secret is shown once.

title: Store builds on Amazon S3 — Step 4: Add the storage in Flightroom
text:
Open **Storages** (under **Cloud** in the sidebar), click **New Storage** and select
**Amazon S3**:

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| **Name** | A label, e.g. *Production S3* |
| **Bucket Name** | `acme-frontends` |
| **Path** | Optional prefix inside the bucket, e.g. `mfe`. Leave blank for the bucket root |
| **Access Key ID** | From step 3 |
| **Secret Access Key** | From step 3 |
| **Region** | The bucket's region, e.g. `eu-west-1` |

![The New Storage form with the Amazon S3 credential fields](../assets/storage-form-aws-s3.png)

Click **Test connection** to check the credentials and the permissions before saving, then
**Create**.

title: Store builds on Amazon S3 — Step 5: Point a frontend at it
text:
Open a frontend, set **Hosting type** to **Custom Source**, select this storage, and save.
Publish a new version — the artifact now lands in your bucket, at:

```
mfe/<projectSlug>-<projectId>/<frontendSlug>/<version>/…
```

Then [deploy](../deployments/overview.md) the environment.

title: Store builds on Amazon S3 — Troubleshooting
text:
**`AccessDenied` on upload**

The key lacks `s3:PutObject` on the path being written. Check the policy's `Resource` ARN covers
your configured **Path** prefix — a policy scoped to `mfe/*` will reject writes if the storage has
no path set, because objects then land at the bucket root.

**`AccessDenied` on serving, but upload worked**

`s3:GetObject` is missing. Both actions are needed: the platform writes on upload and reads on every
request.

**`NoSuchBucket` or region errors**

The **Region** field must match the bucket's actual region. A bucket in `eu-west-1` configured as
`us-east-1` fails to resolve.

**Files upload but the app 404s**

Usually the **Entry Point**. Check what your build actually produces — Vite Module Federation emits
`assets/remoteEntry.js`, not `remoteEntry.js`. You can verify by browsing the version prefix in the
S3 console.

title: Store builds on Amazon S3 — Cost notes
text:
The traffic pattern is `GET` requests from Flightroom to S3, one per file served, plus egress
from S3 to the platform. Both are small for typical bundles, but if your frontends are heavily
trafficked and large, consider a bucket in the same region as your Flightroom installation to
reduce inter-region egress.

title: Store builds on Azure Blob Storage
text:
Flightroom supports three ways of authenticating against Azure Blob Storage. Pick one and
follow the matching section.

| Method | When to use it |
| --- | --- |
| **Connection string** | Quickest to set up; grants access to the whole storage account |
| **Shared key** (*Api Key* in the console) | Account name + key, scoped to one container |
| **Azure AD** (*Enterprise Application*) | Recommended for production — a service principal with a role assignment you control |

title: Store builds on Azure Blob Storage — Prerequisites
text:
- An Azure subscription
- Permission to create storage accounts and, for the Azure AD method, app registrations

title: Store builds on Azure Blob Storage — Step 1: Create the storage account and container
text:
1. In the Azure portal, create a **Storage account** (or reuse one).
   - **Performance**: Standard is fine
   - **Redundancy**: your call; LRS is sufficient for rebuildable artifacts
2. Inside it, open **Data storage → Containers** and create a container, e.g. `frontends`.
3. Set the container's **Public access level** to **Private**.

:::tip[Keep the container private]
Flightroom reads blobs server-side with your credentials and streams them to browsers itself.
The container never needs public access, and no CORS rules are required.
:::

title: Store builds on Azure Blob Storage — Step 2: Choose an authentication method
text:
### Option A — Connection string

1. Open the storage account → **Security + networking → Access keys**.
2. Click **Show keys** and copy the **Connection string** for key1.

Simple, but the connection string grants full access to every container in the account, and rotating
the account key invalidates it. Fine for a trial; prefer Azure AD for production.

### Option B — Shared key

From the same **Access keys** page, copy:

- The **Storage account name**
- The **Key** value

Scoped to the container you name in Flightroom, but still derived from an account-level key.

### Option C — Azure AD (recommended)

1. **Microsoft Entra ID → App registrations → New registration**. Name it e.g.
   `flightroom-storage`. No redirect URI is needed.
2. Note the **Application (client) ID** and **Directory (tenant) ID** from the overview page.
3. **Certificates & secrets → New client secret**. Copy the secret **Value** immediately — it is
   shown once. Note the expiry date and set a reminder to rotate.
4. Grant the app access to the container:
   - Open the **storage account** (or, for tighter scope, the **container**)
   - **Access Control (IAM) → Add role assignment**
   - Role: **Storage Blob Data Contributor**
   - Assign access to: **User, group, or service principal** → select your app registration

Scoping the role assignment at the container rather than the account is the least-privilege choice.

:::info[Why Storage Blob Data Contributor]
The platform needs to read and write blobs. *Reader* is insufficient (uploads fail) and *Owner*
grants more than is needed. Contributor at container scope is the right level.
:::

title: Store builds on Azure Blob Storage — Step 3: Add the storage in Flightroom
text:
Open **Storages** (under **Cloud** in the sidebar), click **New Storage** and select
**Azure Blob Storage**. The fields depend on
the **Authentication Type** you pick:

![The three authentication types offered for Azure Blob Storage](../assets/storage-form-azure-auth-types.png)

**Connection String**

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| **Container Name** | `frontends` |
| **Connection String** | From Option A |
| **Path** | Optional prefix inside the container |

**Api Key** (shared key)

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| **Container Name** | `frontends` |
| **Account Name** | The storage account name |
| **Account Key** | From Option B |
| **Path** | Optional prefix inside the container |

**Azure AD - Enterprise Application**

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| **Container Name** | `frontends` |
| **Account Name** | The storage account name |
| **Tenant ID** | Directory (tenant) ID |
| **Client ID** | Application (client) ID |
| **Client Secret** | The secret value from step C3 |
| **Path** | Optional prefix inside the container |

![The Azure Blob Storage form with Connection String selected](../assets/storage-form-azure-blob.png)

Click **Test connection** to check the credentials and the permissions before saving, then
**Create**.

title: Store builds on Azure Blob Storage — Step 4: Point a frontend at it
text:
Open a frontend, set **Hosting type** to **Custom Source**, select this storage, and save. New
versions land at:

```
<path>/<projectSlug>-<projectId>/<frontendSlug>/<version>/…
```

Then [deploy](../deployments/overview.md) the environment.

title: Store builds on Azure Blob Storage — Troubleshooting
text:
**`AuthorizationPermissionMismatch` (Azure AD)**

The service principal has no suitable role on the container. Confirm the **Storage Blob Data
Contributor** assignment exists and that it is scoped to the account or container you configured.
Role assignments can take a few minutes to propagate.

**`AuthenticationFailed` (shared key)**

Usually a truncated or whitespace-padded account key, or a mismatch between the account name and the
key. Re-copy both from the portal.

**`ContainerNotFound`**

The **Container Name** is wrong, or the container lives in a different storage account than the one
your credentials point at.

**Everything worked, then stopped**

If you used Azure AD, check whether the client secret expired — this is the most common cause of a
storage that worked for months and then failed. Create a new secret and update the storage.

**Files upload but the app 404s**

Check the **Entry Point** on the frontend. Vite Module Federation builds emit
`assets/remoteEntry.js`; you can verify the layout by browsing the version prefix in Storage
Explorer.

title: Store builds on Azure Blob Storage — Secret rotation
text:
Client secrets and account keys both expire or get rotated. When you rotate:

1. Create the new secret/key alongside the old one.
2. Update the storage in Flightroom.
3. Verify a file still serves.
4. Remove the old credential.

Doing it in that order avoids a window where serving is broken.

title: Store builds on Google Cloud Storage
text: Flightroom authenticates to Google Cloud Storage with a **service account JSON key**.

title: Store builds on Google Cloud Storage — Prerequisites
text:
- A Google Cloud project
- Permission to create buckets, service accounts and keys

title: Store builds on Google Cloud Storage — Step 1: Create the bucket
text:
In the Cloud console, open **Cloud Storage → Buckets → Create**:

- **Name** — globally unique, e.g. `acme-frontends`
- **Location** — a region close to your users
- **Storage class** — Standard
- **Access control** — **Uniform** (simpler and recommended; IAM only, no per-object ACLs)
- **Public access prevention** — leave **enabled**

:::tip[Keep the bucket private]
Flightroom reads objects server-side with your credentials and streams them to browsers
itself. The bucket never needs to be public, and no CORS configuration is required.
:::

title: Store builds on Google Cloud Storage — Step 2: Create a service account
text:
1. **IAM & Admin → Service accounts → Create service account**.
2. Name it e.g. `flightroom`.
3. Skip the optional project-level role grant — you will grant access on the bucket instead, which
   is tighter.
4. Create it.

title: Store builds on Google Cloud Storage — Step 3: Grant access on the bucket
text:
1. Open **Cloud Storage → Buckets → your bucket → Permissions**.
2. **Grant access**, with the service account's email as the principal.
3. Assign the role **Storage Object Admin** (`roles/storage.objectAdmin`).

:::info[Why Storage Object Admin]
The platform reads and writes objects. `objectViewer` is insufficient (uploads fail) and
`storage.admin` grants bucket administration the platform does not need. `objectAdmin`, granted on
the single bucket, is the right scope.
:::

Granting at the bucket rather than the project keeps the service account unable to touch anything
else.

title: Store builds on Google Cloud Storage — Step 4: Create a JSON key
text:
1. Open the service account → **Keys → Add key → Create new key**.
2. Choose **JSON** and create. The file downloads once.
3. Keep it safe — it is a long-lived credential.

The file looks like this:

```json
{
  "type": "service_account",
  "project_id": "acme-prod",
  "private_key_id": "…",
  "private_key": "-----BEGIN PRIVATE KEY-----\n…\n-----END PRIVATE KEY-----\n",
  "client_email": "flightroom@acme-prod.iam.gserviceaccount.com",
  "client_id": "…",
  "…": "…"
}
```

title: Store builds on Google Cloud Storage — Step 5: Add the storage in Flightroom
text:
Open **Storages** (under **Cloud** in the sidebar), click **New Storage** and select **Google Cloud
Storage**:

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| **Name** | A label, e.g. *Production GCS* |
| **Bucket Name** | `acme-frontends` |
| **Path** | Optional prefix inside the bucket, e.g. `mfe` |
| **Service Account JSON Key** | Paste the **entire contents** of the JSON key file |

![The New Storage form with the Google Cloud Storage fields](../assets/storage-form-gcs.png)

There is no authentication type to pick: a service account key is the only method offered for Google
Cloud Storage. Paste the whole JSON document, not just the private key — the platform reads
`client_email` and `private_key` out of it.

Click **Test connection** to check the key and the permissions before saving, then **Create**.

title: Store builds on Google Cloud Storage — Step 6: Point a frontend at it
text:
Open a frontend, set **Hosting type** to **Custom Source**, select this storage, and save. New
versions land at:

```
<path>/<projectSlug>-<projectId>/<frontendSlug>/<version>/…
```

Then [deploy](../deployments/overview.md) the environment.

title: Store builds on Google Cloud Storage — Troubleshooting
text:
**`The service account key is not valid JSON`**

Reported by **Test connection** — saving does not parse the key, so a broken one otherwise only shows
up when files fail to upload or serve. The field must contain valid, complete JSON. A common cause is pasting a fragment, or an
editor mangling the `\n` escapes inside `private_key`. Copy directly from the downloaded file
without reformatting.

**`403 does not have storage.objects.create access`**

The service account lacks write permission on the bucket. Confirm the **Storage Object Admin**
binding exists on the bucket and names the correct service account email. IAM changes can take a
minute to propagate.

**`403 does not have storage.objects.get access`**

Read permission is missing. `objectAdmin` covers both read and write — if you granted `objectCreator`
instead, uploads succeed and serving fails.

**`404 Not Found` for the bucket**

Check the bucket name for typos, and that the service account belongs to a project that can see it.

**Files upload but the app 404s**

Check the **Entry Point** on the frontend. Vite Module Federation emits
`assets/remoteEntry.js`; browse the version prefix in the Cloud console to see the actual layout.

title: Store builds on Google Cloud Storage — Key rotation
text:
Service account JSON keys do not expire by default, which makes them convenient and a long-term
risk. Rotate them on a schedule:

1. Create a second key for the same service account.
2. Edit the storage in Flightroom and replace the masked **Service Account JSON Key** with the new
   JSON.
3. Verify a file still serves.
4. Delete the old key in the Cloud console.

If your organisation enforces a key-expiry policy, put the rotation date in the calendar — an
expired key surfaces as a sudden serving failure with no warning.

title: Storage overview
text:
A **bucket** — a *storage* in the console — is a connection to object storage you own. With one
configured, frontend builds are stored in your own cloud account instead of on the platform,
while Flightroom continues to handle versioning, deployments and serving.

Buckets live on the **Storages** page, under **Cloud** in the sidebar. It is also reachable from
**Settings → Resources**, through the **Storages** card.

The page lists the project's storages with their **Name** (and provider logo), **Bucket Name** — the
container name, for Azure — **Path** and **Default**, plus the edit and delete actions.

![The Storages page of a project with no bucket configured yet](../assets/storages-empty.png)

title: Storage overview — Why use your own bucket
text:
| | Flightroom Hub | Your bucket |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Where artifacts live | Platform storage | Your cloud account |
| Data residency control | ❌ | ✅ |
| Your retention & backup policy | ❌ | ✅ |
| Setup effort | None | Bucket + credentials |
| Durability guarantees | Platform's | Your provider's SLA |

For production use — and for anything with compliance requirements — your own bucket is the right
answer. The hub is excellent for getting started and for self-hosted installations where you
already own the disk.

title: Storage overview — Supported providers
text:
| Provider | Authentication methods |
| --- | --- |
| [Amazon S3](./aws-s3.md) | Access key ID + secret access key |
| [Azure Blob Storage](./azure-blob-storage.md) | Connection string, shared key, or Azure AD application |
| [Google Cloud Storage](./google-cloud-storage.md) | Service account JSON key |

title: Storage overview — How it works
text:
Once a storage is configured and selected on a frontend whose hosting type is
**Custom Source**:

```
CI uploads dist.zip
      │
      ▼
Flightroom extracts it and writes to YOUR bucket
      │
      ▼
Browser requests remoteEntry.js
      │
      ▼
Flightroom reads from YOUR bucket with your credentials
and streams the file back
```

Two things follow from this:

- **Your bucket does not need to be public.** Files are read server-side with the credentials you
  configured. Keep the bucket private.
- **Your bucket does not need CORS configuration.** The browser talks to Flightroom, not to
  your bucket, so cross-origin headers are the platform's concern.

title: Storage overview — Path layout
text:
Files are stored under a deterministic path:

```
<storage path>/<projectSlug>-<projectId>/<frontendSlug>/<version>/…
```

For example, with a storage `path` of `mfe`:

```
mfe/my-shop-68f1a2b3c4d5e6f7/catalog/1.4.0/assets/remoteEntry.js
mfe/my-shop-68f1a2b3c4d5e6f7/catalog/1.4.0/assets/index-4f2a.css
mfe/my-shop-68f1a2b3c4d5e6f7/catalog/1.5.0/assets/remoteEntry.js
```

The project id is part of the prefix, so several projects — and several Flightroom
installations — can share one bucket without colliding. Versions sit side by side, which is what
makes rollback instant: nothing is overwritten or deleted on a new release.

title: Storage overview — Adding a storage
text:
1. Open **Storages** and click **New Storage**.
2. Give it a **Name** and pick the **Provider**.

   ![The Provider select open, offering Amazon S3, Google Cloud Storage and Azure Blob Storage](../assets/storage-providers.png)

3. Fill in the provider-specific credentials — see the per-provider pages.
4. Optionally set a **Path** prefix inside the bucket.
5. Optionally click **Test connection**. Flightroom uploads a small probe file,
   `.flightroom-connection-test`, under the folder the project's builds go to, reads it back, then
   tries to delete it — so a pass means uploads and serving will both work. When the credentials are
   not allowed to delete, the probe simply stays where it is. The test runs on the values in the
   form: nothing is saved yet.
6. Click **Create** (**Update** when editing).

![The New Storage form, showing the Amazon S3 credential fields](../assets/storage-dialog.png)

:::caution[The provider cannot be changed later]
A storage's provider type is fixed at creation. To move from S3 to GCS, create a new storage and
re-point your frontends at it.
:::

You can mark one storage as the **default** for the project with the star in the **Default**
column. A new frontend then starts on **Custom Source** with that storage already selected,
instead of on the Flightroom Hub.

Adding, editing, testing, deleting a storage and changing the default are refused to a **Viewer**,
and they need access to the **whole project**: a storage can serve frontends of every domain, so
a member limited to specific domains cannot change one.

title: Storage overview — Using a storage
text:
On the frontend, set **Hosting type** to **Custom Source** and pick the storage. Then upload
as usual — the platform routes the artifact to your bucket. See
[Hosting options](../frontends/hosting-options.md).

Existing versions are not migrated when you change a frontend's storage. Change it, then
publish a new version.

:::caution[Deleting a storage does not check who uses it]
The console deletes a storage without looking at which frontends point at it. Those
frontends keep referencing a storage that no longer exists, and their next deployment has
nothing to serve their files from. Re-point them first, then delete.
:::

title: Storage overview — Credentials and least privilege
text:
Flightroom needs to read and write objects under its prefix, and nothing else. Each provider
page includes a minimal permission set — grant that rather than a broad administrative role.

Credentials are stored by the platform and never returned to the browser once saved: when you edit
a storage, the secret fields — secret access key, account key, connection string, client secret,
JSON key — show a masked placeholder. Leave it as it is to keep the stored value. If you change the
provider account the storage authenticates as — the access key ID on S3, the authentication type,
account name, tenant or client ID on Azure — the stored secret is no longer lent to it and saving
asks you to type it again. Rotate credentials on your provider's normal schedule and update the
storage when you do.

title: Storage overview — Housekeeping
text:
The platform never deletes old versions: every release you have ever published stays in the bucket.
That is what makes rollback reliable, but it does grow without bound. Consider a lifecycle rule that
expires objects older than your rollback window — S3 lifecycle policies, Azure blob lifecycle
management, or GCS object lifecycle.

:::caution
Do not expire objects still referenced by a deployment you might roll back to. A rule that deletes
anything older than 90 days is safe if your rollback window is a fortnight; a rule that keeps only
the two newest versions is not, because an environment may be sitting on an older one.
:::

title: Change code with AI
text:
Every frontend, service and functional domain opens on its **Edit with AI** tab. There you
describe a change, an agent proposes it on a branch of the repository, and you decide what to do
with it. The other tabs are:

| Opened on | Tabs |
| --- | --- |
| A frontend | **Edit with AI**, **Details & settings** |
| A service | **Edit with AI**, **Overview**, **Details & settings** |
| A [functional domain](../domains/overview.md) | **Edit with AI**, **Structure** |

It is available when the project can use an [AI](./ai-models.md) and what you are changing has a
code repository linked. Otherwise, on a frontend or a service the **Edit with AI** tab is
hidden and the page opens on **Details & settings** (on **Overview** for a service). A domain always
shows the tab: without an AI it reads *AI editing is not available in this project: the organization
has no AI it can use.*

title: Change code with AI — Ask for a change
text:
The composer reads **What do you want to change in *name*?**

1. Describe the change in **What should change?**, for example *Add a 404 page with a link back to
   the home page*. Up to 8,000 characters.
2. Check the repository and the branch the agent starts from, shown under the prompt. It is the
   repository's default branch unless you pick another one.
3. Optionally pick another **AI** and **Reasoning effort** (*Low*, *Medium*, *High*, *Extra high*,
   *Max*). Code changes default to *High*; more effort means deeper reasoning, slower answers and
   more tokens.
4. Press **Generate proposal**, or ⌘/Ctrl + Enter.

The request is queued and the agent starts. While it works the console shows where it is (*Preparing
the repository*, *The agent is working*, *Pushing the proposal on its branch*…), and **Show the
agent's progress log** opens the details. Two events only show up when the agent has to wait:

- *Waiting for the repository to be free*: another request is working on the same repository, and
  this one starts when it is done.
- *The model hit its rate limit: retrying shortly*: the AI provider asked to slow down, and the agent
  tries again on its own.

The agent reads the repository together with the AI context of the project, of the domain and of
what it is changing. In a service repository it also follows an `AGENTS.md` or `CLAUDE.md` at the
root, if there is one. Files it reads are cut at 100 KB: past that size a file is usually generated
or vendored, rarely something to edit by hand.

title: Change code with AI — Read the proposal
Change code with AI — Refine it in a chat
text:
Each request is a conversation. Below the proposal, write in **Ask the agent for a change, or ask it a
question…** and press **Send** (Enter; Shift+Enter for a new line).

- A follow-up starts from the files of the previous proposal and knows what was asked before. Its
  proposal **replaces** the previous one, which is marked *Refined by the next message*.
- Every follow-up force-pushes the same branch, so a pull request already open on it shows the latest
  proposal.
- A question that changes no file pushes nothing.
- If a follow-up fails, the previous proposal stays open to apply or refine again.
- Only the **latest** proposal can be applied.

You can pick a different AI or effort for each message.

title: Change code with AI — Apply, open a pull request, or discard
text:
| Action | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| **Apply to *branch*** | Pushes the proposal straight onto the base branch, with no review. All the proposed files go together. The base branch's CI starts right away |
| **Open a pull request** | Opens a pull request (a merge request on GitLab) from the proposal's branch onto the base branch, to review it in the repository. The proposal stays open: you can still refine, apply or discard it |
| **Discard** | Deletes the proposal's branch, unless a pull request is open on it |

Details worth knowing:

- **Apply is never forced.** A protected base branch refuses the push, and the console tells you to
  open a pull request instead.
- **Apply checks for conflicts.** Every file must still be what the agent saw. If someone changed one
  of them on the base branch in the meantime, Apply stops and names the files: ask for the change
  again.
- When the base branch has not moved since the proposal, Apply moves it to the very commit of the
  proposal's branch, so a pull request opened on it shows as merged. After Apply, the proposal's
  branch is deleted unless a pull request is open on it.
- The commit and the pull request are named after the first message, and the pull request
  description quotes every message of the conversation. The commit author is the person who asked.
- If the provider refuses to open the pull request (for example a token without that permission),
  the console shows why, and the branch stays pushed.
- If pushing the proposal on its branch failed, applying it or opening its pull request tries again.

Once a proposal is applied or discarded, the conversation is closed. Press **New change** to start a
fresh one from the base branch.

title: Change code with AI — Change a whole domain
text:
**Edit with AI** on a functional domain starts **one agent on every frontend and service of the
domain that has a code repository**, at most 10. It sees them all at once, so a single request can
span a backend endpoint and the screens that call it.

- The agent still proposes **one change per repository**, each on its own branch, and each one is
  applied or opened as a pull request on its own. One pull request per repository.
- **Apply all (*N*)** pushes every pending proposal of the request onto the base branch of its
  repository in one go, after a confirmation. A repository that cannot be applied goes back to its
  proposal, with the error on it.
- Each message of the conversation shows one tab per repository, with its files and diff.
- Each repository starts from its default branch, or from a branch you pick. One choice can set them
  all: each repository's default branch, or a branch that every one of them has.
- Members without a repository are left out and listed under the request.
- A domain with more than 10 repositories cannot be changed in one go from here: start the job from
  Maestro and pick the ones to change (below).

An empty domain, or one whose members have no repository yet, is handled first by
[Generate a domain](./generate-a-domain.md).

title: Change code with AI — Change several components outside a domain
text:
In [Maestro](./console-assistant.md), the **New AI job** button starts one agent on the
frontends and services you pick, in any domain: choose them (or **All frontends and
services**, every one with a linked repository, at most 10), describe the change and press **Start
job**. The job opens as a tab in Maestro, where you follow it, chat with the agent and apply its
proposals.

title: Change code with AI — Requests and their status
text:
The **AI change requests** list groups requests by where they stand:

| Group | Contains |
| --- | --- |
| **Awaiting approval** | Proposals ready for you to act on |
| **In progress** | Requests queued, being worked on, or being applied |
| **Applied** | Proposals pushed onto their base branch |
| **Discarded** | Proposals you threw away |
| **Failed** | Requests that did not complete. **Try again**, or start a new change |

Proposals nobody acts on are **removed after 7 days**; their branch stays in the repository. Once a
proposal is applied, the whole conversation is kept.

At most 3 AI jobs run at the same time in a project: a fourth is refused with *Too many jobs are
running in this project: wait for one to finish.* Other limits are listed in
[Guardrails](./guardrails.md).

title: Change code with AI — Tips for good requests
text:
- Write the rules the agent should always follow (conventions, vocabulary, what not to touch) in the
  **AI context** of the project, domain, frontend or service, rather than repeating them in
  every request.
- One change per request. Refine it in the chat rather than starting over.
- Read the diff before **Apply**: the agent cannot run your tests, and Apply skips review.

title: AI models
text:
Every AI feature (editing code with AI, generating a domain, Maestro, the AI draft of the new project
wizard) runs on the **AIs of the organization**. Each AI is a provider, a model and the credentials to
reach it. You bring your own: requests go to your account at the provider.

An organization can define several AIs, for example Claude on the Anthropic API and GPT on Azure
OpenAI. Users pick one per request in the **AI** selector, preselected on the default.

title: AI models — Adding an AI
text:
Open **Organization settings** from the organization menu, tab **AI**. The **Artificial intelligences** list is visible to every
member of the organization; only an **Owner** or an **Admin** can add, edit or delete an AI.

Click **Add AI** and fill in:

| Field | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| **Name** | Unique in the organization, for example *Claude for the teams* |
| **Provider** | See the table below |
| Provider settings | The credentials and location the provider needs |
| **Model** / **Deployment** | Which model the requests go to |
| **Maximum effort** | Optional. The highest reasoning effort users can pick with this AI (*Low*, *Medium*, *High*, *Extra high*, *Max*). *No limit* by default |
| **Default AI** | Preselected in every project that can use it. Only one AI of the organization is the default |

### Providers

| Provider | Settings | Model |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Claude (Anthropic)** | **API key** | **Model**, optional: `claude-opus-5-5` when left empty |
| **Claude (Azure AI Foundry)** | **Resource** (the resource name, not a URL) and **API key** | **Model**: the name of the Claude deployment, optional: `claude-opus-5-5` when left empty |
| **Claude (AWS Bedrock)** | **Region**, **Access key ID** and **Secret access key** | **Model**, required: the Bedrock model id or an inference profile. The key needs permission to invoke it |
| **Gemini (Google)** | **API key** | **Model**, required: use a model with function calling |
| **GPT (Azure OpenAI)** | **Endpoint**, **API key** and **Reasoning model** | **Deployment**, required: the name of the GPT deployment |

Notes:

- The Azure OpenAI **Endpoint** must be an Azure HTTPS endpoint, like
  `https://my-resource.openai.azure.com/`. Turn on **Reasoning model** when the deployment is a
  reasoning model (for example GPT-5 or the o-series): it then accepts an effort level.
- Reasoning effort is offered on Claude with all five levels, and on GPT with **Reasoning model** on
  with *Low*, *Medium* and *High*. Without reasoning, and on Gemini, the choice is hidden.
- On Claude, the effort levels need Claude Opus 4.7 / Sonnet 5 or later. The default model is one.
- The prompts and tools of the agent were written and tested with Claude: the quality of the code
  agent depends on the model.

### Credentials

The credentials are never shown again after saving: the form keeps a hidden value, and leaving it as
it is keeps the stored key. A stored key is kept only while the provider, the resource, the endpoint
and the access key stay the same; point the AI elsewhere and you type the key again. The stored keys
are never sent to another provider.

On a self-hosted installation, set `SECRETS_ENCRYPTION_KEY` to have them encrypted at rest with
AES-256-GCM. See [Encryption at rest](../self-hosting/encryption-at-rest.md).

### Deleting an AI

Deleting an AI also removes it from every project that uses it. A project left with no AI has the AI
features turned off.

title: AI models — Which AIs a project can use
text:
Below the list, the **Project access** table shows, for each project of the organization, the AIs it
can use. Owners and admins edit a row and choose:

- **All the AIs of the organization (default)**, including those added later; shown as **All
  (default)**;
- **Only the selected AIs**: an AI added later is not included.

Selecting none turns the AI features off for that project, shown as **AI turned off**: Maestro is
hidden, the AI endpoints answer that AI is not enabled, and nothing is sent to any provider.

The AI preselected in a project is the organization's default when the project may use it, otherwise
the first one available.

title: AI models — The system AI (self-hosting)
text:
A self-hosted installation can offer one more AI to every organization from its environment
variables. It is listed as **System AI**, is read-only in the console (*Configured in the
installation's environment: it cannot be edited here.*), and can be excluded from a project like any
other.

| `AI_PROVIDER` | Required variables | Optional |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `anthropic` | `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` | `ANTHROPIC_MODEL` (`claude-opus-5-5`) |
| `azure-foundry` | `AZURE_FOUNDRY_RESOURCE`, `AZURE_FOUNDRY_API_KEY` | `AZURE_FOUNDRY_MODEL` (`claude-opus-5-5`) |
| `aws-bedrock` | `AWS_BEDROCK_REGION`, `AWS_BEDROCK_ACCESS_KEY_ID`, `AWS_BEDROCK_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY`, `AWS_BEDROCK_MODEL` | |
| `gemini` | `GEMINI_API_KEY`, `GEMINI_MODEL` | |
| `azure-openai` | `AZURE_OPENAI_ENDPOINT`, `AZURE_OPENAI_API_KEY`, `AZURE_OPENAI_DEPLOYMENT` | `AZURE_OPENAI_REASONING` (`false`) |

- `AI_MAX_EFFORT` (`low`, `medium`, `high`, `xhigh` or `max`) caps the effort of the system AI. On an
  installation open to sign-ups it bounds the cost of a single question.
- `AI_PROVIDER` left empty with `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` set means Claude through the Anthropic API.
- A provider named without one of its required variables stops the backend at boot, with the missing
  variables in the error.
- For Azure sovereign clouds, add the endpoint suffixes the installation accepts with
  `AZURE_OPENAI_ENDPOINT_SUFFIXES`, comma separated (for example `.openai.azure.us,.openai.azure.cn`).

With none of these variables set there is no system AI. See also
[Environment variables](../self-hosting/environment-variables.md).

title: Maestro, the console assistant
text:
**Maestro** is the AI assistant of the console. It looks up and changes the frontends, services,
builds, deployments, environments and variables of the project you have open, and searches the
Flightroom documentation. It acts **as you**: with your permissions, on the current project only.

Maestro is available when the project can use at least one [AI](./ai-models.md). Otherwise it is
hidden.

The console opens on Maestro (`/assistant`) when you sign in. In a project without an AI it opens on
**Frontends** instead.

![The Maestro page answering a project overview request, with the tools it called and Recent conversations on the right](../assets/assistant-overview.png)

title: Maestro, the console assistant — Opening it
text:
- As a side panel, from anywhere in the project: **⌘J** on macOS, **Ctrl+J** elsewhere, or the Maestro
  button in the header.
- As a full page: **AI agent**, the first entry of the sidebar. On a wide screen the page keeps
  **Recent conversations** open in a column on the right.

Type in **Ask something about the project…** (up to 4,000 characters) and press **Send**. While
Maestro answers, **Stop** interrupts it: the answer ends with *Answer stopped.*

Suggestions get you started, and they follow the page you are on: *Are there failed builds? Why?* on
Builds, *What changed in the latest deployment?* on Deployments, *Are there conflicts between shared
dependencies?* on Dependencies, *Is any environment missing variables?* on the variables page, then
general ones such as *Give me an overview of the project*. Some pages also offer a button that asks
Maestro for you: **Explain the failure** on a failed build, **Analyze the latest deployment**,
**Analyze the conflicts** on shared dependencies, **Check the variables** across environments.

Next to the message box you can pick the **AI** and the **Reasoning effort**. Maestro starts at
*Medium*; [code changes](./ai-changes.md) start at *High*. The console remembers the last choice of
each. When the AI reasons before answering, its thoughts show in a folded **Reasoning** block above
the answer. Every answer shows the tokens it used.

Conversations are saved per project: **Recent conversations** reopens them, **New conversation**
starts a fresh one, and **Delete conversation** removes one for good.

title: Maestro, the console assistant — Confirming actions
text:
Reads and ordinary writes run directly. Actions that are destructive or that hand out access **stop
and wait for you**. The panel shows a **Confirm this action** card, and nothing happens until you
press **Confirm**; **Cancel** drops it.

Actions that need confirmation include:

- deleting anything, deploying, rolling back (a redeploy of a previous snapshot, which does not
  touch Kubernetes: see [Rolling back a Kubernetes deploy](../kubernetes/rollback.md)), committing
  to a repository;
- changing a member's role, removing a member, revoking an API key or an AI client connection;
- inviting to a project or an organization, resending an invitation, creating an API key;
- applying an AI change or an AI job, opening the pull request of an AI change, discarding an AI
  change;
- scaffolding a repository from a template, renaming a repository;
- setting canary users.

The card names what the action acts on (users, environments, frontends with version and host,
services, domains, the AI change with its request and files) instead of raw ids. A deploy card shows,
for each environment, which versions, hosts and variables change compared with the active deployment.
**Input sent by Maestro** shows exactly what the model asked for.

A card can be answered **once** and **expires after 15 minutes**. After that, ask again.

title: Maestro, the console assistant — Starting AI code changes
text:
The **New AI job** button in the panel starts an agent on frontends and services you pick,
across domains. Jobs open as tabs in Maestro, where you follow them, chat with the agent and apply
the proposals. See [Change code with AI](./ai-changes.md#change-several-components-outside-a-domain).

title: Maestro, the console assistant — What Maestro does not do
Maestro, the console assistant — Permissions
text:
Maestro runs every tool through the same checks as the console. On a project where you are a
**Viewer** it cannot change anything. Member management (inviting, changing roles, removing) takes a
project owner or an administrator of the organization, as in the console pages.

title: Maestro, the console assistant — Audit
text:
Every answer and every write is logged by the server:

| Audit tag | Logged for | Contains |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `assistant_usage` | Every answer | The user, the project, the AI, the effort and the token counts |
| `assistant_tool_call` | Every write, confirmed or refused | The tool, the project or organization, the user, the outcome, and the arguments reduced to ids and short identifying values. Never free text or secrets |

Questions count against `ASSISTANT_RATE_LIMIT_MAX` per user per minute (default 20). Past it,
Maestro answers *Too many questions in a short time. Wait a minute and try again.*

title: Generate a domain with AI
text:
A **functional domain** groups the frontends and services of one business capability. When a
domain is still empty, one request is enough to get a first version: the AI proposes the components
the request needs, you review the list, and on confirmation the console creates each one with its own
repository, scaffolded from a Flightroom template, and the agent writes the code on top.

title: Generate a domain with AI — Before you start
text:
- The project can use at least one AI. See [AI models](./ai-models.md).
- The project has a code repository connection to GitHub, GitLab or Azure DevOps, which the new
  repositories are created through. See [GitHub](../repositories/connect/github.md),
  [GitLab](../repositories/connect/gitlab.md) or [Azure DevOps](../repositories/connect/azure.dev-ops.md).
- Your project role is not **Viewer**.

title: Generate a domain with AI — 1. Create the domain
text:
Open **Domains** in the sidebar and click **New domain**. Give it a **Name** (for example
*Payments*) and, optionally, a **Description** and an **AI context**: notes for the agent about this
domain only, such as its rules and vocabulary. See [Functional domains](../domains/overview.md) for
everything else a domain page offers.

title: Generate a domain with AI — 2. Describe what you need
text:
Open the domain. It opens on the **Edit with AI** tab, which tells you that the domain has no
frontend or service yet and that **Generate** will first ask the AI which ones your request
needs.

Write the request in **What should change?**, the way you would explain it to a colleague. For
example:

- *A page where warehouse leads log late deliveries, with a weekly count per carrier.*
- *An agent that checks each expense claim against the travel policy and flags the ones over the
  limit before approval.*

Pick the **AI** and the **Reasoning effort** if you want something other than the preselected ones,
then press **Generate proposal** (or ⌘/Ctrl + Enter).

title: Generate a domain with AI — 3. Review the components
text:
The console shows *The AI is proposing the components…* while a single model call drafts the list:
usually a frontend and a backend, **at most 3 frontends and 3 services**.

The dialog **Create these components for *domain*?** lists them under **Frontends** and
**Backends (services)**. Nothing exists yet: edit freely.

| Field | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| Checkbox | Untick a component to leave it out |
| **Name** | Display name |
| **Slug** | 2 to 50 lowercase letters, digits or dashes, starting with a letter or a digit. Unique in the project |
| **Repository name** | Letters, digits, `.`, `_` and `-`, up to 100, starting with a letter or a digit, not ending with `.`, `.git` or `.atom`. By convention it ends with `-fe` for a frontend and `-be` for a backend |
| **Template** | The Flightroom template the repository is scaffolded from |

Below the list choose the **Code repository connection** to create the repositories with, and
whether they are **Private repositories** (on by default). Then confirm with **Create *N* components and generate**.

### Templates

| Kind | Default | Also available |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Frontend | React with Vite, as a remote (`vite-remote-react`) | React, Angular and Vue with Vite or Webpack, plus Web Component, single-spa and micro-lc. See the [templates library](../templates/templates-library.md) |
| Service | Node.js & Fastify (`service-node-fastify`) | Python & FastAPI, Spring Boot, Quarkus |

title: Generate a domain with AI — 4. What happens on confirmation
text:
1. Each component is created in the domain, each with a **new repository** scaffolded from its
   template, CI pipeline included. The dialog shows *Creating…*, *Created* or *Not created* per
   component.
2. The agent job starts on the new repositories. One agent sees all of them at once, so it can write
   an API and the screens that call it together.
3. It pushes its work on a branch of its own in each repository, `ai/<slug>-<timestamp>`, and
   proposes **one change per repository**.

From here the domain behaves like any other: review each proposal, refine it by chatting with the
agent, then apply it, open a pull request or discard it. See
[Change code with AI](./ai-changes.md).

title: Generate a domain with AI — Members without repositories
text:
If the domain already has frontends or services but none of them has a code repository, the
console asks **Can I create the repositories?** instead. Each selected member gets a new repository
named `<slug>-fe` or `<slug>-be`, scaffolded from the member's template or from the default of its
kind. Confirm with **Create *N* repositories and generate**, and the job starts as above.

title: Generate a domain with AI — When something is in the way
text:
| Message | What to do |
| --- | --- |
