| **No code repository connected** | The project has no GitHub, GitLab or Azure DevOps connection. Follow **Connect a code repository**, then try again |
| *The AI did not propose anything to create* | Describe in the request what the domain should do and try again |
| *The repository already exists at the provider…* | Possibly left there by an attempt that failed. Pick another name, or delete it at the provider and try again |
| *A frontend (or service) with this slug already exists in the project* | Pick another slug |
| *You do not have permission to create code repositories in this project.* | Your project role is **Viewer**. Ask an Admin or an Editor of the project to run it |
| *The template no longer exists* | Pick another template for the component |
| *The pipeline templates of the project could not be read: nothing was created* | The project uses [its own pipeline templates](../templates/templates-library.md#your-own-pipeline-templates) and their repository or branch cannot be read. Fix them in **Settings**, or go back to the official templates, and try again |
| *…one agent works on at most 10 repositories* | Select fewer components; you can start a job on the others later |
| *AI editing is not available in this project* | The organization has no AI the project can use. See [AI models](./ai-models.md) |

title: AI guardrails
text:
This page is for the people who have to approve the AI features: IT, security, platform owners. It
lists what the agent is allowed to do, what it is not, and where a human stays in the loop.

title: AI guardrails — A person decides what reaches the base branch
text:
- The agent works on a **clone** of the repository and never pushes by itself. The console pushes its
  proposal on a new branch, `ai/<slug>-<timestamp>`, and only there.
- The base branch is written only when a user presses **Apply**. That push is **never forced**: a
  protected branch refuses it, and the console suggests a pull request instead.
- **Apply** first checks that every file is still what the agent saw. A file changed on the base
  branch in the meantime stops the apply with a conflict, so nothing is silently overwritten.
- **Open a pull request** hands the change to your normal review process on GitHub, GitLab (merge
  request) or Azure DevOps.

To force review on every AI change, protect the base branch at your Git provider: Apply is then
refused and a pull request is the only way in.

title: AI guardrails — CI is the judge
text:
The agent **cannot run anything**: no install, no build, no test. Your repository's CI checks the
branch and the pull request, exactly as it does for a person's work.

:::warning[Pushed branches run CI with the repository secrets]
Every proposal is pushed on its branch as soon as the agent is done, before anyone has reviewed it. A
pipeline that runs on every branch therefore runs the agent's code with whatever secrets that
pipeline can reach. Keep deployment secrets, and the pipelines that use them, limited to protected
branches.
:::

The protected paths below keep the agent away from what CI executes directly. Build configuration,
tests and `package.json` scripts also run in CI, and only the human review of the diff covers those.

title: AI guardrails — What the agent cannot read
text:
Files that usually hold credentials:

`.env*`, `.npmrc`, `.netrc`, `id_rsa*`, `id_ed25519*`, `*.pem`, `*.key`, `*.p12`, `*.pfx`,
`*.keystore`, `*.jks`

title: AI guardrails — What the agent cannot write
text:
| Category | Paths |
| --- | --- |
| Git internals | `.git` |
| CI configuration | `.github/workflows/`, `.github/actions/`, `.gitlab-ci.yml`, `.gitlab/`, `azure-pipelines*.yml`, `azure-pipelines*.yaml`, `.azure-pipelines/`, `.circleci/`, `bitbucket-pipelines.yml`, `Jenkinsfile*`, `.husky/` |
| Lockfiles | `pnpm-lock.yaml`, `package-lock.json`, `yarn.lock`, `npm-shrinkwrap.json`, `bun.lock`, `bun.lockb` |
| Registry configuration | `.npmrc`, `.yarnrc`, `.yarnrc.yml`, `.pnpmfile.cjs` |
| Ignored files | Anything the repository's `.gitignore` excludes |

title: AI guardrails — Confined to the working copy
text:
- The agent can list, search, read, write and delete files **inside the working copy only**. Every
  path is resolved after following symlinks: `..`, absolute paths, `.git` and symlinks pointing out of
  the repository are refused.
- Repository credentials are never written to disk: the clone URL holds no token, and the provider
  token is handed to each network call.
- No `git` binary runs and no repository hook is ever executed.

title: AI guardrails — Limits
text:
| Limit | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Request length | 8,000 characters |
| Files changed | 20 per repository |
| Content written | 500 KB per repository, 2 MB per job |
| Model rounds | 40 for one repository, plus 20 for each additional repository, 120 at most |
| Repositories in one job | 10 |
| Jobs running at once | 3 per project |
| Requests per user | `ASSISTANT_RATE_LIMIT_MAX` per minute (default 20), the same ceiling as Maestro questions |
| Unanswered proposals | Removed after 7 days; the branch stays |

title: AI guardrails — Who can do what
text:
| Action | Who |
| --- | --- |
| See AI change requests | Every member of the project |
| Ask for a change, apply, open a pull request, discard | Project **Admin** and **Editor**, plus organization **Owner** and **Admin**. A **Viewer** cannot |
| Manage the organization's AIs and which projects use them | Organization **Owner** and **Admin** |

A member whose access is limited to **Specific domains** (see
[Changing a role](../project-settings/users-and-roles.md#changing-a-role)) sees and starts only the jobs
whose frontends and services all belong to their domains. Jobs on the whole project are hidden
from them.

Maestro and MCP clients act with the user's own permissions: on a project where the user is a Viewer,
every change is refused. See [Console assistant](./console-assistant.md) and
[MCP server](./mcp-server.md).

title: AI guardrails — What leaves your installation
text:
The agent sends the files it reads, and your request, to the **AI provider** of the AI picked for the
request. Which providers a project may use is decided by the organization's administrators; a project
restricted to no AI has the AI features off, and nothing is sent anywhere. See
[AI models](./ai-models.md).

A provider's own error message is never shown to users or stored on a job: users see a generic error,
and the provider's message goes to the server log.

title: AI guardrails — Audit and cost
text:
- The commit author of an AI change is the user who asked; the committer is Flightroom.
- The token usage of each request is stored and shown in the console, next to the effort used.
- The server log carries an `ai_job_usage` line per AI job, with the user, the project, the effort,
  the AI and the token counts.
- Maestro logs every answer (`assistant_usage`) and every write it runs, confirmed or refused
  (`assistant_tool_call`). See [Console assistant](./console-assistant.md#audit).

title: AI guardrails — Self-hosting: where the clones live
text:
The agent works on clones kept on the backend's disk.

| Variable | Default | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `REPOSITORIES_FOLDER` | `/repositories` (`/data/repositories` in the all-in-one image) | Root of the clones |
| `REPOSITORIES_MAX_SIZE_MB` | `500` | A clone bigger than this is refused and deleted |
| `REPOSITORIES_EVICT_AFTER_DAYS` | `14` | Clones not used for this long are deleted |

The folder is a **cache**: deleting it only costs a new clone. Clones are also removed when their
frontend or project is deleted. On Kubernetes the Helm chart mounts an `emptyDir` there
(`repositories.sizeLimit`, 10Gi by default); set `repositories.existingClaim` to keep the clones
across restarts. See also [Environment variables](../self-hosting/environment-variables.md).

title: MCP server
text:
Flightroom can expose its features to AI clients that speak the
[Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io): Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude Code, Cursor
and others. You sign in to the console from the client, pick the projects to share and whether the
client may change things, and the client then works only inside those projects, with your role.

:::info[Self-hosted installations]
The MCP server is **off by default**. It is available on self-hosted installations where an
administrator turns it on. When it is off, the **AI assistants** page of the project settings reads
*AI assistants are not enabled*.
:::

title: MCP server — Turning it on
text:
Set these on the backend:

| Variable | Default | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `MCP_ENABLED` | `false` | Mounts the MCP server, the OAuth endpoints and the discovery documents |
| `FRONTEND_URL` | required | Public URL of the console: the consent page lives there |
| `JWT_SECRET` | required | Your own secret, at least 32 bytes (`openssl rand -hex 32`). With MCP on, the backend refuses to start on a missing, placeholder or short one |
| `MCP_API_KEY_ENABLED` | `true` | Lets clients that cannot do OAuth use a project API key (see below) |
| `MCP_RATE_LIMIT_MAX` | `120` | MCP requests per minute for each grant or API key, on top of the per-IP `RATE_LIMIT_MAX` (default `100`) |
| `MCP_DCR_ENABLED` | `true` | Dynamic client registration, what most clients use today |
| `MCP_CIMD_ENABLED` | `true` | Client ID metadata documents: the client is identified by the URL of a document it publishes |
| `CIMD_ALLOWED_HOSTS` | empty | Comma-separated hosts allowed to publish a client metadata document. Empty accepts any host. A client from a listed host is not flagged *Unverified application* on the consent page |
| `OAUTH_ISSUER_URL` | derived | Public URL of the OAuth authorization server, when it cannot be derived from `BACKEND_URL` or `FRONTEND_URL` (`/api`) |
| `MCP_RESOURCE_URL` | derived | Public URL of the MCP server, when it is not `<issuer>/mcp` |

The discovery documents live at the origin root, outside `/api`
(`/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource`, `/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server`,
`/.well-known/openid-configuration`). The bundled nginx already routes them; if you put another proxy
in front, route them to the backend with the path untouched, and serve `/api/mcp` without buffering.

title: MCP server — Connecting a client
text:
In the project, open **Settings → Access**, then **Manage** on **AI assistants**, and use **Copy MCP
server URL**. With the default layout it is `https://<your console>/api/mcp`.

- **Claude.ai, ChatGPT and Gemini** connect with just this URL: add it as a remote MCP server, and
  they ask you to sign in and approve access.
- **Claude Code**:

  ```bash
  claude mcp add --transport http flightroom https://<your console>/api/mcp
  ```

![The AI assistants page, with the MCP server URL to copy, the API key alternative and no connected assistants yet](../assets/mcp-clients.png)

### The consent page

The client sends you to the console, where you sign in as usual and see **Connect *client***:

1. **Choose the projects to share**: one or more, at most 50, grouped by organization. The checkbox
   next to each organization (**Select all**) selects all its projects. With more than 8 projects
   the list gets a **Search projects** box.
2. **Allow changes**, or leave it off for read-only access. With it, the client can also change the
   projects, deploy, and create new projects in the organizations of the shared projects you
   administer.
3. **Approve** or **Deny**.

The page warns when something deserves a second look: *Unverified application* (the client's name is
self-asserted), *Redirect address differs from publisher*, *Local application*, *Custom link scheme*.

### When the connection fails

If the request cannot go on, the console shows **Connection failed** with the reason:

| Code | Shown as | Means |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `invalid_client` | **Unknown application** | The application that started the request is not recognized |
| `invalid_redirect_uri` | **Invalid redirect address** | The application asked to be sent to an address that is not allowed |
| `invalid_request` | **Request not valid** | The request is invalid, expired or belongs to another account. Start the connection again from your assistant |
| `server_error` | **Something went wrong** | An unexpected error. Also shown for any other code |

![The Connection failed page showing Request not valid for an invalid or expired request](../assets/oauth-error.png)

title: MCP server — What a client can do
text:
| Scope | Granted by | Allows |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `mfe:read` | Always | Reading the project: frontends, services, domains with their links and their deployed versions, environments, deployments, canary users, variables, config maps, secrets (values masked), build status, storages, databases and repository connections (credentials masked), dependency and integration plans |
| `mfe:write` | **Allow changes** | Everything the console does inside a project, **deploy and rollback included**, plus creating projects and creating a frontend or a service with its repository from a template (`frontend_scaffold`, `service_scaffold`). Rollback re-activates a snapshot and does not touch Kubernetes: see [Rolling back a Kubernetes deploy](../kubernetes/rollback.md) |

The role caps each project separately and is read again on every call. On a project where you are a
**Viewer**, every write is refused whatever the grant says, and the consent page tells you which
selected projects stay read-only. Demoting a member takes write access away from their clients
immediately.

Left out on purpose:

- API keys, and listing or revoking MCP clients;
- creating or editing storages, databases, secrets and repository connections (their input is a
  secret);
- organization settings, creating an organization, deleting projects, organizations, members and
  invitations;
- the GitOps and pipeline templates settings of a project;
- bulk creation and deletion, and the layout of the canvas;
- the user profile, bundle upload, and Flightroom's own AI code changes.

These stay in the console, where some of them are available to [Maestro](./console-assistant.md).
One connection creates at most 10 projects.

title: MCP server — Changing code from your own coding agent
text:
Flightroom's AI change jobs run only in the console. A coding agent on your machine (Claude Code,
Cursor…) gets two tools instead, so it can do the work locally and still hand it back as a pull
request:

1. `repository_checkout_get` (read) returns where to clone the repository of a frontend or a
   service (an HTTPS URL without credentials: clone it with your own Git access), its default branch,
   and the AI context the team wrote for it, its domain and the project.
2. The agent edits the clone, following that context.
3. `code_change_submit` (write) pushes the files to a new branch, `mcp/<slug>-<timestamp>`, and opens
   a pull request against the base branch. The base branch itself is never written.

`code_change_submit` takes the commit the clone started from: if the base branch moved since and one
of the submitted files changed there too, the change is refused, so pull and submit again. The same
protected paths as the console agent apply: CI configuration, lockfiles and registry configuration
cannot be changed this way (see [Guardrails](./guardrails.md#what-the-agent-cannot-write)). One
submission carries at most 100 files and 768 KB.

title: MCP server — Fallback: a project API key
MCP server — Managing connections
text:
The **AI assistants** page (`/mcp-clients`, also reached from **Settings → Access → AI assistants**)
lists the connected clients that include the current project: **Assistant**, **Projects**, **User**,
**Access** (*Read only* or *Read and write*), **Connected on** and **Last used**. A project owner or an
organization admin sees and can revoke everyone's connections that include the project; other
members see and revoke their own.

To revoke one, press the trash icon on its row and confirm in the **Revoke access** dialog. It removes
the whole grant, with all its projects, and takes effect on the client's next request.

A grant also ends by itself:

- when you lose access to all its projects;
- after **30 days** without use;
- in any case after **90 days**.

title: MCP server — How it works
text:
- **Authorization**: OAuth 2.1 authorization code with PKCE (S256 only), public clients and resource
  indicators. The authorization code is single use and lives 60 seconds.
- **Tokens**: access tokens are valid 15 minutes and are distinct from console sessions: a console
  session token is refused by the MCP server, and an MCP token cannot open a console session. Refresh
  tokens rotate on every use, and a replayed one revokes the whole grant.
- **Transport**: Streamable HTTP, stateless.
- **Audit**: the log line of every tool call names the grant (OAuth) or the API key.

title: Build with AI overview
text:
Anyone in a project can describe the app or the AI agent they need in their own words. Flightroom's
AI writes the code in **your own Git repositories** (GitHub, GitLab or Azure DevOps), starting from
Flightroom templates, and pushes it to a branch of its own. Engineers review the change where they
already review code, and from there it ships like anything else in the project.

The AI never writes to your base branch by itself. It proposes, and a person applies, opens a pull
request or discards.

title: Build with AI overview — Apps and agents in console terms
text:
The console has no entity called "app" or "agent". What you describe maps to the building blocks
Flightroom already manages:

| What you ask for | What it is in the console |
| --- | --- |
| The web interface of an app | A **frontend**. Its **Kind** is *Bundle* (served by Flightroom) or *Docker* (served by its Docker container) |
| The backend or API of an app | A **service**, listed under **Backend services** |
| An app as a whole | A **functional domain** (**Domains** in the sidebar), which groups the frontends and services of one business capability |
| An AI agent | A **service** whose code the AI writes to call an AI model and your systems |

An agent has no separate runtime. It is a service like any other: it lives in its repository, goes
through your CI, gets versioned and is deployed the same way.

The rest of this section uses the console terms when it describes what to click.

title: Build with AI overview — What the AI does, and what it leaves to you
text:
- It works on a **clone** of the repository, never on the repository itself.
- It commits its proposal on a new branch, `ai/<slug>-<timestamp>`, and pushes it. The branch it
  started from is not touched.
- It does **not** install, build or test anything. Your CI checks the code, as it does for any other
  branch.
- It cannot read files that usually hold credentials, and cannot change CI configuration or
  lockfiles. See [Guardrails](./guardrails.md).

Once the proposal is ready you choose: **Apply** it to the base branch, **Open a pull request**, or
**Discard** it. See [Change code with AI](./ai-changes.md).

title: Build with AI overview — Ways to build
text:
| Starting point | Where | Page |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A new app from nothing | An empty functional domain, **Edit with AI** tab | [Generate a domain](./generate-a-domain.md) |
| A change to a frontend, a service or a whole domain | Its **Edit with AI** tab | [Change code with AI](./ai-changes.md) |
| Questions and actions on the project, in a chat | **Maestro**, ⌘J / Ctrl+J or **AI agent** in the sidebar | [Console assistant](./console-assistant.md) |
| Your own AI client (Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, Cursor…) | The Flightroom MCP server, on installations that turn it on | [MCP server](./mcp-server.md) |

title: Build with AI overview — Set it up once
text:
An administrator prepares the ground; after that, project members build.

1. **Add an AI to the organization.** An owner or an admin of the organization opens
   **Organization settings**, tab **AI**, and adds one with **Add AI**: Claude (Anthropic, Azure AI
   Foundry or AWS Bedrock), Gemini or GPT on Azure OpenAI. Every project of the organization can use
   it unless restricted. See [AI models](./ai-models.md).
2. **Connect a code repository provider to the project.** The AI works in repositories reached
   through a code repository connection:
   [GitHub](../repositories/connect/github.md), [GitLab](../repositories/connect/gitlab.md) or
   [Azure DevOps](../repositories/connect/azure.dev-ops.md).
3. **Optionally, write AI context.** Free markdown notes for AI agents (business domain,
   conventions, rules), up to 20,000 characters each:
   - for the whole project, in **Settings → General → Project AI context**;
   - for a functional domain, in the **AI context** field of the domain form;
   - for a frontend or a service, in its **AI context** tab.

   The agent always receives the context of what it works on, of its domain and of the project.

When a project has no AI available, the AI features are hidden or report that they are not enabled,
and nothing is sent to any provider.

title: Build with AI overview — Who can do what
text:
| Action | Who |
| --- | --- |
| Add, edit or delete the AIs of the organization, and choose which AIs each project can use | Organization **Owner** or **Admin** |
| See the AI change requests of a project | Every member of the project |
| Ask for a change, apply it, open its pull request, discard it | Project **Admin** and **Editor**, and organization Owners and Admins. Not **Viewer** |
| Use Maestro | Every member; it acts with the member's own permissions, so a Viewer cannot change anything through it |
| Connect an AI client over MCP with changes allowed | Members who can write on the projects they share; on a project where they are Viewer the client stays read-only |

:::info[The Viewer role is enforced here]
The AI features check the project role: a **Viewer** can read AI change requests but not start,
apply or discard one. Elsewhere in the console the project role is still a label; see
[Project members and roles](../project-settings/users-and-roles.md).
:::

title: Build with AI overview — From the branch to production
text:
The AI's work ends in your repository. From there the usual path applies: CI builds the branch you
merged or applied to, and you deploy the result to an environment. To run your frontends and
services on your own cluster, see [Deploy to Kubernetes](../kubernetes/overview.md).

title: Build with AI overview — Where to go next
text:
- [Generate a domain](./generate-a-domain.md): from an empty domain to a first version
- [Change code with AI](./ai-changes.md): proposals, chat, apply, pull request, discard
- [Guardrails](./guardrails.md): limits and protections, for IT and security reviewers
- [AI models](./ai-models.md): connecting your AI providers
- [Console assistant](./console-assistant.md): Maestro
- [MCP server](./mcp-server.md): using Flightroom from your own AI client

title: API keys for CI/CD
text:
An API key authenticates a machine — a CI pipeline, a deploy script, an automation job — against a
single project. Keys live on the project's **API Keys** page, reached from **Settings → Access →
API Keys**.

title: API keys for CI/CD — Creating a key
text:
1. Go to **Settings → Access → API Keys** and click **Create API Key**.

   ![The API Keys page with Create API Key and a ci-pipeline key marked Active](../assets/api-keys.png)

2. Give it a **Name** describing where it will be used, e.g. *catalog GitHub Actions*.
3. Pick an **Expiration Date**. The dialog proposes one six months from now. A day you pick
   yourself is sent as the *start* of that day — midnight in your browser's time zone, not UTC — so
   pick the day after the last one you want the key to work on.
4. Click **Create Key**.

   ![The Create API Key dialog, with a name and an expiry date](../assets/api-key-dialog.png)

The key is displayed once, in a dialog with a **Copy & Close** button.

:::caution[Shown exactly once]
The key is stored hashed and can never be retrieved again — the list view has no key column at all.
If you lose it, delete the key and create a new one.
:::

title: API keys for CI/CD — Expiry
text:
Every key carries an expiry date and the list marks it **Active**, **Expiring soon** or **Expired**
from that date. The date is enforced: from the moment it passes, a request with the key is refused
with *API key expired on …*. There is no way to create a non-expiring key.

:::tip
Put the expiry date in whatever calendar your team actually reads. Rotate before it: create the new
key first, update the consumer, then delete the old one.
:::

title: API keys for CI/CD — What a key can call
text:
Exactly these endpoints accept a key — `` is the API URL, e.g.
`https://console.example.com/api`:

| Endpoint | What it does | Body | Role |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `POST /frontends/by-slug/:slug/upload/:version` | [Uploads](./manual-upload.md) the bundle of a frontend version | multipart, field `file` (a ZIP) | any |
| `POST /frontends/by-slug/:slug/versions/:version` | Registers the image of a version of a frontend served by its own Docker container | JSON: `image` (required), `digest`, `commitSha` | `MANAGER` |
| `POST /frontends/by-slug/:slug/environments/:envSlug/deployments` | Reports that a version of that Docker frontend now runs in an environment | JSON: `version` (required), `image`, `commitSha` | `MANAGER` |
| `POST /services/by-slug/:slug/versions/:version` | Registers the image of a [service](../kubernetes/services.md) version | JSON: `image` (required), `digest`, `commitSha` | `MANAGER` |
| `POST /services/by-slug/:slug/environments/:envSlug/deployments` | Reports that a service version now runs in an environment | JSON: `version` (required), `image`, `commitSha` | `MANAGER` |

The two `frontends/…/versions` and `…/deployments` routes refuse a frontend served by
Flightroom — its CI uploads a bundle instead — and the upload refuses a Docker one. The template
pipelines call the right ones for you.

Plus the [MCP server](../build-with-ai/mcp-server.md) at `/mcp`, where a key stands in for
clients that cannot sign in with OAuth. There it goes in `Authorization: Bearer <key>` (or the
`api-key` header); the `?apiKey=` query parameter is **not** accepted on `/mcp`. An operator can turn
this fallback off with `MCP_API_KEY_ENABLED=false` — see
[environment variables](../self-hosting/environment-variables.md#mcp-server-and-oauth).

Everything else on the API — creating a deployment, editing a frontend, reading the build
status — is authenticated with the token of a signed-in user and answers an API key with an
authentication error. So a pipeline can *publish* a version, and it cannot *deploy* it; see
[publishing does not deploy](./manual-upload.md#publishing-does-not-deploy).

title: API keys for CI/CD — Roles
text:
A key carries a role in the database — `MANAGER` or `VIEWER` — and neither the console nor the API
gives you anything to do with it.

- **You cannot choose it in the console.** The create dialog asks for a name and an expiry date,
  nothing else, and every key it produces is a `MANAGER`. `POST /api-keys` accepts an optional
  `role` in its body and defaults to `MANAGER` when it is missing. Keys created automatically for a
  scaffolded repository are `MANAGER` too.
- **It is checked where it matters for CI and AI clients.** Registering the version of a service or
  a Docker frontend, and reporting where it was deployed, require a `MANAGER` key. The
  [MCP server](../build-with-ai/mcp-server.md) gives a `VIEWER` key read-only tools. Uploading a
  frontend bundle does not read the role. A `VIEWER` key can be created through the
  [console assistant](../build-with-ai/console-assistant.md), not from the create dialog.

Treat the *key itself* as the credential to protect. Anywhere the
CI pages ask for a key, any key the console gives you is the right one.

title: API keys for CI/CD — Keys created for you
text:
You often do not need to create a key at all. Connecting a code repository — or editing an existing
connection — creates a key and writes it into your Git provider under the name the generated
pipelines read, `MICROFRONTEND_ORCHESTRATOR_API_KEY`. It happens once per connection, not once per
frontend, and is skipped when a secret of that name already exists.

| Provider | Where the key is written | Scope |
| --- | --- | --- |
| GitHub | Organization secret, visible to all repositories | The organization on the connection |
| GitLab | Group CI/CD variable | The group you selected on the connection |
| Azure DevOps | Variable group `MFE_ORCHESTRATOR_SECRETS` | The Azure DevOps project |

:::caution[A personal GitHub account gets no organization secret]
Each injector needs an organization or group id and returns without doing anything when there is
none. A GitHub connection to a personal account has no organization, so no secret is written and a
pipeline in an existing repository cannot authenticate — the publish step fails with an
authentication error on its first run and nothing in the console says why.

For repositories the console creates itself under a personal connection it falls back to a
**repository** secret of the same name, so those work. Repositories you connected by hand need the
secret added by hand: create an [API key](#creating-a-key) and add it as a repository secret named
`MICROFRONTEND_ORCHESTRATOR_API_KEY`.
:::

You will find these keys in the API Keys list named
`MFE_ORCHESTRATOR_DEPLOY_SECRET - <provider> - <repository>`. Do not delete them unless you intend
to break the corresponding pipeline.

:::caution[Older keys expire after 15 days]
An automatically created key now expires after a year. Older versions of the platform computed 365
*hours* instead, about 15 days, and expiry is enforced: a pipeline whose key was created that way
fails with *API key expired*. Create a new key and update the pipeline secret.
:::

title: API keys for CI/CD — Using a key
text:
Send it in the `api-key` header:

```bash
curl -X POST \
  -H "api-key: $MFE_ORCHESTRATOR_API_KEY" \
  -F "file=@dist.zip" \
  "/frontends/by-slug/catalog/upload/1.4.0"
```

On every endpoint except `/mcp`, a query parameter is also accepted, for clients that cannot set
headers:

```
/frontends/by-slug/catalog/upload/1.4.0?apiKey=…
```

:::caution[Prefer the header]
Query strings end up in access logs, browser history and proxy logs. Use `?apiKey=` only when
setting a header is genuinely impossible.
:::

The project is derived from the key, so requests authenticated this way do not need a `project-id`
header.

title: API keys for CI/CD — Stopping a key
text:
In the console there is one action: **Delete**, the trash button on the key's row in the list.

A key can also be **revoked**: it stays in the list, and every request with it is refused with
*API key revoked*. The console has no Revoke button; the API (`PUT /api-keys/:id/revoke`) and the
[console assistant](../build-with-ai/console-assistant.md) can do it. Revoke when you want to keep the
record for the audit trail, delete when you do not.

title: API keys for CI/CD — Good practice
text:
**One key per consumer.** A key per pipeline, not one shared across the organisation. Rotating or
revoking then affects one thing, and the name tells you what breaks.

**Never commit a key.** Use your CI's secret store. Keys are UUIDs and match no distinctive pattern,
so secret scanners will not catch one you paste into a repository.

**Scope by project.** A key grants access to its project only. Cross-project automation needs one
key per project — which is the correct blast radius, not an inconvenience to work around.

**Treat a leaked key as a live incident.** Any key can publish arbitrary JavaScript to your
production frontends. **Delete it first, investigate second** — deleting is the only thing that
stops it, and nothing else you can do in the console reduces its access at all. Then create a
replacement and update the consumer.

title: Deploy with Azure Pipelines
text:
When Flightroom creates a repository from a template in Azure DevOps, it commits an
`azure-pipelines.yml`, creates the pipeline definition, and stores the deploy key in a variable
group.

title: Deploy with Azure Pipelines — The generated pipeline
text:
```yaml
trigger:
  branches:
    include:
      - main
      - develop
      - development
  tags:
    include:
      - '*'

pool:
  vmImage: 'ubuntu-latest'

stages:
  - stage: Build
    displayName: '🏗️ Build'
    jobs:
      - job: BuildJob
        steps:
          - task: NodeTool@0
            inputs:
              versionSpec: '24.x'

          - script: npm install -g pnpm
            displayName: '📦 Install pnpm'

          - script: pnpm i
            displayName: '📥 Install dependencies'

          - script: pnpm build
            displayName: '🔨 Build project'

          - task: PublishBuildArtifacts@1
            inputs:
              PathtoPublish: 'dist'
              ArtifactName: 'app'
              publishLocation: 'Container'

  - stage: Deploy
    displayName: '🚀 Deploy'
    dependsOn: Build
    condition: and(succeeded(), startsWith(variables['Build.SourceBranch'], 'refs/tags/'))
    variables:
      - group: MFE_ORCHESTRATOR_SECRETS
      - name: VERSION
        value: $[replace(variables['Build.SourceBranch'], 'refs/tags/', '')]
      - name: MICROFRONTEND_ORCHESTRATOR_DOMAIN_RESOLVED
        value: $[coalesce(variables['MICROFRONTEND_ORCHESTRATOR_DOMAIN'], 'https://console.flightroom.dev')]
    jobs:
      - job: Deploy
        steps:
          - task: DownloadBuildArtifacts@1
            inputs:
              buildType: 'current'
              downloadType: 'single'
              artifactName: 'app'
              downloadPath: '$(System.ArtifactsDirectory)'

          - task: flightroom-upload@1
            inputs:
              apiKey: '$(MICROFRONTEND_ORCHESTRATOR_API_KEY)'
              microfrontendSlug: 'catalog'
              filePath: '$(System.ArtifactsDirectory)/app'
              version: '$(VERSION)'
              domain: '$(MICROFRONTEND_ORCHESTRATOR_DOMAIN_RESOLVED)'
```

The template in
[`template-pipelines`](https://github.com/mfe-orchestrator/template-pipelines) carries
`%microfrontendSlug%` and `%domain%` where this example has `catalog` and the console URL. The
scaffolder replaces both before the initial commit, as it does on GitHub: the slug of the
frontend, and the installation's `BACKEND_URL` inserted verbatim — or
`https://console.flightroom.dev` when `BACKEND_URL` is not set. A pipeline variable named
`MICROFRONTEND_ORCHESTRATOR_DOMAIN` wins over that default, so you can publish to another
installation without editing the file.

:::caution[`%domain%` is the API URL, copied as is]
`BACKEND_URL` is the public URL of the API, which normally already ends in `/api`, and nothing strips
that suffix when it becomes `%domain%`. The templates add `/api` themselves where they need it — the
host templates, for instance, build `%domain%/api` — so an installation whose `BACKEND_URL` ends in
`/api` gets URLs with `/api/api` in them. Check the scaffolded file, and if that is the case set
`MICROFRONTEND_ORCHESTRATOR_DOMAIN` to the console URL without `/api`. With `BACKEND_URL` unset the
default points at `https://console.flightroom.dev`, not at your installation, so on a self-hosted
installation set the variable.
:::

title: Deploy with Azure Pipelines — Two stages, deliberately
text:
Unlike the GitHub workflow, this pipeline separates build from publish:

- **Build** runs on branch pushes *and* tags. Every commit to `main` is verified.
- **Deploy** runs only when the trigger was a **tag**, thanks to the `condition` on
  `refs/tags/`.

So branch pushes give you CI feedback without publishing anything, and a tag publishes. The version
is derived from the tag name by stripping `refs/tags/`.

title: Deploy with Azure Pipelines — The variable group
text:
The publish task reads `$(MICROFRONTEND_ORCHESTRATOR_API_KEY)` from a variable group named
**`MFE_ORCHESTRATOR_SECRETS`**. Flightroom creates the group and the key when you connect the
Azure DevOps repository to a project — or edit that connection — not when a frontend is
scaffolded, and it skips the work when the variable already exists.

The group is created at **project** scope, so several frontend repositories in the same Azure
DevOps project share it. That also means the connection must have a project selected: without an
organization and a project id the injector returns without creating anything.

:::note[The key is dated 15 days out, and keeps working anyway]
The generated key expires after a year, and an expired key is refused with *API key expired*.
Keys generated by older versions of the platform expired after 365 *hours*, about fifteen days: if a
publish fails that way, create a new key and update the pipeline secret. See
[Expiry](./api-keys.md#expiry).
:::

:::caution[Pipeline authorization]
A newly created variable group may need to be authorized for the pipeline the first time it runs.
If the Deploy stage fails with a permissions error on the variable group, open
**Pipelines → Library → MFE_ORCHESTRATOR_SECRETS → Pipeline permissions** and grant access.
:::

title: Deploy with Azure Pipelines — The publish task
text:
`flightroom-upload@1` is an Azure DevOps extension and must be installed in your organization
before a pipeline can use it.

| Input | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `apiKey` | A Flightroom [API key](./api-keys.md) |
| `microfrontendSlug` | The slug of the frontend to publish to |
| `filePath` | The directory containing the build output |
| `version` | The version to publish |

The generated pipeline passes exactly these four, and no domain: it publishes to the extension's
default installation. To publish somewhere else, add a `MICROFRONTEND_ORCHESTRATOR_DOMAIN` variable
to the `MFE_ORCHESTRATOR_SECRETS` group and pass it to the task as an additional `domain` input.

:::info[If the task is not available]
Install the extension from the Visual Studio Marketplace into your organization. If your
organization does not permit third-party extensions, replace the task with a script step calling the
[upload endpoint](./manual-upload.md) directly — it does the same thing:

The `curl` needs a base URL, which the generated pipeline does not carry, so declare it in the
`Deploy` stage's `variables` block — or add it to the `MFE_ORCHESTRATOR_SECRETS` group — before using
the step below:

```yaml
- script: |
    cd $(System.ArtifactsDirectory)/app
    zip -qr $(Build.ArtifactStagingDirectory)/dist.zip .
    curl --fail --show-error --silent -X POST \
      -H "api-key: $(MICROFRONTEND_ORCHESTRATOR_API_KEY)" \
      -F "file=@$(Build.ArtifactStagingDirectory)/dist.zip" \
      "$(MICROFRONTEND_ORCHESTRATOR_DOMAIN)/api/frontends/by-slug/catalog/upload/$(VERSION)"
  displayName: '🚀 Upload to Flightroom'
```

`--fail` is not optional: without it `curl` exits 0 on a rejected upload and the stage passes.
:::

title: Deploy with Azure Pipelines — Publishing a version
text:
Tag and push:

```bash
git tag 1.4.0
git push origin 1.4.0
```

Or use the **Build** action on the frontend card in the console, which creates the tag for you.

title: Deploy with Azure Pipelines — Adding this to an existing repository
text:
1. Create an [API key](./api-keys.md).
2. Create a variable group named `MFE_ORCHESTRATOR_SECRETS`
   (**Pipelines → Library → Variable group**) with a secret variable
   `MICROFRONTEND_ORCHESTRATOR_API_KEY`.
3. Commit the pipeline above as `azure-pipelines.yml`, with your slug.
4. Create the pipeline definition pointing at that file.
5. Authorize the variable group for the pipeline.

Variants for other compilers and host types are in
[`template-pipelines`](https://github.com/mfe-orchestrator/template-pipelines) under
`<type>/<compiler>/azure_dev_ops/`.

title: Deploy with Azure Pipelines — Troubleshooting
text:
**Deploy stage skipped**

Expected on a branch push — it runs only for tags. Check `Build.SourceBranch` starts with
`refs/tags/`.

**Variable group not found or not authorized**

The group must exist in the same project and be authorized for the pipeline. See the caution above.

**Task `flightroom-upload` not found**

The extension is not installed in the organization. Install it, or use the `curl` fallback.

**Authentication failure on publish**

The key is missing from the group, misnamed, or names a key that has been deleted, revoked or has
expired. Check **Settings → Access → API Keys** in the console: an expired or revoked key is refused,
with *API key expired on …* or *API key revoked*. If the connection has no Azure DevOps project
selected, the group was never created at all.

**Wrong version published**

`VERSION` comes from the tag name. A tag like `v1.4.0` publishes a version literally called
`v1.4.0` — consistent, but make sure it matches what you select in the console.

title: Deploy with GitHub Actions
text:
When Flightroom creates a repository from a template on GitHub, it commits a
`.github/workflows/build-and-deploy.yml` workflow and creates the secret the workflow needs. This
page explains that workflow, and how to add one to a repository the platform did not create.

title: Deploy with GitHub Actions — The generated workflow
text:
```yaml
name: 🚀 Build and deploy

on:
  push:
    tags:
      - '*'
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      version:
        required: true
        type: string
        description: 'Version to release'

jobs:
  build-and-deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
    - uses: actions/checkout@v3

    - name: 🔄 Setup pnpm
      uses: pnpm/action-setup@v4
      with:
        version: 10

    - name: ⚙️ Setup Node.js
      uses: actions/setup-node@v4
      with:
        node-version: '23.11.1'
        cache: 'pnpm'
        cache-dependency-path: '**/pnpm-lock.yaml'

    - name: 🔧 Install Dependencies
      run: pnpm install

    - name: 🏗️ Build
      run: pnpm build

    - name: 🚀 Publish to Flightroom
      uses: mfe-orchestrator-hub/github-action@0.0.29
      with:
        apikey: ${{ secrets.MICROFRONTEND_ORCHESTRATOR_API_KEY }}
        microfrontend-slug: catalog
        domain: ${{ vars.MICROFRONTEND_ORCHESTRATOR_DOMAIN || 'https://console.flightroom.dev' }}
        file-path: './dist'
        version: ${{ inputs.version || github.ref_name }}
```

The `microfrontend-slug` and `domain` values are substituted for you at scaffold time — the slug you
chose, and the API base URL of the installation you created it from. The domain stays overridable
afterwards: set a `MICROFRONTEND_ORCHESTRATOR_DOMAIN` repository variable
(**Settings ▸ Secrets and variables ▸ Actions ▸ Variables**) and the workflow publishes there
instead, without you having to edit the YAML.

title: Deploy with GitHub Actions — Two ways to trigger it
text:
**Push a tag.** The version is the tag name:

```bash
git tag 1.4.0
git push origin 1.4.0
```

**Run it manually.** From the Actions tab, or from the console's **Build** action on the
frontend card, which creates the tag for you — see
[Versions and builds](../frontends/versions-and-builds.md).

Tag-driven versioning is what makes the console's **Build** button work, so keep the tag trigger even
if you add others.

title: Deploy with GitHub Actions — The publish action
text:
| Input | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `apikey` | A Flightroom [API key](./api-keys.md) |
| `microfrontend-slug` | The slug of the frontend to publish to |
| `domain` | Base URL of your Flightroom installation |
| `file-path` | The build output directory, e.g. `./dist` |
| `version` | The version to publish |

The action zips `file-path` and calls the [upload endpoint](./manual-upload.md). Point it at the
directory, not at a zip you made yourself.

title: Deploy with GitHub Actions — The secret
text:
The workflow reads `secrets.MICROFRONTEND_ORCHESTRATOR_API_KEY`. It is created when you **connect**
the GitHub repository to a project — or edit that connection — not when a frontend is
scaffolded, and it is written as an **organization** secret visible to all repositories. Creating a
second frontend does not create a second key: the injector skips the work when a secret of that
name already exists.

:::caution[A personal GitHub account gets no organization secret]
The injector needs an organization id and returns without doing anything when the connection is to a
personal account. For repositories the console creates itself it falls back to a repository secret,
so those still work — but a pipeline you added to a repository you connected by hand has no secret at
all, and its publish step fails with an authentication error on the first run.

Fix it by hand: create an [API key](./api-keys.md), then add it under
**Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions** as `MICROFRONTEND_ORCHESTRATOR_API_KEY`.
:::

:::note[The key is dated 15 days out, and keeps working anyway]
The generated key expires after a year, and an expired key is refused with *API key expired*.
Keys generated by older versions of the platform expired after 365 *hours*, about fifteen days: if a
publish fails that way, create a new key and update the pipeline secret. See
[Expiry](./api-keys.md#expiry).
:::

title: Deploy with GitHub Actions — Adding this to an existing repository
text:
For a repository Flightroom did not create:

1. Create an [API key](./api-keys.md).
2. Add it as a repository secret named `MICROFRONTEND_ORCHESTRATOR_API_KEY`
   (**Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions**).
3. Copy the workflow above into `.github/workflows/build-and-deploy.yml`, replacing
   `microfrontend-slug` and `domain` with your values.
4. Adjust the package manager and build command if you do not use pnpm.

Ready-made variants for other compilers and host types are in
[`template-pipelines`](https://github.com/mfe-orchestrator/template-pipelines), under
`<type>/<compiler>/github/`.

title: Deploy with GitHub Actions — Adapting it
text:
**npm or yarn instead of pnpm** — replace the pnpm setup and `pnpm install` / `pnpm build` with
`npm ci` / `npm run build`, and set `cache: 'npm'`.

**A monorepo** — build only the package that changed and point `file-path` at that package's output,
e.g. `./packages/catalog/dist`. Publishing several frontends from one repository means one
publish step per frontend, each with its own slug.

**Tests before publishing** — add the step between build and publish. A failing test then stops the
release, which is the behaviour you want.

**Deploying automatically** — the workflow cannot do it with the API key it already holds:
`POST /deployment` is authenticated with a signed-in user's token, while an API key
authenticates the upload endpoint only. Automating a development environment therefore means
supplying a user token of your own. For production, leave the deployment manual; the separation
between *published* and *live* is the platform's main safety property.

title: Deploy with GitHub Actions — Troubleshooting
text:
**Publish step fails with an authentication error**

The secret is missing, misnamed, or names a key that has been deleted, revoked or has expired. Check
the exact spelling of `MICROFRONTEND_ORCHESTRATOR_API_KEY`, and that the key still exists in
**Settings → Access → API Keys** without an **Expired** badge: the error message says *API key
expired on …* or *API key revoked* when that is the cause. On a personal GitHub account, suspect the
missing organization secret described above.

**"Entity not found" for the slug**

`microfrontend-slug` does not match a frontend in the key's project. Slugs are lowercase; check
for a typo or a stale value after a rename.

**Publishes, but the app still serves the old version**

Publishing is not deploying. Select the version and
[deploy](../deployments/overview.md) the environment.

**Publishes, but requests 404**

Almost always the **Entry Point** on the frontend not matching the build output. Vite Module
Federation emits `assets/remoteEntry.js`; Webpack emits `remoteEntry.js`.

**Workflow does not run**

The generated workflow triggers only on tags and manual dispatch. A push to `main` does nothing by
design.

title: Deploy with GitLab CI
text:
When Flightroom creates a repository from a template in GitLab, it commits a `.gitlab-ci.yml`
and creates a group-level CI/CD variable holding the deploy key.

title: Deploy with GitLab CI — The generated pipeline
text:
The scaffolded `.gitlab-ci.yml` covers install, test and build:

```yaml
stages:
  - install
  - lint
  - test
  - build

variables:
  PNPM_VERSION: "9.15.0"
  NODE_VERSION: "20"

.pnpm_cache:
  cache:
    key:
      files:
        - pnpm-lock.yaml
    paths:
      - .pnpm-store
  before_script:
    - corepack enable
    - corepack prepare pnpm@${PNPM_VERSION} --activate
    - pnpm config set store-dir .pnpm-store
    - pnpm install --frozen-lockfile

install:
  stage: install
  image: node:${NODE_VERSION}
  extends: .pnpm_cache
  script:
    - echo "Dependencies installed"
  artifacts:
    paths:
      - node_modules/
      - .pnpm-store
    expire_in: 1 hour

test:
  stage: test
  image: node:${NODE_VERSION}
  extends: .pnpm_cache
  dependencies:
    - install
  script:
    - pnpm run test
  coverage: '/All files[^|]*\|[^|]*\s+([\d\.]+)/'
  artifacts:
    when: always
    reports:
      junit:
        - coverage/junit.xml
      coverage_report:
        coverage_format: cobertura
        path: coverage/cobertura-coverage.xml
  allow_failure: false

build:
  stage: build
  image: node:${NODE_VERSION}
  extends: .pnpm_cache
  dependencies:
    - install
  script:
    - pnpm run build
  artifacts:
    paths:
      - dist/
    expire_in: 7 days
  only:
    - main
    - develop
    - tags
```

:::caution[Host repositories stop at build]
Frontend repositories get the `deploy` stage below already committed. Host repositories do not
— like their GitHub and Azure DevOps counterparts they build and containerise, but do not publish
themselves to Flightroom. Add the job below if you want a host published as a remote too.
:::

title: Deploy with GitLab CI — The publish job
text:
A `deploy` stage uploads the built `dist/` on tags:

```yaml
stages:
  - install
  - lint
  - test
  - build
  - deploy

deploy:
  stage: deploy
  image: alpine:latest
  dependencies:
    - build
  variables:
    FRONTEND_SLUG: "catalog"
    MICROFRONTEND_ORCHESTRATOR_DOMAIN: "https://console.flightroom.dev"
  before_script:
    - apk add --no-cache curl zip
  script:
    - cd dist && zip -qr ../dist.zip . && cd ..
    - |
      curl --fail --show-error --silent -X POST \
        -H "api-key: ${MICROFRONTEND_ORCHESTRATOR_API_KEY}" \
        -F "file=@dist.zip" \
        "${MICROFRONTEND_ORCHESTRATOR_DOMAIN%/}/api/frontends/by-slug/${FRONTEND_SLUG}/upload/${CI_COMMIT_TAG}"
    - echo "published ${FRONTEND_SLUG} ${CI_COMMIT_TAG}"
  only:
    - tags
```

The template in
[`template-pipelines`](https://github.com/mfe-orchestrator/template-pipelines) carries two
placeholders, which the scaffolder replaces before the initial commit, as it does on GitHub:

| Placeholder | Replaced with |
| --- | --- |
| `%microfrontendSlug%` | The slug of the frontend, as it appears in the console |
| `%domain%` | The value of the installation's `BACKEND_URL`, inserted verbatim; `https://console.flightroom.dev` when `BACKEND_URL` is not set |

If you add this job to a repository by hand, write those two values in yourself.

:::caution[`%domain%` is the API URL, and the job appends `/api` to it]
`BACKEND_URL` is the public URL of the **API** — usually the console URL followed by `/api` — and
the scaffolder copies it into `%domain%` as it is, without removing anything. The job above then
appends `/api/frontends/…`, so an installation whose `BACKEND_URL` ends in `/api` produces
uploads to `…/api/api/frontends/…`, which fail. Two more cases to check:

- With `BACKEND_URL` unset, `%domain%` is `https://console.flightroom.dev` — not your installation,
  even if `FRONTEND_URL` is set.
- Either way, the fix is the same: make `MICROFRONTEND_ORCHESTRATOR_DOMAIN` the console URL
  **without** `/api` (e.g. `https://console.example.com`), in the file or as a project CI/CD
  variable.
:::

Both are plain job variables, so a **project** CI/CD variable of the same name wins over them: once
the YAML is correct you can set `MICROFRONTEND_ORCHESTRATOR_DOMAIN` in the project settings to publish
somewhere else without touching the file again.

Points worth noting:

- `only: tags` keeps publishing tied to tags, which is what makes the console's **Build** action work
  — see [Versions and builds](../frontends/versions-and-builds.md).
- `CI_COMMIT_TAG` is the version. It is only set on tag pipelines, which is another reason for
  `only: tags`.
- `--fail` on `curl` is essential: without it the job passes even when the upload is rejected.
- The `zip` is created from **inside** `dist`, so the archive has no directory prefix. See
  [Uploading a build](./manual-upload.md) for why this matters.

title: Deploy with GitLab CI — The CI/CD variable
text:
The job reads `MICROFRONTEND_ORCHESTRATOR_API_KEY`. It is created as a **group-level** CI/CD variable
when you connect the GitLab repository to a project — or edit that connection — not when a
frontend is scaffolded, and it is skipped if a variable of that name already exists in the group.

Group scope means every frontend repository in that GitLab group can publish without further
setup. It also means the connection must have a group selected: without a group id the injector
returns without creating anything.

:::note[The key is dated 15 days out, and keeps working anyway]
The generated key expires after a year, and an expired key is refused with *API key expired*.
Keys generated by older versions of the platform expired after 365 *hours*, about fifteen days: if a
publish fails that way, create a new key and update the pipeline secret. See
[Expiry](./api-keys.md#expiry).
:::

:::caution[Protected variables and tags]
If you mark the variable as **Protected**, it is only exposed to pipelines on protected branches and
tags. Since publishing happens on tags, protect your release tag pattern
(**Settings → Repository → Protected tags**) or the variable will be empty in the deploy job.
:::

title: Deploy with GitLab CI — Publishing a version
text:
```bash
git tag 1.4.0
git push origin 1.4.0
```

Or use the **Build** action on the frontend card in the console, which creates the tag for you.

title: Deploy with GitLab CI — Adding this to an existing repository
text:
1. Create an [API key](./api-keys.md).
2. Add it as a CI/CD variable named `MICROFRONTEND_ORCHESTRATOR_API_KEY`, at group or project level
   (**Settings → CI/CD → Variables**). Mark it **Masked**.
3. Add the `deploy` job above to your `.gitlab-ci.yml`, with your slug and API base URL.
4. If the variable is protected, protect your tag pattern too.

Base pipelines for other compilers and host types are in
[`template-pipelines`](https://github.com/mfe-orchestrator/template-pipelines) under
`<type>/<compiler>/gitlab/`.

title: Deploy with GitLab CI — Troubleshooting
text:
**Deploy job does not run**

`only: tags` means branch pushes skip it. Confirm you pushed a tag.

**The upload URL contains `%domain%`, or the slug is `%microfrontendSlug%`**

The repository was scaffolded by a console older than the one that replaces the placeholders on
GitLab, or the job was copied by hand from `template-pipelines`. Replace them as described
[above](#the-publish-job).

**The upload URL contains `/api/api/`, or points at the wrong installation**

`%domain%` was filled from `BACKEND_URL`, which already ends in `/api`, or from the default used
when `BACKEND_URL` is unset. Set `MICROFRONTEND_ORCHESTRATOR_DOMAIN` to the console URL without
`/api` — see [the caution above](#the-publish-job).

**`api-key` empty / authentication failure**

Either the variable is not defined at a scope the project can see, or it is **Protected** and the tag
is not. Check both, and confirm the key still exists in **Settings → Access → API Keys** and is not
**Expired**: an expired or revoked key is refused, with *API key expired on …* or *API key revoked*.

**`dist/` missing in the deploy job**

The `dependencies: [build]` declaration is what carries the artifact across stages. Also check the
`build` job's `expire_in` has not lapsed for a re-run of an old pipeline.

**Upload succeeds, app 404s**

The **Entry Point** on the frontend does not match the build output. Vite Module Federation
emits `assets/remoteEntry.js`.

**Upload succeeds, users see the old version**

Publishing is not deploying — [deploy the environment](../deployments/overview.md).

title: Upload a build from any CI system
text:
Everything the provider-specific pipelines do reduces to one HTTP call. This page documents it, so
you can publish from any CI system — or from your laptop when debugging.

title: Upload a build from any CI system — The endpoint
text:
```http
POST /frontends/by-slug/{frontendSlug}/upload/{version}
```

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Authentication** | `api-key` header (see [API keys](./api-keys.md)) |
| **Body** | `multipart/form-data` with a single ZIP file |
| **Project** | Derived from the API key — no `project-id` header needed |

title: Upload a build from any CI system — Minimal example
text:
```bash
cd dist
zip -r ../dist.zip .
cd ..

curl -X POST \
  -H "api-key: $MFE_ORCHESTRATOR_API_KEY" \
  -F "file=@dist.zip" \
  "https://console.flightroom.dev/api/frontends/by-slug/catalog/upload/1.4.0"
```

title: Upload a build from any CI system — Zipping correctly
text:
This is where most first attempts go wrong. The archive must contain the **contents** of your build
output, not the folder itself:

```
✅ dist.zip
   ├── index.html
   └── assets/
       └── remoteEntry.js

❌ dist.zip
   └── dist/
       ├── index.html
       └── assets/
           └── remoteEntry.js
```

The second produces an entry point at `dist/assets/remoteEntry.js`, which does not match the
configured entry point, and every request 404s.

```bash

cd dist && zip -r ../dist.zip . && cd ..

# ❌ zips the directory itself
zip -r dist.zip dist
```

Verify before uploading:

```bash
unzip -l dist.zip | head
```

The first entries should be your files, not a directory prefix.

title: Upload a build from any CI system — Requirements and behaviour
text:
- The file must be a **ZIP**: it is accepted when its MIME type is `application/zip` **or** its
  file name ends in `.zip`, and rejected only when neither holds.
- The frontend must already exist in the project, matched by **slug**.
- The archive is extracted into the version's folder, wherever that frontend is
  [hosted](../frontends/hosting-options.md) — the platform's own storage or your bucket.
- Uploading a version that already exists overwrites its files in place. The target folder is not
  cleaned first, so a file that was in the previous upload and is absent from the new one survives
  under the same version and is still served.
- **Custom URL** frontends cannot be uploaded to; the request fails. Publishing is entirely
  yours in that case.
- Frontends served by **their own Docker container** cannot be uploaded to either: the request
  fails with `DOCKER_FRONTEND_UPLOAD_NOT_ALLOWED`. Their pipeline registers the version of the pushed image
  instead — see [what a key can call](./api-keys.md#what-a-key-can-call).

:::caution[Overwriting a deployed version]
Re-uploading a version that some environment is currently serving changes what those users get,
without any deployment. Publish a new version instead — versions are cheap, and it keeps rollback
meaningful.
:::

title: Upload a build from any CI system — Publishing does not deploy
text:
After a successful upload the version exists and is selectable, but nothing changes for your users.
Select the version on the frontend and [deploy](../deployments/overview.md) the environment.

:::caution[An API key cannot deploy]
`POST /api/deployment` — the endpoint behind the **Deploy** button, which takes
`{ "environmentIds": ["…"] }` — is authenticated with the token of a signed-in user. An API key
authenticates the upload endpoint and nothing else, so a pipeline holding one can publish a version
but cannot make it live. Automating the deployment of a development environment means driving that
call with a user token of your own, obtained outside the CI key mechanism.
:::

For production the manual step is the point: the separation between *published* and *live* is the
platform's main safety property.

title: Upload a build from any CI system — A generic pipeline step
text:
For a CI system with no dedicated integration:

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

: "${MFE_ORCHESTRATOR_API_KEY:?missing API key}"
: "${VERSION:?missing version}"

SLUG="catalog"
API_BASE="https://console.flightroom.dev/api"

npm ci
npm run build

( cd dist && zip -qr ../dist.zip . )

curl --fail --show-error --silent \
  -X POST \
  -H "api-key: ${MFE_ORCHESTRATOR_API_KEY}" \
  -F "file=@dist.zip" \
  "${API_BASE}/frontends/by-slug/${SLUG}/upload/${VERSION}"

echo "published ${SLUG} ${VERSION}"
```

`--fail` matters: without it `curl` exits 0 on an HTTP error and your pipeline reports a green build
that published nothing.

Deriving `VERSION` from the Git tag keeps the version and the source in step:

```bash
VERSION="${GITHUB_REF_NAME}"      # GitHub Actions
VERSION="${CI_COMMIT_TAG}"        # GitLab CI
VERSION="${BUILD_SOURCEBRANCHNAME}"  # Azure DevOps
```

title: Upload a build from any CI system — Troubleshooting
text:
| Symptom | Cause |
| --- | --- |
| `401` / authentication error | Missing, wrong, revoked or **expired** `api-key` |
| `File must be a ZIP archive` | Wrong MIME type or extension — send a real `.zip` |
| Entity not found for the slug | No frontend with that slug in the key's project |
| `Frontend host type is not supported` | The frontend is **Custom URL** |
| Upload succeeds, app 404s | Entry point mismatch, or the ZIP has a directory prefix |
| Upload succeeds, users see the old version | You have not deployed |

For the entry point: Vite Module Federation emits `assets/remoteEntry.js`, Webpack emits
`remoteEntry.js`. The **Entry Point** field on the frontend must match what your build actually
produces.

title: Core concepts and object model
text:
Before diving into the individual features, it helps to understand the handful of objects
Flightroom is built around. Everything you do in the console — and every call you make
to the API — maps onto one of them.

:::info[Apps and agents, in the console's words]
The site talks about *apps* and *AI agents*. The console names what they are made of: a web
interface is a **frontend**, a backend is a **service**, and an agent is a service that calls
the AI model your organization chose. A **functional domain** groups the frontends and
services of one business capability. There is no separate agent runtime: an agent is built,
reviewed and deployed like any other service.
:::

:::tip[Prefer a picture?]
[Architecture](./architecture.md) draws the same objects as running components: the orchestrator,
its database, the storage options and how a deployment reaches each environment.
:::

title: Core concepts and object model — The object model
text:
```
Organization
├── Members (Owner, Admin, Member)
├── AI (the models the organization may use)
└── Project
    ├── Functional domain (groups frontends and services)
    ├── Frontend (web interface: served by Flightroom, or as a Docker container)
    │   └── Built version (one record per bundle or image)
    ├── Service (backend or agent, runs as a Docker container)
    │   └── Config maps and Secrets (one value per environment)
    ├── Environment (dev, uat, prod, …; a Kubernetes namespace each)
    │   ├── Environment Variables (key/value, read by the browser)
    │   └── Deployment #1, #2, #3 …  (immutable snapshots)
    ├── Code Repository (GitHub, GitLab, Azure DevOps)
    ├── Database (registered connections, tested from the console)
    ├── Storage / Bucket (S3, Azure Blob, GCS)
    ├── API Key (for CI/CD, automation and MCP clients)
    └── Members (Admin, Editor, Viewer)
```

One line in that tree is worth expanding, because the console does not spell it out. A
frontend carries a single `version` field: the version *currently selected*, the one the next
deployment would freeze. The versions you can select are separate records, one per bundle that has
reached the platform, keyed by frontend and version string. That is why the version of a
frontend is a list you pick from rather than free text, and why a version stays selectable long
after another has been deployed over it.

### Organization

An **organization** is the tenant that owns projects. A project belongs to exactly one organization,
and a user can belong to any number of them with a different role in each. It is the level that
decides *which projects a person can reach at all*: whoever administers the organization
(`OWNER`, `ADMIN`) reaches every project inside it, while a plain `MEMBER` reaches only the projects
they were explicitly invited to.

The organization is selected in the console header, and it scopes everything below it — the project
switcher only offers projects of the organization you are in. See
[Organizations](./organizations/overview.md).

### AI

An **AI** is a model the organization allows Flightroom to use, with the organization's own
credentials: Claude through Anthropic, Azure AI Foundry or AWS Bedrock, GPT through Azure OpenAI,
or Gemini. Organization owners and admins add them under **Organization settings → AI**, and can
restrict a project to some of them or turn AI off for it. A self-hosted installation can also
provide a read-only **System AI** from its configuration. See
[AI models](./build-with-ai/ai-models.md).

### Project

A **project** is the container every configuration object belongs to, and the boundary the project
roles are written against: frontends, environments, storages, repositories and API keys belong
to exactly one project. A project has a `name`, a `slug` and an `id` — all three, plus its free-text
`description`, live under **Settings → General → Project Information**, where only the name and the
description can be edited. The same tab holds the project's AI `context`, under **Project AI
context**, and **Settings → Delivery** holds its `gitOps`, `exposure` and `pipelines` settings. Two
more fields are not editable anywhere in the console: the `organizationId` of the organization that
owns it, fixed at creation, and an `isActive` flag. See
[Projects and access control](./project-settings/projects.md#project-settings).

Access to a project is granted either by an explicit project membership or by administering the
organization that owns it — see
[Organization roles and project visibility](./organizations/roles-and-visibility.md).

When you call the API directly, the project is selected with the `project-id` HTTP header.

### Environment

An **environment** is a deployment stage inside a project — typically `dev`, `uat` and `prod`,
but you can define as many as you like. Each environment has:

| Field | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `name` | Display name, e.g. *Production* |
| `description` | Free text |
| `slug` | URL-friendly identifier used in the public serve API, e.g. `prod` |
| `color` | Colour used to tag the environment throughout the console |
| `isProduction` | Marks the environment as a production stage |
| `domains` | The domains your application is served from — used to resolve which environment a browser request belongs to |
| `order` | Sort order in the environment selector |

The `slug` is unique within a project. When you deploy to Kubernetes, each environment also
maps to a **Kubernetes namespace** (by default its slug) and can carry a **subdomain** its apps
answer on — see [Deploy to Kubernetes](./kubernetes/overview.md).

:::info[Why domains matter]
Some public endpoints resolve the environment automatically from the browser's `Referer`
header, by matching it against the environment's **Allowed Domains**. This is what lets a
single frontend URL serve the right version to `app.example.com` and to
`staging.example.com`. See [Environments → Allowed domains](./environments/domains.md).
:::

### Functional domain

A **functional domain** groups the frontends and services that work on the same business
capability, such as *Payments* or *Onboarding*. It is the natural unit for building with AI: on an
empty domain, one request makes the AI propose the components it needs and create their
repositories, and a single AI job can change every repository of the domain at once. A domain can
also be deployed on its own. See [Generate a domain with AI](./build-with-ai/generate-a-domain.md).

### Service

A **service** is a backend that runs as a Docker container: an API, a worker, or an agent that
reasons with your AI model and calls your systems. New services start from a template — Node.js &
Fastify, Python & FastAPI, Spring Boot or Quarkus — with health checks and an OpenAPI description
already in place. Its configuration comes from **config maps** and **secrets**, one value per
environment, delivered as environment variables. See
[Deploy to Kubernetes](./kubernetes/overview.md).

### Frontend

A **frontend** is a web interface registered in a project. Its **kind** says how it is
served: **Bundle**, a static bundle served by Flightroom, or **Docker**, its own Docker container
deployed to Kubernetes like a service. A frontend served by Flightroom is either:

- a **host** — the shell application that loads other frontends, or
- a **remote** — a frontend consumed by a host.

Hosts and remotes are wired together by declaring parent/child relations in the console, and
Flightroom turns those relations into the `remotes` block of your Module Federation
configuration.

![The frontends of a project, drawn as a host with its remotes](./assets/frontends-diagram-view.png)

Each frontend has a `slug` (unique per project), a `version`, and a **hosting type** that
tells the platform where its files actually live. See
[Frontends → Hosting options](./frontends/hosting-options.md).

### Environment variable

An **environment variable** (also called a *global variable*) is a `key`/`value` pair scoped to
a single environment. Unlike build-time variables baked into your bundle, these are read at
runtime by the browser, which means the same artifact can be promoted from `uat` to `prod`
without a rebuild. See [Runtime configuration](./integration/runtime-configuration.md).

### Storage (bucket)

A **storage** is a connection to an object storage bucket you own — Amazon S3, Azure Blob
Storage or Google Cloud Storage. Frontend builds can be uploaded to your own bucket
instead of to the hub, which keeps your artifacts inside your own cloud account. See
[Buckets](./buckets/overview.md).

### Code repository

A **code repository** is a connection to GitHub, GitLab or Azure DevOps. With one connected,
Flightroom can scaffold a new repository from a template, inject a build pipeline, and
create the deploy secret the pipeline needs. It is also where the AI writes: every AI change is
pushed to a branch of one of these repositories. See [Code Repositories](./repositories/connect/github.md).

### Deployment

A **deployment** is an immutable snapshot of everything an environment needs at a point in
time: the full list of frontends with their versions and hosting configuration, the
environment's variables, and the storage configuration.

This is the single most important idea in Flightroom:

:::tip[Editing is not deploying]
Changing a frontend's version, adding a variable, or connecting a bucket does **not**
affect what your users see. Those changes sit in the project configuration until you press
**Deploy**, which freezes them into a new snapshot and activates it.
:::

Deployments are numbered per environment (`#1`, `#2`, `#3` …) and exactly one of them is
**active** at any time. Because a snapshot is immutable, rolling back is just a matter of
re-activating an older one. See [Deployments](./deployments/overview.md).

![A deployment snapshot with the versions and variables it froze](./assets/deployments-overview.png)

### API key

An **API key** authenticates machines rather than people — CI pipelines, scripts, deploy jobs.
Keys are project-scoped, and they are shown once at creation and stored hashed. They also carry a
role and an expiry date. The console creates `MANAGER` keys; the role is read by the
[MCP server](./build-with-ai/mcp-server.md) and when CI registers the version of a service or a
Docker frontend. An expired or revoked key is refused. Treat a key as access to its project until it
expires, and see
[API Keys](./ci-cd/api-keys.md).

### Members and roles

Membership is recorded at two levels, and both are checked.

At **organization** level, the role decides which projects a person reaches:

| Role | In the API | Reaches |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Owner | `OWNER` | Every project of the organization; can also delete it and hand over ownership |
| Admin | `ADMIN` | Every project of the organization; can manage members and create projects |
| Member | `MEMBER` | Only the projects they were invited to |

At **project** level, the role decides what they can do inside one:

| Role | In the API | Can do |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Admin | `OWNER` | Everything, including managing members and the GitOps and Argo CD settings |
| Editor | `MEMBER` | Build with AI, manage frontends, services, variables and storages, and deploy |
| Viewer | `VIEWER` | Cannot use the AI, create repositories, change storages or databases, or deploy with GitOps on. Other project settings are not role-checked |

See [Roles and project visibility](./organizations/roles-and-visibility.md) and
[Members and roles](./project-settings/users-and-roles.md).

title: Core concepts and object model — The lifecycle of a change
text:
Putting it together, this is the path a change takes from a request to a running app on
Kubernetes:

```
1. Describe              A project member asks for an app, an agent or a
      │                  change, on a domain, frontend or service
      │
2. Propose               The AI writes it on an ai/… branch of your
      │                  repositories; your CI checks the branch
      │
3. Review                Open a pull request, or apply it where branch
      │                  protection allows; or discard it
      │
4. Deploy                One click commits manifests and Helm values to
      │                  your GitOps repositories
      │
5. Sync                  Argo CD applies the commit; the app answers on its
                         URL in that environment, with TLS
```

Steps 1 to 3 are described in [Build with AI](./build-with-ai/overview.md), steps 4 and 5 in
[Deploy to Kubernetes](./kubernetes/overview.md).

For a frontend served by Flightroom, the path from commit to browser is different:

```
1. Commit                Your frontend repository
      │
2. Build & upload        CI builds the bundle and uploads it to
      │                  Flightroom (hub or your own bucket),
      │                  tagged with a version
      │
3. Register version      The version becomes selectable on the
      │                  frontend in the console
      │
4. Deploy                You create a deployment for an environment,
      │                  snapshotting versions + variables
      │
5. Serve                 The host application asks the public serve API
                         which URLs to load; the active deployment answers
```

Steps 2 and 3 are automated by the pipelines Flightroom injects into your repository —
see [CI/CD](./ci-cd/api-keys.md). Step 5 is described in
[Integration](./integration/overview.md).

title: Core concepts and object model — Two ways to run the platform
text:
Everything above applies identically whether you use the hosted console at
[console.flightroom.dev](https://console.flightroom.dev) or run the container
yourself. The only difference is the base URL of the API:

| Setup | API base URL |
| --- | --- |
| Hosted console | `https://console.flightroom.dev/api` |
| Self-hosted | `/api`, or `BACKEND_URL` if you set it explicitly |

Throughout this documentation, `` refers to whichever of the two applies to you.

title: Build status of your frontends
text:
Every frontend is built by the CI of the provider its repository lives on. Without a place
that collects those runs, checking whether the last pipeline passed means one browser tab per
repository.

The **Builds** page is that place: one row per frontend and per backend service, the outcome
of its latest run, the recent history behind it, and the version each environment is currently
serving.

![The Builds page: one row per frontend and backend service, with its type, last build, last built version and the version each environment serves](../assets/builds-page.png)

:::info[Nothing is stored]
The runs are read from the providers when you open the page, and re-read while you keep it open.
Flightroom keeps no build history of its own, so the page shows what the providers show and
nothing more.
:::

title: Build status of your frontends — Reading the table
text:
One row per frontend of the current project, then one per backend service, each group sorted
by name:

| Column | Content |
| --- | --- |
| **Name** | Name and slug |
| **Type** | **Frontend** or **Backend** (a service) |
| **Last build** | Status label of the most recent run, with a link to it on the provider, or why no run could be read |
| **Tag / branch** | The ref that run was started from, tags included |
| **Last built version** | The most recent version whose bundle actually reached the platform |
| One column per environment | The version that environment serves — for a frontend, taken from its **active deployment** |

The environment columns come after the fixed ones, in the order the environments are configured on
the project, and the production one is flagged with a badge.

Three version columns sound redundant until an incident makes the difference matter:

- **Last built version** is the newest bundle uploaded to the platform.
- The **environment columns** are what a [deployment](./overview.md) froze. A deployment ships a
  fixed set of versions, so an environment keeps serving what it was given even after a newer
  bundle exists.
- Expand a row and a third one appears, the **selected version**: what the frontend currently
  points at, which is what the next deployment would pick up.

A newer *last built version* than the one in the production column is not a fault — it is the gap
between "built" and "deployed", and this page is where you see it.

Expanding a row also shows the repository the frontend is linked to and the **last five runs**
of that repository, newest first, each with its status, ref, workflow name, start moment, who
started it, and a link to the run on the provider. *Who started it* never appears on GitLab: the
pipelines list endpoint does not carry it, so the field is left unset and the run is shown without
it.

title: Build status of your frontends — Status labels
text:
Each provider describes a run in its own vocabulary; the console reduces all of them to six
statuses. The API returns the code in the first column, the page shows the label in the second.

| Status | Label | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `QUEUED` | Queued | Accepted but not started — including a GitLab pipeline waiting on a manual action |
| `RUNNING` | Running | In progress |
| `SUCCESS` | Succeeded | Finished and passed (Azure `partiallySucceeded` counts as passed) |
| `FAILED` | Failed | Finished and failed, timed out, or failed to start |
| `CANCELED` | Canceled | Canceled or skipped — and a GitHub run whose conclusion is `neutral` |
