| `UNKNOWN` | Unknown | The provider reported a state this platform does not know |

When the project has an AI provider, a **Failed** run in an expanded row carries **Explain the
failure**, which asks the [console assistant](../build-with-ai/console-assistant.md) to read the logs
of the failed jobs, explain the cause and suggest a fix.

A run still in progress is `RUNNING`, whatever result the provider left on it from a previous
attempt: GitHub and Azure DevOps both split the outcome over two fields, and the second one only
means something once the first says the run is over.

Cancellation is the exception, on both providers that report it as a state of its own. Azure DevOps
`cancelling` and GitLab `canceling` are runs that have not finished yet, and both are shown as
**Canceled** rather than **Running**, because the outcome is already decided.

title: Build status of your frontends — When a row has no runs
text:
A row without runs says why, instead of showing an empty history:

| Reason | Shown as | Cause |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `NO_REPOSITORY` | No linked repository | No code repository is connected to the frontend or service, or the connection is disabled |
| `REPOSITORY_NOT_FOUND` | Linked repository not found | It points at a code repository connection that no longer exists |
| `PROVIDER_ERROR` | Unable to read builds from the provider | The provider call failed — revoked token, network error, missing Azure configuration |

`PROVIDER_ERROR` is confined to the row that produced it: one unreachable provider never blanks the
page, and the row keeps its versions. A frontend whose repository is reachable but has never
run a pipeline carries no reason at all and an empty run list.

title: Build status of your frontends — Where the runs come from
text:
The runs are read through the [code repository connection](../repositories/connect/github.md) the
frontend points at, with the token stored on that connection:

| Provider | Addressed by | Read from |
| --- | --- | --- |
| GitHub | The repository **name**, under the organization or user of the connection | `GET /repos/:owner/:repo/actions/runs` |
| GitLab | The repository **id** | `GET /projects/:id/pipelines` |
| Azure DevOps | The repository **id**, inside the organization and project of the connection | `GET /_apis/build/builds?repositoryId=…&repositoryType=TfsGit` |

Runs are read repository-wide: every workflow, pipeline or build definition attached to the
repository is in scope, and there is no way to select "the build pipeline" among them.

title: Build status of your frontends — Live updates
text:
The page opens a Server-Sent Events stream and keeps it for as long as it stays open. The header
shows whether the stream is connected and the moment of the last snapshot received.

Two things are worth knowing about what "live" means here:

- The server re-reads the providers **every 15 seconds** and only sends a frame when something
  actually changed. No provider webhook is involved, so a run that starts is visible within 15
  seconds, not instantly.
- A snapshot is reused for 15 seconds and shared by everyone watching the same project, so
  **Refresh** inside that window returns the cached snapshot rather than hammering the provider.
  The *last update* moment is when the snapshot was read, which is how you tell a fresh one from a
  reused one.

A provider failure during a poll ends that round, not the connection: the last snapshot stays on
screen and the next poll retries.

title: Build status of your frontends — API
text:
Both endpoints are authenticated and scoped to the project carried by the `Project-Id` header.

| Method | Path | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `GET` | `/api/builds` | Current build status of the project, as one snapshot |
| `GET` | `/api/builds/stream` | The same snapshot, pushed over SSE as it changes |

Neither takes a query parameter or a body. The snapshot carries the environments of the project,
then a `frontends` and a `services` list; each entry has its `selectedVersion`,
`latestBuiltVersion`, a `versionByEnvironmentId` map and up to five `builds`, and one that could not
be read carries `unavailableReason` and an empty `builds`. For a service, `latestBuiltVersion` is the
last image its CI registered and the environment versions are the latest deploys its pipeline
reported there.

:::note[`EventSource` cannot be used]
The API requires an `Authorization` and a `Project-Id` header on every call — the console sends an
`issuer` header alongside them, naming the identity provider the token came from — and `EventSource`
cannot send any of them. Consume the stream with `fetch`, as the console does.
:::

title: Build status of your frontends — Limits worth knowing
text:
- Only the **last five runs** per frontend are read, and only for the repository as a whole.
- On Azure DevOps only builds of **Azure Repos Git** repositories are matched; a pipeline defined
  on a repository hosted elsewhere is not listed.
- Nothing is persisted: no trend, no duration, no failure rate.
- The status is at most 15 seconds old.
- A token without access to the CI of a repository yields `PROVIDER_ERROR` even when the repository
  itself is readable.

title: Build status of your frontends — Where to go next
text:
- [Versions and builds](../frontends/versions-and-builds.md) — how a version comes into
  existence and reaches the platform
- [Deployments overview](./overview.md) — turning built versions into what an environment serves

title: Deployments overview
text:
A **deployment** is an immutable snapshot of everything an environment needs, taken at the moment
you press **Deploy** and activated for your users.

This is the mechanism that makes the rest of the platform safe to use. Understanding it is worth
five minutes.

title: Deployments overview — What gets captured
text:
When you deploy an environment, Flightroom copies into the snapshot:

- **Every frontend** in the project — its selected version, hosting configuration, entry
  point, canary settings and relation graph
- **Every backend service** of the project — its name, slug, domain, image and the version its CI
  registered last
- **Every config map and secret** of the project, as they apply to that environment: the keys set
  for it, with their values for a config map and **key names only** for a secret
- **Every environment variable** of that environment
- **Every storage configuration** of the project

The snapshot is a copy, not a set of references. Editing a frontend afterwards does not
reach back into it.

### Deploying one domain

A deploy limited to a [functional domain](../core-concepts.md#functional-domain) — and any deploy by
a member whose access is limited to specific domains — ships only the frontends and services of
those domains. Everything else the environment serves, environment variables and storages included,
is carried over unchanged from the deployment it is serving now, so one team's deploy never ships
what another domain has not released yet. Config maps and secrets are still recorded for the whole
project.

title: Deployments overview — Editing is not deploying
text:
The single most important consequence:

:::tip
Changes you make in the console — a version bump, a new variable, a rewired remote, a bucket
swap — are **drafts**. They sit in the project configuration and affect nothing until you deploy
the environment you want them in.
:::

This is why the same project can serve `1.2.0` to production while you stage `1.4.0` for UAT: the
production snapshot was taken when `1.2.0` was selected, and it does not change under you.

title: Deployments overview — Creating a deployment
text:
Open **Deployments** in the sidebar, select an environment in the selector, and press **Deploy**.
When the project has an AI provider, **Analyze the latest deployment** next to it asks the
[console assistant](../build-with-ai/console-assistant.md) to compare the latest deployment of the
selected environment with the previous one.
The action applies to the environment currently selected — moving `dev` and `uat` together is two
deployments, one after the other. (The API behind it, `POST /api/deployment`, takes a list of
environment ids and creates them in one transaction.)

Each deployment is numbered per environment: `#1`, `#2`, `#3` … The new deployment becomes
**active**, and any previously active deployment for that environment is deactivated. Exactly one
deployment is active per environment at any moment. The endpoints that answer *what should I load*
resolve against that flag; the ones that stream the files themselves resolve the deployment
differently, which only diverges after a rollback — see
[Serving from the active deployment](#serving-from-the-active-deployment) below.

:::caution[With GitOps on, the commit comes first]
When the project has [GitOps](../kubernetes/gitops.md) enabled, a deploy first commits what it ships
to the GitOps repositories. If that commit does not go through, nothing is deployed: the environment
keeps serving its current deployment and the deploy fails with the error the commit returned. A **Viewer**
cannot deploy a project with GitOps on.
:::

One thing travels with the new deployment without being part of your draft configuration: the
**canary enrolment** of the deployment being replaced is copied into the new one, inside the same
transaction, so deploying never silently drops the users you enrolled. See
[canary users](../frontends/canary-releases.md#canary-users).

title: Deployments overview — Reading the deployments page
text:
The page has two parts:

**Active deployment** — the snapshot currently serving this environment, expandable to show:

- **Frontends** — one card each, with the version frozen in this snapshot and, when a canary
  is configured, the share of traffic it takes — or *Enrolled users*, for a
  [*User* canary](../frontends/canary-releases.md#who--the-canary-type), which splits nothing
  — next to its canary type, its deployment type and its target version or URL
- **Backends** — one card per backend service, with the version frozen in this snapshot
- **Environment variables** — the values frozen in this snapshot
- **Config maps** and **Secrets** — the keys each map sets in this environment; config maps with
  their values, secrets with key names only, since secret values are not kept in the deployment
- **View canary users** — the enrolment list of this deployment

Each section appears only when the snapshot has something in it.

**History** — every previous deployment of this environment, newest first, with the same detail
plus a **Redeploy** action.

**Redeploy** and changes to the canary users both need access to the **whole project**: re-activating
an older snapshot rolls back every domain at once, so a member limited to specific domains can read
the history but not redeploy from it.

![The Deployments page: the active deployment expanded, with the canary badges of Catalog and Checkout, the backends, the environment variables and the config maps](../assets/deployments-overview.png)

Inspecting an old deployment answers "what exactly was live last Tuesday?" without archaeology
through Git.

:::tip[Which version is where]
The deployments page answers the question one environment at a time. For the whole project at a
glance — every frontend, the version each environment serves, and whether its last CI run
passed — use [Build status](./build-status.md).
:::

title: Deployments overview — Promoting between environments
text:
There is no dedicated "promote" button, because promotion is just a deployment:

1. Note the version live in the source environment (visible in its active deployment).
2. Select that version on the frontend.
3. Deploy the target environment.

The artifact is not rebuilt or copied — both environments point at the same stored files. What
differs is the environment variables each snapshot carries, which is exactly the difference you
want between stages.

title: Deployments overview — Serving from the active deployment
text:
Most of the public serve API resolves against the active deployment:

| Question from your app | Answered from |
| --- | --- |
| Which remotes do I load, and from where? | Active deployment's frontends |
| What is my runtime configuration? | Active deployment's variables |
| Give me this frontend's files | The **newest** deployment of the environment, which is not always the active one |

The third row is not a slip. The queries behind the manifest, the per-frontend configuration
and the variables filter on the `active` flag. The three routes that stream files do not: each takes
the newest deployment of the environment, and they do not agree on what "newest" means.

| File route | Newest by | After a rollback |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `/serve/mfe/files/:projectId/:envSlug/:mfeSlug/*` | Deployment time | Follows the rollback |
| `/serve/mfe/files/auto/:projectId/:mfeSlug/*` | Creation time | Does not follow the rollback |
| `/serve/mfe/files/:mfeId/*` | Creation time | Does not follow the rollback |

A **Deploy** stamps both times at once, so as long as you only ever deploy forwards the newest
deployment is the active one on either ordering and all three routes agree. A **Redeploy** bumps the
deployment time only, which is where they part company — described in full, with the mitigation, in
[Rollback and redeploy](./rollback-and-redeploy.md#the-file-routes-do-not-all-follow-a-rollback).
The routes themselves are listed in [Serve API](../integration/serve-api.md).

If an environment has never been deployed, these endpoints return an *Active deployment not
found* error, and the console's Integration page tells you to deploy first.

title: Deployments overview — Where to go next
text:
- [Rollback and redeploy](./rollback-and-redeploy.md)
- [Build status](./build-status.md) — what is built, and what each environment serves
- [Integration](../integration/overview.md) — consuming a deployment from your application

title: Rollback and redeploy
text:
Because deployments are immutable snapshots, rolling back is not a rebuild, a revert commit, or a
re-upload. It is re-activating a snapshot that already exists.

title: Rollback and redeploy — Rolling back
text:
1. Open **Deployments** and select the affected environment.
2. Find the last known-good deployment in **History**.
3. Expand it and check its frontend versions and variables are what you expect.
4. Choose **Redeploy** on that deployment.

**Redeploy** lives on the deployments in **History**, next to **View canary users**. The active
deployment has no Redeploy button — re-activating what is already active would be a no-op.

Redeploying needs access to the **whole project**: an older snapshot rolls back the frontends
and services of every domain at once, so a member limited to specific domains is refused.

![The active deployment collapsed above deployment #1 expanded in History, with its frontend and backend versions](../assets/deployments-history.png)

Reading the two snapshots against each other is the whole point. Above, `#2` and `#1` carry the same
versions, because nothing was edited between the two deployments — which is itself the answer to
"did anything actually change?". When they differ, the line you are looking for is the version badge
on a frontend card: `#2` serving `catalog` at `2.2.0` while `#1`, one click away, still holds
`2.1.0`.

That deployment becomes active again and the broken one is deactivated. The manifest, the
per-frontend configuration and the variables endpoints answer from the restored snapshot
immediately. The routes that stream the files themselves do not all follow — read the next section
before you rely on a rollback in production.

Because the frontend entry point is always served with
`Cache-Control: no-cache, no-store, must-revalidate`, browsers pick up the change on their next
request rather than after a cache expiry.

title: Rollback and redeploy — The file routes do not all follow a rollback
text:
:::caution[A rollback is not honoured by two of the three file routes]
The manifest, the per-frontend configuration and the global-variables endpoints filter
deployments on the `active` flag, so **Redeploy** moves them at once. The three routes that stream
the bytes of a frontend do not filter on it: each takes the newest deployment of the
environment, and they order "newest" differently.

| File route | Newest by | After a rollback |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `/serve/mfe/files/:projectId/:envSlug/:mfeSlug/*` | Deployment time | Serves the restored snapshot |
| `/serve/mfe/files/auto/:projectId/:mfeSlug/*` | Creation time | Keeps serving the snapshot you rolled back *from* |
| `/serve/mfe/files/:mfeId/*` | Creation time | Keeps serving the snapshot you rolled back *from* |

**Redeploy** sets the active flag and stamps a new deployment time, but the creation time stays the
moment the snapshot was first taken. The two creation-time routes therefore keep pointing at the
most recently *created* snapshot — the broken one.
:::

Because the manifest *does* honour the rollback, the outcome is worse than a rollback that has not
landed yet: the manifest reports the restored version while those two routes stream the files of the
version you rolled back from. The version your host believes it is running and the code it actually
runs disagree, which is not a state any error message will point you at.

**Whether this reaches you depends on which URL your host asks for.** Every frontend URL the
manifest hands out carries the environment slug, and that is the route ordered by deployment time —
so a host wired through the [client SDK](../integration/client-sdk.md), or through any code that
loads the URLs the manifest returned, lands on the behaviour that is correct. Only a consumer that
calls the `auto` or `:mfeId` file URLs directly — hardcoded in an `index.html` or in a Module
Federation `remotes` block — is exposed.

If you are in that position, do not stop at the rollback. Set the frontend's selected version
back to the good one and press **Deploy**: a new snapshot is the newest by both orderings, so every
route follows it. See [Serve API](../integration/serve-api.md) for the routes themselves.

title: Rollback and redeploy — What a rollback restores
text:
Everything in the snapshot, together:

- Frontend versions
- Backend service versions
- Hosting configuration and entry points
- Canary settings
- Environment variables
- Storage configuration

The **canary enrolment** comes back with it too, but for a different reason: enrolment rows are
stored per deployment, and the one you re-activate still holds its own. That is the list as it was
on that deployment, which is not necessarily the list you had a minute ago — if you enrolled
someone after the deployment you are rolling back to was replaced, check
[canary users](../frontends/canary-releases.md#canary-users) afterwards.

This matters when an incident has more than one cause. If a bad release changed both a version
and a feature-flag variable, rolling back the deployment undoes both — you do not have to
remember which variables moved.

title: Rollback and redeploy — What a rollback does not do
text:
| Not restored | Why |
| --- | --- |
| Your project's draft configuration | The console keeps showing the versions and variables you last selected. Only the *active snapshot* changes |
| Deleted frontends | A frontend deleted from the project is gone from the project, even if older snapshots mention it |
| Data outside Flightroom | Database migrations, backend deployments and CDN state are yours to manage |

Point one is a common surprise: after a rollback, the console still shows the version you were
trying to ship, because that is still what you have selected. Reconcile the draft afterwards, or
your next deployment will re-ship the bad version.

:::tip[After rolling back]
Set the frontend's selected version back to the good one straight away. It costs ten seconds
and prevents the next deployment from re-introducing the incident.
:::

title: Rollback and redeploy — Redeploy does not publish your edits
text:
**Redeploy** re-activates an existing snapshot, with a fresh timestamp, exactly as it was stored.
It never picks up draft changes: a version you selected, a variable you edited or a remote you
rewired since that snapshot was taken are not in it.

To publish edits you want **Deploy**, which takes a new snapshot of the current configuration. The
two buttons sit on different things for that reason — **Deploy** at the top of the page, on the
selected environment, and **Redeploy** inside a deployment of the history.

title: Rollback and redeploy — Deployment numbering
text:
Numbers are assigned per environment and never reused: `#1`, `#2`, `#3` … A rollback does not
create a new number — it re-activates an existing one. So a history where `#7` is active after
`#9` existed is entirely normal, and tells you at a glance that a rollback happened.

title: Rollback and redeploy — A rehearsal worth doing
text:
Roll back once in a non-production environment before you need to do it under pressure:

1. Deploy a version, note the deployment number.
2. Bump the version and deploy again.
3. Redeploy the first snapshot and confirm your app serves the old version.

Ten minutes now buys confidence during an incident.

title: Functional domains
text:
A **functional domain** groups the frontends and services of one business capability, for
example *Payments* or *Catalog*: the screens and the backends that call each other. A frontend or
a service belongs to one domain at most, and can belong to none.

A domain is what you hand to the AI to change a whole capability in one request, what you deploy on
its own without touching the rest of the project, and what you can limit a member to.

title: Functional domains — The domains of a project
text:
Open **Domains** in the sidebar (`/domains`). The page header has a view switcher, **Deployed
versions** and **New domain**. An empty project shows *No functional domains* with a **New domain**
button instead.

### Galaxy view

The default view is a map of the project: every domain is a galaxy, and its frontends and services
are the stars.

![The Galaxy view: the Storefront, Checkout and Customer care domains with their stars, the links across domains and two labelled domain relations](../assets/domains-galaxy.png)

- Click a galaxy to fly to it, and click it again to open the domain.
- Click a star to open the frontend or the service.
- Scroll to zoom; **Show everything** zooms back out to the whole project.
- The legend tells apart the stars with a canary on (**Canary on**), the links between frontends
  or services of two different domains (**Link across domains**), and the relations you drew between
  domains (**Domain relation**).

To relate two domains, press **Link domains**, click the galaxy the relation starts from, then the one
it goes to (Esc cancels). The **New domain relation** dialog takes an optional **Label**, such as
*uses* or *publishes events to*. A relation goes one way: a relation back is a relation of its own.
Click a relation to delete it; the domains and their members stay.

### Cards view

One card per domain, with its name, slug, description and the number of frontends and services.
Each card has:

- **Edit with AI**, which opens the domain;
- the pencil, to edit its **Name**, **Description** and **AI context**;
- the trash icon, to delete it. Its frontends and services stay, without a domain, and its
  relations are deleted with it.

![The Cards view: one card per domain with its slug, description, member counts, Edit with AI, pencil and trash icon](../assets/domains-cards.png)

### Creating a domain

**New domain** asks for a **Name** (required, and unique in the project), a **Description** and an
**AI context**: notes for the AI agents about this domain only, in Markdown, up to 20,000 characters.
What applies to the whole project belongs in the project context, in **Settings**.

title: Functional domains — Deployed versions
text:
**Deployed versions** opens `/domains/deployments`, a matrix of which version of each frontend
and service runs in each environment:

- **Rows** are the domains, then **No domain** for the frontends and services in none (shown only
  when there are some).
- **Columns** are the environments, in their order, each with its colour, a **Production** badge where
  it applies, and the deployment it serves with its date, or *Never deployed*.
- Each cell lists the members of the domain as `slug version`.

![The Deployed versions matrix: one row per domain, one column per environment, with not reported where no pipeline reported a backend version](../assets/domains-deployed-versions.png)

Where the versions come from is not the same for the two halves:

| Member | Version shown | When there is none |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Frontend of kind **Bundle** | The one in the deployment the environment serves (the active one), with its canary if one is on, for example `1.2.0 · canary 1.3.0 (10%)` | *not deployed* |
| Frontend of kind [**Docker**](../frontends/create-a-frontend.md#bundle-or-docker) | The latest version its deploy pipeline reported for that environment, through `POST /api/frontends/by-slug/:slug/environments/:environmentSlug/deployments` | *not deployed* |
| Service | The latest version a deploy pipeline **reported** for that environment, through `POST /api/services/by-slug/:serviceSlug/environments/:environmentSlug/deployments` | *not reported* |

:::info[A GitOps deploy alone shows "not reported"]
The backend versions come **only** from that call. A **Deploy** through
[GitOps](../kubernetes/gitops.md) does not write it, so a project that deploys its services with
GitOps and nothing else shows *not reported* in every backend cell. Add the call to your deploy
pipeline: see [Reporting where a version runs](../kubernetes/services.md#reporting-where-a-version-runs).
:::

The same information, for one domain, is on the **Overview** of its structure (below).

title: Functional domains — A domain's page
text:
A domain has two tabs, **Edit with AI** and **Structure**, and a **Deploy** button on both.

### Edit with AI

`/domain/:id` (also `/domain/:id/ai`) is where you ask the AI for a change across the whole domain: one
agent works on every frontend and service of the domain that has a code repository, at most 10,
and proposes one change per repository. See
[Change a whole domain](../build-with-ai/ai-changes.md#change-a-whole-domain).

The tab is always there. Without an AI it reads *AI editing is not available in this project: the
organization has no AI it can use.* A domain with no member, or none with a repository, is handled by
[Generate a domain](../build-with-ai/generate-a-domain.md), which creates them first.

### Structure

`/domain/:id/structure` shows the members of the domain, split into **Frontend** (its frontends)
and **Backend** (its services), in four views:

| View | Shows |
| --- | --- |
| **Diagram view** (the default) | Frontend and backend on one canvas. Drag from a frontend's dot to another frontend or to a service to link them; drop the link on empty canvas to create a new frontend under it. Select a link and press Delete to remove it, double-click a block to open it. Positions are shared with the Frontends page |
| **Overview** | Two cards listing the members with their version, and the **Deployed versions** of the domain per environment |
| **Grid view** | The members as cards |
| **Table view** | The members as a table |

![The Diagram view of the Checkout domain structure, with the checkout frontend above the Orders API service](../assets/domain-structure-diagram.png)

**Edit** in the header changes the name, description and AI context of the domain.

### Adding frontends and services

**Add frontend** and **Add service** open the same menu:

| Entry | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| **Create a new frontend** / **Create a new service** | Opens the creation form with the domain already set |
| **Add existing** | Picks frontends or services of the project to put in this domain. Those in another domain are moved here |
| **Import from repository** | Creates one frontend or one service per repository of a code repository connection, in this domain. Shown only when the project has a connection. See [Import repositories](../repositories/import-frontends.md) |

### Deploying a domain

**Deploy** opens **Deploy *domain***: pick the environment and press **Deploy**. Only the
frontends and services of this domain are deployed; the other domains keep the versions the
environment serves now. Config maps and secrets are still deployed as they are now. The button is
hidden while the project has no environment. See [Deployments](../deployments/overview.md) and
[Deploy to Kubernetes](../kubernetes/overview.md).

title: Functional domains — Members limited to some domains
text:
A project member can be given access to the **Whole project** or to **Specific domains** only (see
[Changing a role](../project-settings/users-and-roles.md#changing-a-role)). A member limited to some
domains:

- sees only those domains, their frontends and services, and the relations between two of them.
  The **No domain** row of the matrix never shows for them;
- cannot create, edit or delete domains, relate them, or move members into them;
- sees and starts only the AI jobs on their domains. See
  [Guardrails](../build-with-ai/guardrails.md#who-can-do-what).

title: Allowed domains and environment resolution
text:
**Allowed Domains** is the least obvious field on an environment, and the one that unlocks the
cleanest integration. It lets Flightroom work out *which environment a browser request
belongs to* without the URL saying so.

title: Allowed domains and environment resolution — The problem it solves
text:
Your host application needs to load remotes. The straightforward way is to build the environment
into the URL:

```
https://api.example.com/serve/mfe/files/<projectId>/prod/catalog/remoteEntry.js
                                                    ^^^^
```

That works, but it means the deployed artifact of your host differs per environment — the very
thing composing frontends at runtime is supposed to avoid. You end up with an environment-specific
build, or with runtime string surgery in the host.

title: Allowed domains and environment resolution — How it works
text:
Instead, register the domains each environment is served from:

| Environment | Allowed Domains |
| --- | --- |
| Development | `localhost`, `dev.example.com` |
| UAT | `uat.example.com` |
| Production | `www.example.com` |

Production registers `www.example.com` and not the bare `example.com` on purpose: matching is a
substring test, and a bare apex domain is contained in every subdomain of it registered on another
stage. [Overlapping domains](#overlapping-domains) explains what that costs.

Then use the environment-less form of the URL:

```
/serve/mfe/files/auto/<projectId>/<frontendSlug>/<entryPoint>
```

When that request arrives, Flightroom reads the browser's `Referer` header and matches it
against the registered domains to find the environment, then answers from that environment's
active deployment.

One artifact, every stage. The host built once and deployed to `uat.example.com` gets UAT
remotes; the identical artifact on `www.example.com` gets production remotes.

The same mechanism is what makes `environment` optional in the
[client SDK](../integration/client-sdk.md): a `configure()` call without a slug asks the serve API
in this environment-less form, and the answer comes from whichever environment claims the domain the
page is on.

title: Allowed domains and environment resolution — Adding domains
text:
Open the environment and type a domain into **Allowed Domains**, pressing `Enter` or `,` after
each one. Add every hostname the environment is genuinely reachable at, including `www`
variants and any vanity domains. Then read [Overlapping domains](#overlapping-domains) below,
because what you register on one stage constrains what the others may hold.

![The Allowed Domains field on the environment dialog](../assets/environment-dialog.png)

The domains of every environment are visible together on the Environments page, which is the
quickest way to spot a stage that is still missing one:

![The Environments page with its Allowed Domains column, still empty on every environment](../assets/environments-list.png)

title: Allowed domains and environment resolution — Overlapping domains
text:
:::caution[No domain may be a substring of a domain on another environment]
Matching is not an equality test. The domain the request comes from is compiled into a
case-insensitive regular expression, and each **registered** domain is tested against it with no
anchors — so an environment matches when one of its registered domains *contains* the calling one.

A request from `example.com` therefore matches a Development environment holding `dev.example.com`
just as well as a Production environment holding `example.com`. The lookup takes the first document
the database returns and applies no ordering, so which of the two answers is arbitrary — and because
the preset environment sets create Development before Production, the arbitrary answer tends in
practice to be the development one. Production traffic answered by the development deployment is the
failure this produces, and nothing raises an error or logs a warning when it happens.

So the rule is stronger than one environment per domain: **no domain registered on one environment
may be a substring of a domain registered on another**. Two hostnames on the *same* environment
never fight each other — either match resolves to the same place. The dangerous shape is a bare apex
domain on one stage while a subdomain of it lives on another: `example.com` on Production against
`dev.example.com` on Development. Register a subdomain for production too (`www.example.com`, with
the apex redirecting to it) and no stage contains another.
:::

Note which way the containment runs: it is the *caller* that has to be contained. A request from
`dev.example.com` will not match a registered `example.com`, which is why the stage with the longer
hostname is never the one that gets hijacked.

title: Allowed domains and environment resolution — Which endpoints use it
text:
Domain resolution applies to the endpoints that do not name an environment:

| Endpoint | Resolution |
| --- | --- |
| `/serve/all/auto/:projectId` | From `Referer` (falls back to the request host) |
| `/serve/global-variables/auto/:projectId` | From `Referer` (falls back to the request host) |
| `/serve/global-variables/auto/:projectId/index.js` | From `Referer` (falls back to the request host) |
| `/serve/mfe/config/auto/:projectId/:mfeSlug` | From `Referer` (falls back to the request host) |
| `/serve/mfe/files/auto/:projectId/:mfeSlug/*` | From `Referer` (falls back to the request host) |
| `/serve/mfe/files/:mfeId/*` | From `Referer` — **required** |
| `/serve/mfe/config/:mfeId` | From `Referer` — **required** |

Endpoints that name the environment explicitly — anything with `:environmentId` or
`:environmentSlug` in the path — ignore the domain list.

The first three are what the [client SDK](../integration/client-sdk.md) uses when `configure()` is
called without an `environment`, which is the point at which the domain list stops being a
convenience for asset URLs and becomes the thing your whole host depends on to find its remotes.
Keep it accurate: registering the domain is part of standing up a new stage, not an afterthought.

title: Allowed domains and environment resolution — Troubleshooting
text:
**"Referer not found"**

The request arrived without a `Referer` header. This happens with `curl` unless you pass one, and
with strict referrer policies. Either send a `Referer`, or switch to an endpoint that names the
environment explicitly.

```bash
curl -H "Referer: https://www.example.com" \
  "/serve/mfe/files/auto/<projectId>/catalog/remoteEntry.js"
```

**"Environment not found"**

No environment of this project had a registered domain matching the request. Check for typos, and
check the domain is registered at all.

Note what this error does *not* cover. When more than one environment matches, nothing is raised:
one of them is picked and the response looks entirely normal. An ambiguous domain list fails
silently, not loudly — see [Overlapping domains](#overlapping-domains).

**Local development**

Add `localhost` to your development environment. A port does not get in the way, though not through
the origin: the request is tried as four candidates in turn — the raw `Referer`, its origin, its host
and its **hostname** — and for `http://localhost:3000/` the origin (`http://localhost:3000`) and the
host (`localhost:3000`) both still carry the port. It is the hostname candidate, `localhost`, that
matches a bare `localhost` entry.

:::tip
Matching is case-insensitive, and the request is tried as its raw `Referer`, its origin, its host and
its hostname. Register bare hostnames (`example.com`) rather than full URLs: because the registered
value is the one that has to contain the caller, a longer entry matches *more* callers rather than
fewer.
:::

title: Runtime environment variables
text:
Environment variables in Flightroom are **runtime** configuration: `key`/`value` pairs
scoped to an environment, read by the browser after the bundle has loaded.

:::info[Not to be confused with…]
These are the variables of *your application*. The variables that configure the Flightroom
container itself are documented under
[Self Hosting → Environment Variables](../self-hosting/environment-variables.md).
:::

title: Runtime environment variables — Why runtime and not build time
text:
A variable baked in at build time (`import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL`, `process.env.API_URL`) makes
the artifact environment-specific. Promoting a build from UAT to production then means rebuilding
it, which means the thing you tested is not the thing you shipped.

Serving the values at runtime instead means one artifact travels through every stage, and the
stage supplies its own configuration:

```
        one build of catalog@1.4.0
                   │
    ┌──────────────┼──────────────┐
    ▼              ▼              ▼
   dev            uat            prod
API_URL=…dev   API_URL=…uat   API_URL=…com
```

title: Runtime environment variables — Managing variables
text:
Open **Environment Variables** in the sidebar and use **Add Variable**. Each variable is a `key`
with one value per environment; keys are unique per environment.

![The Environment Variables page, one column per environment](../assets/environment-variables-list.png)

The dialog asks for the key once and then for its value in each environment, which is the shape
you almost always want — the same key with a different value per stage. Every environment has to get
a value: `value` is a required field on the model, so an empty box is rejected, and the values of all
environments are written in one batch — so a single empty box fails the whole variable rather than
creating it without that environment. The dialog validates nothing and starts with an empty box for
each environment, so pressing **Create** with one left blank returns a validation error and stores
nothing.

:::note[Leaving a variable out of one environment]
There is no way to do this from the console. The creation endpoint, though, writes only the
environments you send it: `POST /api/global-variables`, with the project in the `project-id` header
and a `values` array carrying no entry for one environment, creates the variable in every other
environment and leaves that one without it. That is where the code reading it genuinely finds
`undefined`.

Editing afterwards will not fill the gap: the update endpoint only rewrites rows that already exist,
and the console's delete removes the key from every environment at once. If the variable has to be
present everywhere, give it an empty-ish value your code treats as off rather than trying to omit
it.
:::

![The Add Variable dialog, with a value per environment](../assets/environment-variable-dialog.png)

:::caution[Not a secret store]
Environment variables are served to the browser by a **public, unauthenticated** endpoint. Anyone
who knows your project and environment id can read them. Never put API secrets, private keys,
database credentials or tokens here. Use them for public configuration only: API base URLs,
feature flags, tracking ids, public keys.
:::

title: Runtime environment variables — Reading them in your application
text:
Variables are exposed in two forms. The full details, including examples, are in
[Runtime configuration](../integration/runtime-configuration.md); in short:

**As a script that populates `window.globalConfig`** — add it to your `index.html` before your
bundle:

```html
<script src="/serve/global-variables/auto/<projectId>/index.js"></script>
```

```js
const apiUrl = window.globalConfig?.API_URL
```

**As JSON**, if you prefer to fetch them yourself:

```js
const vars = await fetch('/serve/global-variables/auto/<projectId>')
  .then(r => r.json())
```

Neither address names an environment: the platform resolves it from the domain the page is
served on, so one `index.html` covers every stage. The console's
**Integration → Environment variables** tab shows both snippets with your project id already
filled in.

title: Runtime environment variables — Variables and deployments
text:
Like everything else, variables are captured in the deployment snapshot. Adding or changing a
variable does not affect a running environment until you deploy.

This is deliberate: it means a configuration change is as auditable and as reversible as a code
change. Rolling back a deployment rolls back its variables along with its versions.

:::tip
If you have changed a variable and your application still reads the old value, check that you
have deployed. Both variables endpoints above answer from the **active deployment** of the resolved
environment, never from the current draft configuration.

That is a property of the variables endpoints, not of the serve API as a whole: the routes that
stream frontend files resolve the deployment differently and can disagree with the active one
after a rollback — see
[Rollback and redeploy](../deployments/rollback-and-redeploy.md#the-file-routes-do-not-all-follow-a-rollback).
:::

title: Environments overview
text:
An **environment** is a deployment stage of your project: `dev`, `uat`, `prod`, or whatever your
release process calls them. Environments are where versions and configuration diverge — the same
frontend can be at `1.2.0` in production and `1.4.0-rc1` in UAT at the same time.

Environments live under **Settings → Resources → Environments**.

title: Environments overview — Creating an environment
text:
Click **New Environment** and fill in:

| Field | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| **Name** | Display name, e.g. *Production* |
| **Slug** | URL-friendly identifier, e.g. `prod`. Unique within the project, part of your public serve URLs, and read-only once the environment exists |
| **Kubernetes namespace** | Only while [GitOps](../kubernetes/gitops.md) is on. The namespace the environment is deployed to: up to 63 lowercase letters, digits and dashes. Left empty, the slug in lowercase |
| **Subdomain** | Only while GitOps is on. The host of the environment under the project's [exposure](../kubernetes/exposure.md) domain. Left empty, the domain itself for a production environment, the slug in lowercase for the others |
| **Description** | Free text |
| **Allowed Domains** | The domains your app is served from — see [Allowed domains](./domains.md) |
| **Color** | Used to tag the environment throughout the console |
| **Production environment** | Marks this as a production stage |

![The Edit Production dialog: name, read-only slug, description, allowed domains, colour and the Production environment switch](../assets/environment-dialog.png)

The environments of a project are listed together, with their slug, production flag, allowed
domains and colour. With GitOps on, the list also shows the **Host** of each environment, a link to
it, or its **Subdomain** while the project has no exposure domain yet. Drag a row to change the order
they appear in throughout the console:

![The Environments page listing Development, Staging and Production](../assets/environments-list.png)

When you set up a project through the wizard you are offered a set of **default environments**
to start from, and you can add your own alongside them.

:::caution[Slugs are public]
The environment slug appears in serve URLs such as
`/serve/all/<projectId>/<environmentSlug>`. The console will not let you rename it — the
field is disabled when you edit an existing environment — precisely because renaming it breaks any
consumer using that form of the URL. `PUT /api/environments/:id` does accept a new slug, so through
the API the breakage is yours to manage.
:::

title: Environments overview — The environment selector
text:
Most pages in the console are scoped to one environment, chosen from the selector in the page
header. Environment Variables, Deployments and Integration all follow it — if you are wondering
why a page shows nothing, check which environment is selected.

The order of environments in the selector is configurable, so you can list them in the order
they appear in your release flow rather than alphabetically.

title: Environments overview — What is environment-specific and what is not
text:
This distinction matters, and it is not obvious at first:

| Object | Scope |
| --- | --- |
| Frontends | **Project** — one definition, shared by all environments |
| Services | **Project** — one definition, shared by all environments |
| Environment variables | **Environment** |
| Config maps and secrets | **Project** — but each key holds a value per environment |
| Deployments | **Environment** — each has its own numbering and history |
| Kubernetes namespace and subdomain | **Environment** |
| Storages / buckets | **Project** |
| Databases | **Project** |
| Code repositories | **Project** |
| API keys | **Project** |
| Members | **Project** |

So a frontend exists once, but the **version that is live** is a property of each
environment's active deployment. That is the mechanism by which one definition serves many
stages.

title: Environments overview — Deleting an environment
text:
Deleting an environment removes it together with everything that belongs to it, in a single
transaction: either all of it goes, or nothing does. A confirmation dialog names the environment you
are about to delete — you do not have to type the name — and there is no undo.

| Object | What happens to it |
| --- | --- |
| Deployments of that environment | Deleted, with their history |
| Canary users enrolled in those deployments | Deleted |
| Environment variables of that environment | Deleted |
| Service deployments reported for that environment by your pipelines | Deleted |

Recreating an environment with the same slug starts from scratch: a new environment gets a new id,
and nothing of the old one comes back.

With [GitOps](../kubernetes/gitops.md) on, the folder of the deleted environment is removed from the
configuration repository on the next deploy of the project.

title: Environments overview — Who can change environments
text:
Environments belong to every functional domain of the project. A member scoped to a functional domain
can see them but cannot create, edit, reorder or delete them.

title: Environments overview — Where to go next
text:
- [Allowed domains](./domains.md) — how the platform resolves an environment from a browser request
- [Environment variables](./environment-variables.md) — per-environment runtime configuration
- [Deployments](../deployments/overview.md) — activating configuration in an environment

title: Canary releases for frontends
text:
A canary release serves a new version of a frontend to a fraction of your traffic while
everyone else keeps the stable one. Flightroom takes that decision per frontend and
entirely server-side: the host page never learns which side of the split it got, and does not need
to.

title: Canary releases for frontends — Enabling a canary
text:
Open the frontend's form — **Configuration** on its card, or **Details & settings** when the
card opens the AI workspace. **Release** is the first card of the form and it sits *above* the tabs,
so it is on screen whichever tab is selected: the version and the canary decide which bytes a
browser gets, and they are not something you should have to go looking for. Under the version, past
a divider, is **Canary Settings** and its switch. A frontend of the **Docker** kind has no
canary: its container serves every request.

![The Canary Settings section of the frontend form with the switch on, the percentage slider and its presets, the canary type and deployment type selects and the canary version field](../assets/frontend-canary.png)

Turned on, the section asks for four things, in this order:

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Canary Percentage** | Share of traffic that should receive the canary, as a slider with 5, 10, 25 and 50 presets. Not asked for by *User*, which enrols people instead of splitting traffic |
| **Canary Type** | Who gets the canary — *Random*, *Session* or *User* |
| **Deployment Type** | What the canary is — *Based on Version* or *Based on URL* |
| **Canary Version** / **Canary URL** | The target, depending on the deployment type |

A sentence under the two selects spells out what the selected type does, because the three names
are not enough to tell them apart. The percentage has to be between 1 and 100 while the canary is
enabled — 0 is refused, which is deliberate: a canary configured to reach nobody is a
misconfiguration and not a way to switch it off. Turning the switch off is.

Canary configuration is part of the frontend, so like everything else it is captured in a
[deployment](../deployments/overview.md) and only becomes live once you deploy. Expanding a
deployment under **Deployments** shows a card per frontend with its stable version, the two
types, and the canary share — or *Enrolled users*, for a *User* canary, which has no share. It is
the quickest way to confirm what a deployment will actually do.

![The frontend cards of an expanded deployment, each with its stable version; Catalog and Checkout add their canary share or enrolled users, canary type and deployment type badges and canary version](../assets/deployment-canary-cards.png)

The frontends list carries the same information in shorter form. A grid card shows the share
as a bar with the canary version underneath; the table view gives it a column of its own, next to
a **Canary Version** column, and says *No canary* for the frontends that have none.

![A frontend card in grid view showing the canary block: the share as a percentage, a progress bar and the canary version](../assets/frontend-canary-card.png)

title: Canary releases for frontends — Who — the canary type
text:
The three types answer two different questions, and it is worth being clear about which one you are
asking.

![The Canary Type select open, showing the three options Random, Session and User](../assets/frontend-canary-type.png)

| Canary Type | Who gets the canary | Sticky? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Random** | A share of every page load, drawn fresh each time | No — the same browser flips between versions on every refresh |
| **Session** | A share of browsers, drawn once per browser | Yes — survives a reload, a new tab and a browser restart |
| **User** | Only the users you enrol, no matter how many they are | Yes — it is a decision, not a draw |

*Random* and *Session* are the same percentage split and differ only in whether the draw is
remembered. *User* is not a split at all: the percentage plays no part in it.

The identity the split is computed on travels in the query string of the calls your host makes to
the serve API, and the [client SDK](../integration/client-sdk.md) generates, persists and sends it
for you:

| Query parameter | What it identifies | Where the host keeps it | Used by |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `mfeDeviceId` | The browser | `localStorage` | *Session* |
| `mfeUserId` | The logged-in user | Supplied by your application | *User* |
| `mfeSessionId` | The browsing session | `sessionStorage` | No canary strategy — the SDK still sends it, and exposes it, for your own telemetry |

The host sends **every identity it holds** and is never told which one was used, nor the
percentage, nor whether a canary exists at all. Switching a frontend from one type to another
is therefore a console change only — nothing to redeploy on the host side.

:::info[No cookie is involved, and none can be]
An earlier version of this feature had a *Cookie Based* type, and the name was misleading:
**no cookie is involved anywhere here, and none can be.** Frontends are loaded with a
cross-site `import()`, and module scripts are fetched with a fixed `same-origin` credentials mode,
so a cookie belonging to the Flightroom domain is never attached to those requests and a
`Set-Cookie` on their responses is never stored. This is how module scripts are specified in every
browser, not a Safari or ITP quirk — verified in Chromium with third-party cookies enabled and a
`SameSite=None; Secure` cookie already in the jar. The host page is the only place that can hold
this state, and the URL is the only way to hand it over.

That is why *Session* means "an identity that outlives the browser session", kept in `localStorage`
by the SDK. If you would rather keep it in a first-party cookie of your own domain, read it
yourself and pass it as `mfeDeviceId`.

The old *On Sessions* and *Cookie Based* types no longer exist. Frontends still configured with
either of them — and the frontend snapshots inside deployments already shipped — are converted
to *Session* automatically, by a migration the backend runs when it connects to the database.
Nothing to do on your side.
:::

title: Canary releases for frontends — What — the deployment type
text:
| Type | Behaviour |
| --- | --- |
| **Based on Version** | The canary is a different **version** of the same frontend, served through its normal hosting configuration |
| **Based on URL** | The canary is a completely separate **URL**, which can point anywhere |

*Based on Version* is the natural choice when the canary is simply the next build. *Based on URL*
is useful when the candidate lives on separate infrastructure — a preview environment, a different
CDN — and you want to send a slice of traffic there without registering it as a version.

title: Canary releases for frontends — How the split is computed
text:
*Random* is what it says: a draw against the percentage, taken once per page load when the manifest
is fetched, with nothing stored anywhere.

*Session* is **sticky**, and gets there without server-side state and without a draw per request.
The identity and the frontend id are concatenated (`identity:frontendId`), hashed with
FNV-1a into one of 100 buckets, and the request gets the canary when `bucket < percentage`.

Three properties follow from that, and they are the reason it is done this way:

- **Stable.** The same identity always lands in the same bucket, so a returning browser stays on
  the side it was on, without anything being stored.
- **Monotonic.** Raising the percentage only ever *adds* browsers to the canary; it never moves one
  back to stable. Measured going from 20% to 40%: zero browsers moved out.
- **Independent per frontend.** The frontend id is part of the hashed string, so a
  browser can be on the canary of one frontend and on the stable version of another. A single
  unlucky user does not get every canary at once.

The distribution is accurate enough to trust the number you type: 25% configured measured 25.1%
actual over 4000 identities.

### When no identity arrives

- **Session** falls back to a plain draw **per page load**, which is to say it degrades into
  *Random*. The page load itself stays coherent, because the resolved version is pinned into the URL
  immediately — but the next reload draws again. Stickiness is exactly what requires the host to
  send an identity, which is what the SDK is for.
- **User** does not fall back. Without `mfeUserId` there is nobody to look up, so every request gets
  the stable version. That is the intended behaviour for anonymous visitors, not a degradation.

title: Canary releases for frontends — How the version reaches the browser
text:
This is the subtle part, and worth understanding before you debug a rollout.

A canary that rolls out one of *your* versions does **not** change the URL of the frontend. The
manifest returns the usual serve URL with the resolved version already pinned into it as a **path
segment**:

```
https://console.flightroom.dev/api/serve/mfe/files/auto/68f1a2b3c4d5e6f7a8b9c0d1/checkout-new/_v/1.5.0-rc1/assets/remoteEntry.js
```

Use that URL verbatim. Never rebuild it, and never strip the `_v/<version>/` segment.

**A frontend is many files, and they all come from one build.** The draw happens exactly once,
on the entry point, and its result is pinned into that URL; every chunk imported from it inherits
the `_v/<version>/` segment, because relative specifiers resolve against the entry point's URL. The
server never draws again for the individual files — a file arriving without a version in its path
is served the **deployed** version, not a fresh coin flip. With a *Random* canary that distinction
is the whole ball game: redrawing per file would let one page load half of build A and half of
build B.

**Why a path segment and not a query parameter.** The entry point imports its chunks with relative
specifiers (`./chunk.js`), which the browser resolves against the entry point's URL — and that
resolution drops the query string. A version carried in the query would be lost by the first chunk
request.

**Why the URL is pinned up front rather than redirected to.** The entry point of a canary
frontend also answers the *versionless* URL with a `302` (uncacheable) to the pinned one, as a
fallback for anyone holding a raw URL. That redirect is enough for an ES module, whose relative
imports resolve against the **post-redirect** URL. It is *not* enough for a classic script:
`document.currentScript.src` is the URL *before* redirects, so a webpack build with
`publicPath: 'auto'` would compute its chunk base from the versionless URL and fetch chunks from a
different version — two builds mixed into one page. Verified in Chromium: the classic script saw
`/mfe/assets/entry.js` while an ES module saw `/mfe/_v/1.5.0-rc1/assets/entry-esm.js`. Pinning the
URL in the manifest removes the redirect from the picture entirely, so both module systems resolve
their chunks on one version.

A **Based on URL** canary is decided in the manifest instead: there is no version of yours to pin,
so the host is simply handed either the canary URL or the stable one.

title: Canary releases for frontends — Verifying which version a browser got
text:
| Tool | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `x-mfe-version` response header | Present on every file served for a frontend, naming the version those exact bytes came from |
| `?mfeVersion=<version>` query parameter | Forces a specific version, for testing |

`mfeVersion` is accepted only when the value is one of the versions that deployment can serve —
the deployed version or the configured canary version — so it cannot be used to reach an arbitrary
build.

In practice: open the network panel, find the entry point request, and read `x-mfe-version`. That
is the ground truth, and it is the only thing the browser is ever told about the rollout.

title: Canary releases for frontends — Canary users
text:
**User** targeting is an enrolment list, not a split. A user sees the canary when the deployment
carries a row enabling them, and everyone else — including every anonymous visitor — gets the stable
version. Because the decision is taken on `mfeUserId`, it follows that person onto any browser and
any device.

The list lives on the deployment and covers every frontend of it configured as *User*. Open a
deployment under **Deployments** — the active one or any in the history — and press
**View canary users**.

![The Canary Users page: the Add users field and four enrolled users, each with its canary switch and delete button](../assets/canary-users.png)

- **Add** one or more user ids. Paste a list separated by commas, spaces or new lines — semicolons
  work too — to enrol a whole group in one go; the input de-duplicates, so a list copied out of a
  spreadsheet or a query result works as it is.
- **Toggle** a row between *Canary* and *Excluded* to suspend someone without losing the entry.
- **Remove** a row to send that person back to the stable version.
- **Select rows** with the checkboxes to enable, disable or remove all of them at once — the same
  three actions, applied to the selection.

Removing a row and disabling it are different entries in the table and the same thing to the
resolver: a user with no row and a user with a disabled row both get the stable version.

The ids are the ones **your application** knows — whatever it passes to the client SDK as `userId`.
They are opaque strings to the console, which is why the page shows them back rather than names or
email addresses.

### Enrolment survives a new deployment

Enrolment is stored **per deployment**, which taken literally would mean that every deploy starts
with nobody on the canary. It does not: creating a deployment copies the rows of the deployment the
environment is serving right now into the new one, inside the transaction that creates it. Each row
keeps its state, so someone you had disabled stays disabled rather than being re-enrolled.

A [redeploy](../deployments/rollback-and-redeploy.md) is a different operation — it re-activates a
deployment that already holds its own rows, so there is nothing to carry over.

### Telling the SDK who is logged in

The host is the only place that knows this, so it has to hand it over. Three shapes, depending on
when the user becomes known:

```ts
// Known at bootstrap
configure({ backendUrl, projectId, userId: currentUser.id })

// Known after an auth round trip — the getter is resolved right before the manifest request
configure({ backendUrl, projectId, userId: () => authStore.getState().user?.id })

// Changing while the page is alive: a login, a logout, an account switch

auth.onLogin(user => setUserId(user.id))
auth.onLogout(() => setUserId(undefined))
```

[`setUserId()`](../integration/client-sdk.md#changing-the-user-without-a-reload) drops the memoised
manifest, so the next remote resolved is decided on the new identity. What it cannot do is move a
frontend that is **already on the page**: the federation runtime keeps the container it loaded,
so an enrolment that arrives after the remote was imported takes effect on the next resolution or on
a reload. Resolving your remotes behind your own auth guard avoids the question entirely.

title: Canary releases for frontends — Limits worth knowing
text:
- **Based on URL canaries cannot be inspected the same way.** The split itself works exactly as
  described — the type decides it, and *Session* is as sticky there as anywhere else — but there is
  no version of ours in play: the host is simply handed one URL or the other. Nothing serves those
  files, so they carry no `x-mfe-version` header and `?mfeVersion=` has nothing to force. The
  manifest is no help either — with no version of ours to report, its `version` field names the
  frontend's stable version whichever of the two URLs it just handed out. Prefer *Based on
  Version* when you want to watch a rollout rather than just perform one.
- **The manifest is fetched once per page load and is not retried.** If that request fails, the
  remotes of that page load fail with it; the SDK clears its memo so the next call tries again.

title: Canary releases for frontends — Practical advice
text:
**Pick the type before the percentage.** *Random* is for exercising both builds against the same
browser — a smoke test you can refresh, and a poor fit for anything a user is halfway through.
*Session* is what a rollout normally means. *User* is for a named group: your own team, one
customer, a support case.

**Pick a percentage you can read.** With a sticky split, the useful question is how many sessions
you need before your dashboards say anything. 5% is a smoke test, 25% is a measurement, 50% is a
decision you have already made. The presets on the slider exist for that reason.

**Roll forward in steps, and lean on monotonicity.** 5 → 10 → 25 → 50 → 100 is safe in a way that
matters: every step keeps the browsers already on the canary where they are and only adds new ones,
so you are never re-running the split on people who have been fine for an hour.

**Roll back by turning the canary off, not by rewriting the version.** The switch is the stop
button: the fields keep what you typed, so the next attempt starts from the configuration you
already had. Lowering the percentage is the gentler version of the same move, but it does not reach
zero — the form refuses a canary that is enabled and set to 0%. For anything worse than a bad
canary there is [rollback and redeploy](../deployments/rollback-and-redeploy.md).

**Verify with the header, not by counting.** Before you trust a rollout, load the host twice — once
in a normal window and once in a fresh private window — and read `x-mfe-version` on the entry point
of each. Two different values is the split working. With a *Random* canary a plain refresh is
enough. Use `?mfeVersion=` when you need to see the canary on demand rather than by luck.

**Promote by making the canary the version.** Once you are convinced, set the frontend's
version to what the canary was pointing at and turn the canary off. Nothing about the URLs your
host holds changes.

title: Create a frontend
text:
There are two ways to add a frontend to a project: start from a **template**, which
scaffolds a working repository and a build pipeline for you, or register a frontend whose
code already exists somewhere else.

title: Create a frontend — From a template (recommended)
text:
This is the fastest path from nothing to a deployable frontend. Flightroom creates
the repository in your Git provider, fills it with a working Module Federation project, adds a
build-and-deploy pipeline, and injects the API key the pipeline needs to upload artifacts back
to the platform.

### Prerequisites

A connected code repository. If you have not connected one yet, follow
[GitHub](../repositories/connect/github.md), [GitLab](../repositories/connect/gitlab.md) or
[Azure DevOps](../repositories/connect/azure.dev-ops.md) first.

### Steps

1. From the **Frontends** page, click **Add New Frontend**. Next to it,
   **Import from repository** takes the other route, starting from code you already have.

   ![The Frontends page header with the search field, the domain filter, the view switcher and the Add New Frontend button](../assets/add-new-frontend.png)

   Both depend on a connected code repository. Without one, **Import from repository** is hidden and
   **Add New Frontend** skips the templates library and opens the empty form directly — the
   [from scratch](#from-scratch) route.

2. Choose a template from the [templates library](../templates/templates-library.md), which opens
   as a page of its own. Templates are grouped by framework and filtered by framework, compiler
   and host type, so you can narrow down to, for example, *Vite + React + remote*. **Create From
   Scratch**, the first card, skips the template.

   ![The templates library page: the framework, compiler and type filters above the template cards grouped by framework](../assets/choose-a-template.png)

3. Fill in the frontend details. The form is the same one you get when editing later, minus
   the danger zone: a **Release** card on top, then the tabs.

   **Release**

   - **Version** — required, the version this frontend starts on. Pre-filled with `1.0.0`
   - **Canary Settings** — off by default, and there is no reason to turn it on while creating.
     When you do, the type starts on **Session** and the deployment type on **Based on Version**.
     See [canary releases](./canary-releases.md)

   **General**

   - **Kind** — **Bundle** (served by Flightroom, the default) or **Docker** (served by
     its Docker container). See [Bundle or Docker](#bundle-or-docker)
   - **Name** — the display name, 3 to 100 characters
   - **Slug** — 3 to 50 characters. While you type the name, the slug is derived from it: lowercase,
     with every character other than a letter or a digit turned into `-`. You can still edit it
     before saving. It ends up in your public URLs, so choose carefully
   - **Description** — optional
   - **Domain** — optional, the [functional domain](../core-concepts.md#functional-domain) the
     frontend belongs to

   ![The creation form: the Release card with the version, then the General tab with kind, name Wishlist, slug wishlist, description and domain](../assets/frontend-fill-information.png)

   **AI context** — optional Markdown notes for the AI agents that work on this frontend, at
   most 20,000 characters. What applies to every frontend belongs in the project context, in
   **Settings**.

   **Hosting** — see [hosting options](./hosting-options.md). A **Docker** frontend has a **Container**
   tab here instead.

   **Repository** — only shown when the project has a code repository connection. Created from a
   template, its **Code Repository** switch is already on:

   - **Source Code Provider** — which connected repository the new repo is created in
   - **GitLab Group** — on a GitLab connection that can see more than one group, the group to
     create it under
   - **Repository Name** — the name of the repository to create, pre-filled from the slug.
     Availability is checked as you type
   - **Private Repository** — a switch, on GitHub. Off creates a public repository

4. Click **Save**.

### What happens behind the scenes

Creating from a template is not just a `git init`. Flightroom:

1. **Creates the repository** in the selected provider, under the user account, organization or
   group you chose.
2. **Downloads the template** archive and pushes its contents as the initial commit.
3. **Injects a build pipeline** matching your provider and compiler — a GitHub Actions workflow
   (`.github/workflows/build-and-deploy.yml`), a GitLab CI file (`.gitlab-ci.yml`) or an Azure
   DevOps pipeline (`azure-pipelines.yml`). The pipeline is pre-filled with your frontend's
   slug and the API base URL of this installation.
4. **Registers the frontend** in the project, linked to the new repository, with the
   template's entry point and stack.

The pipeline authenticates its upload with the secret `MICROFRONTEND_ORCHESTRATOR_API_KEY`. Most of
the time that secret already exists before you create anything: an API key with the `MANAGER` role,
valid for one year, is created when the code repository **connection** is made, and stored where
every repository of the connection can read it — an organization secret on a GitHub organization, a
CI/CD variable of the group on GitLab, the variable group `MFE_ORCHESTRATOR_SECRETS` on Azure
DevOps. Scaffolding adds a key of its own, as a secret of the new repository, only on a **personal
GitHub account**, where there is no organization to hold one. See
[keys created for you](../ci-cd/api-keys.md#keys-created-for-you).

:::info
Because the deploy secret is in place, the generated pipeline works on its first run — you do not
have to copy any key by hand. Keys expire after a year: when the pipeline's upload starts failing
with an authentication error, that is the first thing to check.
:::

title: Create a frontend — From scratch
text:
Pick **Create From Scratch** in the templates library — or click **Add New Frontend** in a
project with no code repository connection — when the code already exists, or when you want to
bring your own project layout. You fill in the same release and general information, plus the
hosting configuration:

- **Flightroom Hub** — you will upload builds to the platform
- **Custom Source** — you will upload builds to your own bucket
- **Custom URL** — the files are already served from a URL you control

See [Hosting options](./hosting-options.md) for the details of each, and
[Versions and builds](./versions-and-builds.md) for how to get artifacts in.

The **Code Repository** switch of the **Repository** tab starts off. Turned on at creation, it
creates a **new, empty** repository; there is no template to push and no pipeline to add. To link a
repository that already exists, save first and pick it under **Select Repository** when editing, or
use **Import from repository** on the Frontends page, which creates one frontend for each
repository you tick among those of a connection — repositories already linked to a frontend or
a service are skipped. A linked repository enables the
**Build** action on the frontend card, but Flightroom will not add a pipeline to a repository
it did not create. To use the same automation, copy the relevant pipeline from the
[template-pipelines repository](https://github.com/mfe-orchestrator/template-pipelines); the API key
it needs is usually already there from the connection (see above), and otherwise you
[create one](../ci-cd/api-keys.md) yourself.

title: Create a frontend — Bundle or Docker
text:
The **Kind** at the top of the **General** tab decides who serves the code:

| | Bundle | Docker |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Served by | Flightroom, from the hub, your bucket or a custom URL | Its own Docker container |
| Configured in | **Hosting** tab | **Container** tab — runtime, image, URLs, environment, config maps and secrets, as for a [service](../kubernetes/services.md) |
| Version | Chosen in **Release** | Read-only: set by the pipeline each time it registers an image version |
| Canary | Available | None: Flightroom cannot split the traffic of a container |
| Parents | Any | None. It cannot be the remote of a host, so in the Diagram view no link can end on it |
| Bundle upload | Accepted | Refused with `DOCKER_FRONTEND_UPLOAD_NOT_ALLOWED`: its pipeline registers the image of each version instead |

A frontend created under a parent — from a link dropped on empty canvas in the Diagram view —
is always a **Bundle**, and one that already has parents cannot be switched to **Docker**.
The templates scaffold a pipeline that uploads a bundle: pick **Docker** on a template and the
form warns you to change the pipeline so it builds the Docker image and registers its version.

A Docker frontend never appears in the manifest of [`/serve/all`](../integration/serve-api.md): no host
loads it as a remote.

title: Create a frontend — Editing a frontend
text:
Opening a frontend from its card leads to the same form in edit mode — directly through
**Configuration**, or, when the card offers **Edit with AI**, through the **Details & settings** tab
next to the AI workspace. **Release** sits at the top, outside the tabs, because the version and the
canary are what decide which bytes a browser gets; everything else is behind a tab:

| Where | Contains |
| --- | --- |
| Release (above the tabs) | Version, and **Canary Settings** — progressive rollout, see [Canary releases](./canary-releases.md). A Docker frontend shows its version read-only and no canary |
| General | Kind, name, slug (read-only), description, domain |
| AI context | Markdown notes for AI agents, at most 20,000 characters |
| Hosting | Hosting type, storage or URL, entry point. **Container** instead, for a Docker frontend |
| Repository | The linked repository — only when the project has a code repository connection |
| Danger Zone | Delete this frontend |

In **Repository**, **Select Repository** lists the repositories of the chosen connection, so you can
link one or change it. Once a repository is linked and saved, **Rename repository** renames it at the
provider; local clones then have to update their remote URL — GitHub and GitLab redirect the old one,
Azure DevOps does not. The card of a frontend with a linked repository also carries **Clone
repo**, with the HTTPS and SSH clone commands and shortcuts to clone in VS Code or IntelliJ IDEA.

Switching tab keeps what you typed: every panel stays mounted, so a value entered under **Hosting**
survives a detour through **General**. A tab whose fields failed validation is marked with a dot,
and submitting an invalid form jumps to the first one — an error is never hidden behind an inactive
tab.

![The Add New Frontend form: the Release card with the version and the canary switch, above the General, AI context and Hosting tabs](../assets/frontend-form.png)

Remember that edits take effect for your users only after the next
[deployment](../deployments/overview.md).

title: Hosts and remotes in Module Federation
text:
Frontends composed with Module Federation only form an architecture once the pieces know about each
other.
This page covers how Flightroom models those relationships, and what it does with them.

title: Hosts and remotes in Module Federation — The relation graph
text:
Every frontend can have **parents** — the hosts that load it. In the **Diagram view** on
the Frontends page, relations are the arrows between nodes; you create and remove them
there directly.

A typical setup looks like this:

```
        shell  (host)
       ╱   │   ╲
 catalog  cart  account   (remotes)
              ╲
             payments     (remote of a remote)
```

In the console the same graph looks like this — `payments` is a remote of `cart`, which is
itself a remote of `shell`:

![Diagram view showing the relation graph between host and remotes](../assets/frontends-diagram-view.png)

Nothing stops a remote from being a host of other remotes, and nothing stops a remote from
having several parents — a shared design-system remote consumed by three hosts is a perfectly
normal shape. The one exception is a frontend of the **Docker** kind, served by its own Docker
container: it can have children but no parents, so in the Diagram view no link can end on it.

In the Diagram view, drag from a node's bottom handle to another node to make the second a remote
of the first. Dropping the link on empty canvas starts a new frontend already set as a child of
the node you dragged from. To remove a relation, select the link and press **Delete**.

title: Hosts and remotes in Module Federation — Why the graph matters
text:
The graph is what lets Flightroom generate your Module Federation configuration. When a
host asks the platform for its remotes, the answer is computed as:

> all frontends in the **active deployment** whose parents include this host

and each of them is resolved to a concrete URL, based on that frontend's hosting type and
the version frozen in the deployment.

The consequence worth internalising: **your host's build configuration does not contain version
numbers or URLs**. It contains the remote names and a call into the
[client SDK](../integration/client-sdk.md), which fetches the URLs at import time. Bumping a remote
from `1.3.0` to `1.4.0` in production is a deployment, not a host rebuild.

title: Hosts and remotes in Module Federation — Remote naming
text:
Module Federation remote names cannot contain `/` or `-`, so Flightroom derives the name
from the slug by replacing every `/` with `_` and removing every `-`:

| Slug | Remote name |
| --- | --- |
| `catalog` | `catalog` |
| `product-catalog` | `productcatalog` |
| `shop/catalog` | `shop_catalog` |

This derived name is what appears in the generated config and what you use in your `import`
