Unlike the rest of this page, this endpoint requires authentication. It is a convenience for
tooling, not something your application calls at runtime.

title: Serve API reference — Error responses
text:
Branch on the **`code`** field, not on the message. The messages are written for a human reading a
log and get reworded as they get more helpful; `code` is the discriminator.

| `code` | Status | Message | Cause |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `ENTITY_NOT_FOUND` | 404 | `Entity not found with id Active deployment` | The environment has never been deployed, or has no active deployment |
| `ENTITY_NOT_FOUND` | 404 | `Entity not found with id <slug or id>` | No such frontend, or the frontend is absent from the deployment that answered |
| `ENVIRONMENT_NOT_FOUND` | 404 | `No environment of project <id> has "<domain>" among its registered domains, …` | An `auto` form was called from a domain registered on no environment of that project |
| `ENVIRONMENT_NOT_FOUND` | 404 | `Environment not found: <slug or id>` | An explicit slug or id form named an environment that does not exist |
| `PROJECT_NOT_FOUND` | 404 | `Project not found: <id>` | The project id in the path is not a project of this console |
| *none* | 500 | `Referer not found` | A `Referer`-required endpoint was called with neither a `Referer` nor a `Host` header |

Note the shape of the first message: `Active deployment` is the *entity id* slotted into a generic
template, which is why it reads the way it does. There is no `Active deployment not found` message.

`Referer not found` is the odd one out. It is thrown as a plain error with no status attached, so it
surfaces as a **500** rather than as the 4xx its neighbours return, and it carries no `code`. Only
the two `/serve/mfe/…/{mfeId}/…` forms demand a `Referer` outright; the `auto` forms fall back to the
`Host` header first, so in practice only a request carrying neither reaches this.

A frontend that exists in the project but was added *after* the last deployment falls into the
second row: deploy the environment to include it.

title: Serve API reference — Building runtime discovery
text:
Use the [client SDK](./client-sdk.md). It calls this endpoint for you, once per page load, with the
identity parameters generated and persisted, and returns URLs you can hand straight to your
federation runtime:

```js
// src/main.js

configure({ backendUrl: API_BASE, projectId: PROJECT_ID, environment: ENV_SLUG })
// environment is optional: drop it and the SDK calls the auto form instead,
// letting the domain decide which environment answers.

window.globalConfig = await globalVariables()

const catalog = await remoteUrl('catalog')   // already version-pinned, use as is

await import('./App')
```

The generated bundler configuration already goes through `remoteUrl()`, so in most hosts there is
nothing to write beyond the `configure()` call.

If you do call the endpoint yourself, remember what the SDK was written to get right: generate and
persist a session id and a device id, send them on every manifest request, and pass each `url`
through untouched.

With this in place, adding a remote to the host is a deployment rather than a release: the roster
is discovered, not compiled in.

title: Get started with Flightroom
text:
Flightroom is an open-source enterprise platform where anyone can build applications and AI agents by describing them in plain language. The AI writes the code in your own Git repositories, your engineers review it, and one click deploys it to your Kubernetes through GitOps and Argo CD, with your single sign-on, your roles and your AI models. This tutorial guides you through your first steps with the platform. :::tip[In a hurry?] The **[quick start](./quick-start.mdx)** is the condensed version of this page: describe an app, review it, deploy it. ::: **Flightroom can be used in two ways:**

🌐 Online Console

Recommended for Tutorial

Use our hosted version - no installation required!

  • ✅ No setup needed
  • ✅ Always up to date
  • ✅ Perfect for getting started
Go to console

🔧 Self-Hosted

Deploy on your own infrastructure for full control.

  • ✅ Complete control
  • ✅ Custom configuration
  • ✅ Production ready
View Installation Options
In this tutorial, we'll use the **online console** available at [https://console.flightroom.dev](https://console.flightroom.dev) to explore Flightroom's features.

title: Get started with Flightroom — Step 1: Access the Console & Register
text:
Open your browser and navigate to:

**[https://console.flightroom.dev](https://console.flightroom.dev)**

To get started, you need to create an account. You have two options:

![The Flightroom sign-in page](./assets/console-login.png)

**Option 1: Register with Email**
1. Click **Register**, next to *Don't have an account?* under the login form
2. Enter your email address and create a password
3. Open the activation email and follow its link, within 24 hours. Until you do, the account cannot
   be used: the password is accepted, but the console sends you straight back to the login form.
   This applies on the hosted console and on any self-hosted instance with SMTP configured; without
   SMTP there is no activation step at all. See
   [Registration and activation](./account/email-flows.md#registration-and-activation)
4. Sign in with your credentials
5. Create your organization on the **Create your organization** screen. The
   [five-step project wizard](./project-settings/projects.md#creating-a-project) then opens inside
   it: name, environments, storage, repositories, collaborators
6. On **Project ready!**, choose **Start deploying your frontends**. The console opens on the
   **AI agent** page, or on **Frontends** while your organization has no AI yet — Step 3 adds one

![Creating an account with email and password](./assets/console-register.png)

**Option 2: Sign in with Google SSO**
1. Under **Or continue with**, click **Google**
2. Select your Google account
3. Authorize Flightroom to access your basic profile
4. You'll be automatically signed in — there is no activation email for an account created this way
5. Create your organization, then go through the
   [five-step project wizard](./project-settings/projects.md#creating-a-project) exactly as in
   Option 1

:::tip[Recommended]
Using Google SSO is faster and you don't need to remember another password!
:::

If you already have an account, simply sign in with your email or Google account.

title: Get started with Flightroom — Step 2: Connect Your Code Repository
text:
The AI writes your apps into repositories Flightroom creates in your Git provider, so the first thing to connect is that provider.

1. Navigate to **[Code Repositories](https://console.flightroom.dev/code-repositories)** or open **Settings → Resources → Code Repositories**

   ![The Code Repositories page before any provider is connected](./assets/code-repositories.png)

2. Click the **Add Repository** button and pick your provider

   ![Choosing a provider in the Add Repository dialog](./assets/add-repository-provider.png)

Flightroom supports multiple repository providers:

- **[GitHub](https://github.com)** - Most commonly used for public and private repositories
  - [See detailed setup guide →](/docs/repositories/connect/github)
- **[GitLab](https://gitlab.com)** - Self-hosted or GitLab.com
  - [See detailed setup guide →](/docs/repositories/connect/gitlab)
- **[Azure DevOps](https://dev.azure.com)** - Microsoft Azure Repos
  - [See detailed setup guide →](/docs/repositories/connect/azure.dev-ops)

:::tip[Quick Start]
For most users, we recommend starting with GitHub as it has the simplest setup process.
:::

title: Get started with Flightroom — Step 3: Add an AI to Your Organization
text:
Flightroom uses the AI model your organization chooses, with your own credentials.

1. Open the organization menu in the header and choose **Organization settings**
2. Open the **AI** tab and choose **Add AI**
3. Pick a provider — Claude through Anthropic, Azure AI Foundry or AWS Bedrock, GPT through Azure
   OpenAI, or Gemini — and enter its credentials

Only organization owners and admins can add an AI. Once one exists, every project of the
organization can use it, unless an admin restricts a project to some models or turns AI off for
it. See [AI models](./build-with-ai/ai-models.md).

title: Get started with Flightroom — Step 4: Build Your First App with AI
text:
1. Open **Domains** in the sidebar and create a **New domain**. A domain groups the web interfaces
   and services of one business capability, for example *Expenses* or *Onboarding*
2. On the domain's **Edit with AI** tab, describe what the team needs and press
   **Generate proposal**
3. The AI proposes the components the request needs: up to three **frontends** (web
   interfaces) and three **services** (backends and agents). Adjust names, repositories and
   templates, then confirm
4. Flightroom creates each repository from its template, CI pipeline included, and the AI writes
   a first version on an `ai/…` branch
5. Keep refining through chat, then **Open a pull request**, apply the change, or discard it

Your base branch is untouched until someone acts on the proposal. See
[Generate a domain with AI](./build-with-ai/generate-a-domain.md) and
[AI changes](./build-with-ai/ai-changes.md).

**Congratulations!** 🎉 You have your first app in your own repositories. To put it in front of
users, [deploy it to Kubernetes](./kubernetes/overview.md).

title: Get started with Flightroom — Alternative: Create a Frontend by Hand
text:
If you would rather start from a template without the AI — for example a web interface served by
Flightroom and composed into a host with Module Federation — create a frontend directly.

1. Open **Frontends** in the sidebar
2. Click **Add New Frontend**, at the top right of the page

   ![The Frontends page header with the search field, the domain filter, the view switcher and the Add New Frontend button](./assets/add-new-frontend.png)

3. Choose a template from the list

   ![The Templates library, with the framework, compiler and type filters above the template cards](./assets/choose-a-template.png)

4. Fill in the required information. The form is split into tabs — **General**, **AI context**,
   **Hosting** and, when the project has a code repository connection, **Repository** — and what
   the template needs is spread over two of them.

   ![The creation form: the Release card with the version, then the General tab with kind, name Wishlist, slug wishlist, description and domain](./assets/frontend-fill-information.png)

   * **General → name**: A descriptive name for your frontend
   * **General → slug**: A URL-friendly identifier (e.g., "my-app"). It is filled in from the name as
     you type, and cannot be changed after creation
   * **Repository → source code provider**: The repository connection to create the new repository in.
     Already selected when the project has only one, or when one of them is the default
   * **Repository → repository name**: The name of the repository to create. Also pre-filled from the
     name, so you only touch it if you want a different one

   Because you came from a template, the **Repository** tab arrives with its switch already on. If the
   tab is missing entirely, the project has no repository connection yet — go back to Step 2.

5. Click **Save** to finalize the setup

:::info[Automatic Setup]
Flightroom will automatically:
- ✅ **Create the repository** in your selected source code provider with the chosen template
- ✅ **Initialize the frontend** with all necessary configurations
- ✅ **Set up the deployment pipeline** ready for your first deployment

This process usually takes a few seconds. You'll see a success message once everything is ready!
:::

Your frontend now exists. The [frontend quick start](./frontends/quick-start.mdx) takes it from here to a deployed version and a rollback.

title: Get started with Flightroom — Next steps
text:
1. **[Understand the model](./core-concepts.md)** — organizations, projects, domains,
   environments and deployments, and how they relate.
2. **[Set up your environments](./environments/overview.md)** — dev, UAT, production or your own
   stages, each its own Kubernetes namespace.
3. **[Deploy to Kubernetes](./kubernetes/overview.md)** — connect a GitOps repository and your
   Argo CD once, then ship with one click.
4. **[Keep improving with AI](./build-with-ai/ai-changes.md)** — ask for the next change on any
   frontend, service or domain.

### Going further

- **[Guardrails](./build-with-ai/guardrails.md)** — what the AI can and cannot touch, and how
  review and roles keep it in check
- **[Console assistant](./build-with-ai/console-assistant.md)** — ask the console to act for you,
  with a confirmation before anything destructive
- **[Frontends](./frontends/overview.md)** — versions, hosting options, canary releases
  and generated [Module Federation configuration](./integration/overview.md)
- **[Organizations](./organizations/overview.md)** — the tenant that owns your projects, and who
  reaches which one
- **[Members and roles](./project-settings/users-and-roles.md)** — invite your team
- **[Self hosting](./self-hosting/helm.md)** — run the platform on your own infrastructure

title: Argo CD
text:
**Initialize Argo CD** hands the GitOps repositories of a project to an Argo CD you already run, so
that what each deploy commits is what the cluster runs. Argo CD stays on its own cluster: the console
talks to its API over HTTPS, holds no credentials for your cluster, and every environment is deployed
to the cluster Argo CD runs in.

The section is under **Settings → Delivery → Argo CD**, and appears once [GitOps](./gitops.md) is on
and its configuration repository is saved. Only an owner of the project or an administrator of its
organization can initialize it; the other members see its status.

title: Argo CD — Requirements
text:
- **Argo CD 2.8 or later.**
- **Its API reachable from the Flightroom backend over HTTPS**, through an Ingress, a load balancer
  or a private link between the clusters. Argo CD itself never calls Flightroom: it reads the
  repositories from your Git provider.
- **A certificate Node.js trusts.** For a private CA, set `NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS` on the Flightroom
  backend.
- **The URL Argo CD answers at**, without `/api/v1` and without redirects: for example
  `https://argocd.example.com`.

Plain `http` is refused, since the token and the repository credentials would cross the network in
the clear. For a local cluster only, the installation can allow it with
`ARGOCD_ALLOW_INSECURE_HTTP=true` on the backend.

title: Argo CD — Preparing Argo CD
text:
The console acts in Argo CD as a local account named `orchestrator`, with an API key and no
password. The **Argo CD account permissions** panel in the section shows the same steps. If these
ConfigMaps already hold other keys, add the lines rather than replacing them.

**1. The account**, in `argocd-cm`:

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: argocd-cm
  namespace: argocd
data:
  accounts.orchestrator: apiKey
```

**2. Its permissions**, in `argocd-rbac-cm`. Everything the console creates is named `mfe-…`, so the
account can touch only its own objects:

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: argocd-rbac-cm
  namespace: argocd
data:
  policy.csv: |
    p, role:orchestrator, projects, *, mfe-*, allow
    p, role:orchestrator, applications, *, mfe-*/*, allow
    p, role:orchestrator, applicationsets, *, mfe-*/*, allow
    p, role:orchestrator, repositories, *, *, allow
    g, orchestrator, role:orchestrator
```

The repositories rule cannot be narrowed the same way: the applications repository is registered
globally, and the rule applies to its URL.

**3. The policy per ApplicationSet**, in `argocd-cmd-params-cm`, then restart
`argocd-applicationset-controller`:

```yaml
data:
  applicationsetcontroller.enable.policy.override: "true"
```

Without it, Argo CD ignores the policy that keeps an application from being deleted when its values
file disappears from a branch by mistake.

**4. The token**, to paste in the settings:

```bash
argocd account generate-token --account orchestrator
```

title: Argo CD — Initializing
text:
| Field | What to enter |
| --- | --- |
| **Argo CD URL** | The URL of the Argo CD server, e.g. `https://argocd.example.com` |
| **Argo CD API token** | The token of the `orchestrator` account. Checked against Argo CD before anything is written, stored encrypted when `SECRETS_ENCRYPTION_KEY` is set, and never sent back to the browser |
| **Read-only repository token** | For GitHub and Azure DevOps repositories, a token Argo CD can clone with. Not needed for GitLab |

Argo CD reads the repositories with read-only credentials of its own, never with the token of the
project's connection, which can write:

| Provider | Read-only credentials |
| --- | --- |
| GitLab | Nothing to do. The console creates a deploy token with `read_repository` on each repository and replaces it on every initialization. The connection's token needs the **Maintainer** role on the repositories and the `api` scope |
| GitHub | A fine-grained personal access token with **Contents: Read-only** on the two repositories |
| Azure DevOps | A personal access token with **Code: Read** |

The repository token is required on the first initialization and whenever the URL changes; leave it
empty otherwise to keep the stored one.

Press **Initialize Argo CD**. Once it has gone through, the button becomes **Re-align Argo CD** and
the section shows the date of the last initialization.

Before writing anything, the console checks that every name it is about to take in Argo CD is free
or already its own, and that no repository it registers was registered by someone else. Anything
taken stops the initialization with nothing changed.

title: Argo CD — What gets created
text:
`<project>` below stands for `mfe-<project slug>-<hash>`: the hash keeps two projects with the same
slug, in two organizations, apart.

| Object | Name | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| AppProject | `<project>` | Lets the applications of the project read its two repositories only, and deploy only to the namespaces of its environments |
| Repository credentials | One per repository | Read-only, over HTTPS |
| ApplicationSet | `<project>.environments` | One Application per environment, `<project>.<environment>`, syncing the environment's folder of the configuration repository into its namespace |
| ApplicationSet | `<project>.<application>` | With an applications repository, one per service and Docker frontend that has an image and a version. One Application per environment, `<project>.<application>-<environment>`, installing `microservice-chart/` with `<application>.yaml` from the environment's branch |

Every Application syncs automatically, with **prune** and **self-heal**: Argo CD applies each commit
and puts back anything changed by hand in the cluster. The Applications of the services create their
namespace if it does not exist yet.

### What is never deleted

- **Namespaces are never pruned or deleted** by Argo CD, so an emptied repository or a deleted
  Application cannot take running apps down with it.
- **The ApplicationSet of a service never deletes its Applications**, with the policy override
  above. An application whose values file is gone for good is deleted by hand in Argo CD.

### Names and lengths

Argo CD names fit 63 characters; a longer part is cut and ends with a hash. The Helm release of an
application is its slug, and Helm refuses a release name over **53 characters**: an application with a
longer slug fails to sync, with that error in Argo CD. Keep service and Docker frontend slugs shorter.

Two objects of the project that would get the same name stop the initialization: a service
`orders-api` in environment `dev` and a service `orders` in environment `api-dev` would both be
`<project>.orders-api-dev`. Rename one of them.

:::warning[Keep secrets out of the Helm values]
The applications repository is registered globally, so every AppProject of the Argo CD instance can
read it. Secrets belong in the [secrets](./config-maps-and-secrets.md) of the project, which go to the
configuration repository.
:::

title: Argo CD — Re-aligning
text:
**After adding or deleting an environment, or changing the GitOps repositories, press Re-align Argo
CD.** A new environment's namespace joins the AppProject only then, and until then deploys leave it
out of the ApplicationSets.

New services and Docker frontends need nothing: every deploy updates the ApplicationSet of each one, so a
service deployed for the first time gets its Applications on its own. A deploy that cannot update
Argo CD still goes through, and the reason shows in the section as *The last deploy did not update
the applications in Argo CD*, until a deploy that does clears it.

When you re-align:

- New environments join the ApplicationSets, once their branch exists.
- Deleted environments leave them. Argo CD deletes the environment's Application, but what it
  deployed stays in the cluster until you remove it; the Applications of the services in that
  environment are left for you to delete by hand.
- The ApplicationSet of a deleted service or Docker frontend is deleted with its Applications; its
  workloads stay in the cluster.
- The credentials of a repository no longer linked are removed from Argo CD, and a GitLab deploy
  token is revoked.

One initialization of a project runs at a time.

title: Argo CD — Moving to another Argo CD
text:
Pointing the project at another URL asks for the Argo CD token and the repository token again: the
stored ones are never sent to another server. What the console created on the old instance stays
there: remove its AppProject, ApplicationSets, Applications and repository credentials by hand. GitLab
deploy tokens are revoked for you; a GitHub or Azure DevOps token you pasted is yours to revoke.

title: Argo CD — When it fails
text:
The error shows in the section, under *The last initialization failed*, until an initialization goes
through.

| Error | What to check |
| --- | --- |
| Argo CD cannot be reached | The URL, its DNS name, and that the Flightroom backend can reach the Argo CD API |
| The certificate is not trusted | The certificate of Argo CD, or `NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS` |
| The token is not accepted | That it is a token of the `orchestrator` account, not expired or revoked |
| The account lacks permissions | The policy in `argocd-rbac-cm` above |
| Argo CD already has an object with that name | An AppProject, Application or ApplicationSet not created by this project: rename or delete it |
| The repository is already registered | A registration made by hand or by another project: remove it from Argo CD |
| The GitLab deploy token was not created | The role and scopes of the GitLab connection |
| Argo CD is already being initialized | Another initialization of the project: wait for it to end |
| Argo CD was initialized with other repositories, or by an earlier version | Initialize again |

title: Argo CD — Where to go next
text:
- [Exposure](./exposure.md): give each environment a host and each app a path
- [Rollback](./rollback.md): what a rollback means once Argo CD is in charge

title: Config maps and secrets
text:
Config maps and secrets hold the configuration of your services, with a value per environment. They
reach the container as environment variables, through Kubernetes ConfigMaps and Secrets that every
deploy commits to the configuration repository.

| | Config maps | Secrets |
| --- | --- | --- |
| For | Non-sensitive values: URLs, feature flags, log levels | Sensitive values: API keys, passwords, tokens |
| In the console | Visible to anyone who can see the project | Encrypted at rest and never shown again once saved |
| In Kubernetes | A ConfigMap per environment | A Secret per environment, values base64 encoded |

:::info[Not the same as frontend environment variables]
These values are for containers running in Kubernetes. The variables a frontend reads in the
browser are [runtime environment variables](../environments/environment-variables.md), served by
Flightroom and never committed to Git.
:::

title: Config maps and secrets — Creating one
text:
Open **Config maps** or **Secrets** in the **Backend services** section of the sidebar, and press
**New config map** or **New secret**. The form opens at `/config-map/new` or `/secret/new`.

| Field | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| **Name** | At most 63 lowercase letters, digits or dashes, starting and ending with a letter or digit: it becomes the name of the Kubernetes object as it is. Unique in the project |
| **Description** | What these values are for, at most 2000 characters |
| **Keys** | Each **Key** with a value per environment. Keys take letters, digits and underscores, and do not start with a digit |

| Limit | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Keys per map | 200 |
| Length of one value | 32,768 characters (32 KiB) |
| Maps attached to one service | 50 config maps, and 50 secrets |

A secret value cannot start with `enc:v1:`, the prefix the console gives to the values it encrypts.

The list of maps can be searched by name, key or service using the map. Inside a map, the keys can be
searched too: a config map by key or value, a secret by key only, since its saved values are never
shown.

![The Config maps list with the orders-api-config map, its description, three keys and the Orders API service under Used by](../assets/config-maps-list.png)

A key left empty in an environment is not set there: the container in that environment does not get
it.

![The orders-api-config config map, with its name, description and keys holding a value for Development, Staging and Production](../assets/config-map-detail.png)

A saved secret value is never shown again: leave it as it is to keep it. To rename a saved key of a
secret, remove it and add it again, then type its values again.

![The orders-api-secrets secret, with saved keys locked against renaming and their values masked in every environment](../assets/secret-detail.png)

title: Config maps and secrets — Attaching them to a service
text:
A config map or a secret belongs to the project, and any number of services can attach it. Attach
them in the settings of the service, under **Config maps and secrets**, or in the **Container** tab
of a Docker frontend. The page of each map lists the services that use it, under **Used by**.

No key may be set by two of the maps a service attaches: the console refuses the pair.

Every key of every attached map reaches the container as an environment variable of the same name,
through `envFrom` in the chart. A service's own **Environment variables** list documents which names
the container expects; it holds names only, never values.

To delete a map, detach it from every service first, then confirm by typing its name.

title: Config maps and secrets — Who can change them
text:
A member scoped to a functional domain sees only the maps attached exclusively to services and
Docker frontends of their own domains. A map shared with a component of another domain, or of no
domain, or attached to nothing, is hidden from them. They can edit the maps they see and attach them
to their components, but cannot attach any other map, and cannot create or delete maps.

Every other member of the project can create, edit and delete config maps and secrets, a **Viewer**
included: the console does not refuse a viewer here as it does for [databases](./databases.md) and
GitOps deploys.

title: Config maps and secrets — When the values reach the cluster
text:
Saving a map commits nothing. The values reach the cluster on the next **Deploy** of each
environment, when the console commits:

- `<environment>/configMaps/<name>.yaml` for each config map
- `<environment>/secrets/<name>.yaml` for each secret

to the configuration repository, in the namespace of the environment. Argo CD applies them, and a
map you deleted disappears from the repository on that same deploy.

A **Deploy <domain>** of one functional domain still commits every config map and secret of the
environment as they are now.

The deployments page shows, for each deployment, the **Config maps** and **Secrets** it shipped.
Secret values are not kept in the deployment.

title: Config maps and secrets — How secrets are protected
text:
**In the console**, the values of every secret are encrypted at rest in the database when the
installation sets `SECRETS_ENCRYPTION_KEY`. See
[Encryption at rest](../self-hosting/encryption-at-rest.md).

**In Git**, they are not. A Kubernetes Secret manifest stores its values base64 encoded, which is an
encoding, not encryption.

:::danger[Keep the configuration repository private]
Anyone who can read the configuration repository, or its history, can decode every secret in it.
Use a private repository with restricted access. The console warns about this in the GitOps
settings, and creates new GitOps repositories private.
:::

The console deletes its working copy of the repository after each deploy, so the plaintext values
do not stay on the Flightroom server.

title: Config maps and secrets — An agent's model key
text:
An agent calls a model, and the model's API key is a secret like any other. Create a secret, say
`support-agent-model`, with a key such as `MODEL_API_KEY`, give it a value in each environment, and
attach it to the agent's service. With a different key per environment, a test in `dev` never spends
the production key, and a key leaked from one environment can be revoked without touching the others.

title: Config maps and secrets — Where to go next
text:
- [GitOps repositories](./gitops.md): what else each deploy commits
- [Databases](./databases.md): registering the databases your services work with

title: Databases
text:
A project can register the SQL databases its apps work with, so that the data your company already
has is known to the project. Flightroom stores the connection and tests it. It does not create
databases, and it does not wire a registered database into a service for you: give a service its
connection details through a [secret](./config-maps-and-secrets.md).

Databases live under **Databases**, in the **Cloud** section of the sidebar, and are also reachable
from **Settings → Resources**. The list shows each database's **Name**, **Engine** and **Address**:
`host:port/database` for one registered with host and credentials, *Connection string* for the others.

![The Databases list with the orders-db PostgreSQL database and its host:port/database address](../assets/databases-list.png)

title: Databases — Registering a database
text:
Press **New database** and fill in:

| Field | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| **Name** | How the project calls it, e.g. `orders-production` |
| **Engine** | **PostgreSQL**, **MySQL**, **MariaDB**, **SQL Server** or **Oracle**. **PostgreSQL** by default |
| **Connection mode** | **Host and credentials**, the default, or **Connection string** |

With **Host and credentials**:

| Field | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| **Host** | Required |
| **Port** | A number between 1 and 65535. It follows the default port of the engine you pick (`5432` PostgreSQL, `3306` MySQL and MariaDB, `1433` SQL Server, `1521` Oracle) until you change it by hand |
| **Database name** | Required |
| **Username** | Required |
| **Password** | Required |
| **Encrypted connection (SSL/TLS)** | Connects over TLS. On by default |

![The New database form in Host and credentials mode, with the PostgreSQL default port, the SSL/TLS switch on and Test connection](../assets/database-new.png)

With **Connection string**, paste the string in the format of the engine; the form shows an example
for each one.

title: Databases — Testing the connection
text:
**Test connection** connects from the Flightroom server with what the form holds, without saving it,
and runs `SELECT 1`. The connection times out after 5 seconds, and the result says what the database
answered when it fails.

Tests are limited to 10 per minute per user, counted together with the connection tests of the other
screens of the console.

The test runs from the Flightroom server, not from your cluster: a database reachable only from
inside the cluster fails the test even though your services can reach it.

title: Databases — Credentials
text:
Passwords and connection strings are never shown again once saved: leave them as they are to keep
the stored ones. They are encrypted at rest when the installation sets `SECRETS_ENCRYPTION_KEY`. A stored password is kept only while the engine and the address stay the
same. Change the engine, the host, the port, the database name or the username, and you are asked to
type it again, so that a stored password is never sent to another host.

Removing a database from the project disconnects it only: the database and its data are not touched.

title: Databases — Who can change databases
text:
Viewers, and members scoped to a functional domain, can see the databases of the project but cannot
create, edit, test or delete them: databases belong to the whole project, not to one of its domains.

An administrator of the organization is the exception among viewers: even with the **Viewer** role in
the project, they act there as an owner and can change its databases.

title: Databases — Where to go next
text:
- [Config maps and secrets](./config-maps-and-secrets.md): passing connection details to a service
- [Encryption at rest](../self-hosting/encryption-at-rest.md): how stored credentials are protected

title: Exposure
text:
Exposure puts each environment of a project on a host of its own and each service under a path of
that host, through the Kubernetes Gateway API as Traefik implements it. Every deploy commits the
Gateway and the routes, and Argo CD applies them with the rest of the environment.

```
https://<subdomain>.<domain><exposure path>

https://dev.example.com/api/orders   → orders-api in dev
https://example.com/api/orders       → orders-api in production
```

title: Exposure — The three settings
text:
| Where | Field | Example | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Settings → Delivery → Exposure** | **Domain** | `example.com` | The domain every environment is exposed under |
| The environment | **Subdomain** | `dev` | The host of the environment: `dev.example.com` |
| The service or Docker frontend | **Exposure path** | `/api/orders` | Where the app answers on the host of every environment |

The **Exposure** section lives on **Settings → Delivery**, below the GitOps section. It appears once
[GitOps](./gitops.md) is on **and** its configuration repository is saved: turning the switch on is
not enough until you press **Save**. Changes apply from the next deploy of each environment.

### Domain and certificate issuer

| Field | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| **Domain** | A lowercase domain of at least two labels. Left empty, the environments are not exposed, and the next deploy removes their Gateway |
| **Certificate issuer** | The cert-manager ClusterIssuer each environment's certificate is asked of: **None (HTTP only)**, `letsencrypt`, `letsencrypt-staging`, or **Other…** to type the **ClusterIssuer name** |
| **Traefik ports** | **HTTP port** and **HTTPS port**: the ports Traefik's `web` and `websecure` entry points listen on inside the pod. `80` and `443` by default |

A Traefik Helm chart left at its defaults listens on `8000` and `8443`: write those under **Traefik
ports** rather than changing Traefik.

### Subdomain of an environment

Set it in the environment form, next to **Kubernetes namespace**. Both fields appear only while GitOps
is on. Left empty, a **Production**
environment takes the domain itself, and any other environment takes its slug in lowercase, so `UAT`
lands on `uat.example.com`. Two environments of the project cannot share a host: the deploy is
refused.

### Exposure path of a service

Set it in the service settings, or in the **Container** tab of a Docker frontend. The path is the same
in every environment, and the prefix is stripped before the request reaches the container, so the app
answers at its root: a request to `/api/orders/items` reaches the container as `/items`.

A service without an exposure path gets no route: it is reachable only inside the cluster, through
its Kubernetes Service. Two applications of the project at the same path, `/api` and `/api/`
included, refuse the deploy.

title: Exposure — What each deploy commits
text:
| Repository | File | Content |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Configuration | `<environment>/gateway.yaml` | The Gateway of the environment on its host, with an `http` listener and, with an issuer, an `https` one, the cert-manager Certificate it serves, and a route redirecting HTTP to HTTPS |
| Applications, branch of the environment | `<application>.yaml` | The route of the app: the Gateway, the listener and the path |
| Applications, branch of the environment | `microservice-chart/templates/httproute.yaml` | The HTTPRoute template, written once with the rest of the chart |

With an issuer, HTTPS answers carry `Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000`, without
`includeSubDomains`, since an environment on the bare domain would otherwise force HTTPS on every host
under it. Without an issuer, the environments answer in plain HTTP.

title: Exposure — What the cluster needs
text:
1. **The Gateway API CRDs** (`gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1`).
2. **Traefik v3 with its Gateway provider on**, which registers the `traefik` GatewayClass:

   ```yaml
   providers:
     kubernetesGateway:
       enabled: true
   ```

   The Traefik version must support the `URLRewrite` and `ResponseHeaderModifier` filters of
   HTTPRoute: check the Gateway provider page of the Traefik documentation for your version.
3. **For TLS, cert-manager** and the ClusterIssuer set on the project. An issuer that solves HTTP-01
   through an Ingress class (`http01.ingress.class: traefik`) keeps working as long as Traefik's
   Ingress provider stays on. For an issuer that would solve it through the Gateway API, prefer
   DNS-01: it would otherwise have to name the Gateway of each project.

On a cluster still without the Gateway API or cert-manager CRDs, the config maps and secrets of the
environment keep syncing: the Gateway manifests are skipped in Argo CD's dry run rather than failing
the whole Application.

title: Exposure — Where to go next
text:
- [Config maps and secrets](./config-maps-and-secrets.md): configuration for the apps you just exposed
- [Environments](../environments/overview.md): the environment form

title: GitOps repositories
text:
With GitOps on, every **Deploy** commits what it ships to Git first. The repositories, not the
console, say what each environment runs, and Argo CD applies them to the cluster.

GitOps lives under **Settings → Delivery**, in the section **GitOps for environments, config maps
and secrets**.

The same tab holds, once GitOps is saved, the [Exposure](./exposure.md) and [Argo CD](./argo-cd.md)
sections, and, whether GitOps is on or not, the **Pipeline templates** a new frontend or service
gets when its repository is created. See
[Your own pipeline templates](../templates/templates-library.md#your-own-pipeline-templates).

title: GitOps repositories — Turning it on
text:
1. Turn on **Commit to a repository on every Deploy**.
2. Under **Configuration repository**, pick a **Connection** of the project and a **Repository**, or
   choose **+ Create a new repository** and type the **Name of the new repository**. A new repository
   is created private, when you save, with a first commit holding a README.
3. To deploy services to Kubernetes, turn on **Also commit the applications** and pick, or create,
   the **Applications repository** the same way.
4. Press **Save**.

The connections are the [code repository connections](../repositories/connect/github.md) of the
project. Without one, the section asks you to add one in **Code Repositories** first.

Saving commits nothing. Each **Deploy** commits what it ships, and the repositories fill up one
environment at a time as you deploy them.

Only an owner of the project (**Admin** in the console) or an administrator of its organization can
change these settings: they decide where the secrets of the project are pushed. Anyone else gets
*Only an owner of the project can change the GitOps settings*.

title: GitOps repositories — What a deploy commits
text:
### Configuration repository

On its default branch, one folder per environment, named as the environment slug:

| File | Content |
| --- | --- |
| `<environment>/namespace.yaml` | The Namespace of the environment |
| `<environment>/gateway.yaml` | The Gateway, Certificate and HTTPS redirect of the environment, when the project has an [exposure](./exposure.md) domain |
| `<environment>/configMaps/<name>.yaml` | A ConfigMap per config map of the project, with the values of that environment |
| `<environment>/secrets/<name>.yaml` | A Secret per secret of the project, with the values of that environment, base64 encoded |

A key left empty in an environment is left out of its manifest, so the container does not get it
there.

### Applications repository

One branch per environment, named as its slug. A branch that does not exist yet is created from the
default branch on the first deploy of that environment.

| Path | Content |
| --- | --- |
| `<application>.yaml` | The Helm values of each service and Docker frontend: image, version, port, probes, the config maps and secrets it attaches and, when exposed, its route |
| `microservice-chart/` | The Helm chart every application is installed with |

The chart is written only when the branch does not have it yet. After that it is yours: change its
resources or templates as your cluster needs, and deploys leave it alone. The values files, on the
other hand, are rewritten by every deploy.

:::warning[Do not edit the generated files]
The manifests in the configuration repository and the values files in the applications repository
are overwritten by the next deploy of the environment. Change the configuration in the console
instead, and deploy.
:::

### What is cleaned up

A deploy also removes the files the console wrote that no longer correspond to anything: the
manifest of a deleted config map or secret, the folder of a deleted environment, the values file of
a deleted service. A file without the console's `app.kubernetes.io/managed-by: mfe-orchestrator`
marker is someone else's and is never touched.

title: GitOps repositories — When it fails
text:
The commits come before the deployment is recorded, so the console and Git cannot disagree:

- **A commit fails:** the deploy does not start, with *The commit to <repository> did not go
  through (…): nothing was deployed or saved*.
- **The deployment cannot be recorded after the push:** the console commits the files back to what
  the branches held before, so Git does not claim a deploy that did not happen.
- **Another deploy of the project is being committed:** the second one waits up to 30 seconds, then
  stops with *Another deploy is being committed to the GitOps repository: try again in a moment*.

Some deploys are refused before anything is pushed, because the cluster would not accept them:

| Refusal | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| The environment slug cannot be a Kubernetes namespace | Set a valid **Kubernetes namespace** on the environment: up to 63 lowercase letters, digits and dashes |
| The subdomain of an environment is not valid | Fix its **Subdomain**. See [Exposure](./exposure.md) |
| Two environments are exposed on the same host | Give each one a subdomain of its own |
| Two services are exposed at the same path | Give each one an exposure path of its own |

title: GitOps repositories — Who can deploy
text:
With GitOps on, a deploy pushes to your Git provider with the token of the connection. A **Viewer**
of the project is refused with *A viewer cannot deploy what is committed to the GitOps
repositories*. Every other member can deploy.

A member scoped to a functional domain writes the values of their own domain's applications only,
and a **Deploy <domain>** writes the values of that domain only. In both cases the config maps
and secrets of the environment are still committed as they are now.

title: GitOps repositories — Git as the audit trail
text:
Every deploy is a commit named `Deploy <environment>`, authored by the person who pressed
**Deploy**; a deploy made with an API key is signed by the console itself. Only the files that
changed are committed, so the history of a repository reads as the history of its environments:
who changed which value, and when.

title: GitOps repositories — Keep the configuration repository private
text:
:::danger[Secrets are committed base64 encoded, not encrypted]
Base64 is an encoding: anyone who can read the configuration repository, or its history, can decode
the values of the secrets. Use a private repository and restrict who can read it. The console
creates new repositories private for this reason.
:::

Never put a secret in a service's Helm values either: the applications repository is readable by
every project of the Argo CD instance. Secrets belong in the [secrets](./config-maps-and-secrets.md)
of the project.

title: GitOps repositories — Where to go next
text:
- [Argo CD](./argo-cd.md): hand these repositories to Argo CD
- [Config maps and secrets](./config-maps-and-secrets.md): what ends up in `configMaps/` and `secrets/`

title: Deploy to Kubernetes
text:
Flightroom deploys the backends of a project to your Kubernetes cluster with the same **Deploy**
button that activates frontends. Behind the button, every deploy is a Git commit, and the Argo
CD you already run applies that commit to the cluster.

An **agent** is deployed exactly like any other backend: it is a **service** that happens to call a
model. Everything on this page applies to both. How a service is created and configured in the
console is covered in [Services](./services.md). How apps and agents get written in the first place
is covered in [Build with AI](../build-with-ai/overview.md).

title: Deploy to Kubernetes — What one click does
text:
```mermaid flowchart LR A["Deploy pressed
in the console"] --> B["Commit to the
configuration repository"] B --> C["Commit to the
applications repository"] C --> D["Deployment recorded
in Flightroom"] D --> E["Argo CD syncs
the cluster"] E --> F["App answers on
https://host/path"] ``` 1. **A member of the project presses Deploy.** Open **Deployments** in the **DevOps** section of the sidebar, pick the environment in the selector and press **Deploy**. A functional domain can be deployed on its own with **Deploy <domain>**. The console assistant can deploy too, after you confirm the action it proposes. 2. **Flightroom commits to Git.** The manifests of the environment go to the configuration repository, and the Helm values of each service to the applications repository. See [GitOps repositories](./gitops.md). 3. **Flightroom records the deployment**, only once the commits are pushed. If a commit fails, nothing is deployed. 4. **Argo CD syncs the cluster.** It watches the repositories through the objects Flightroom set up in it. See [Argo CD](./argo-cd.md). 5. **The app answers on its URL**, `https://`, with a certificate from cert-manager. See [Exposure](./exposure.md). The console never connects to your cluster. It talks to the Argo CD API over HTTPS, and Argo CD deploys to the cluster it runs in.

title: Deploy to Kubernetes — What runs in Kubernetes, and what does not
text:
| In the console | Kind | Where it runs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Backend service, or agent | Service | A container in Kubernetes, deployed through GitOps |
| Web interface served by its container | Frontend of kind **Docker** | A container in Kubernetes, deployed like a service |
| Web interface served by Flightroom | Frontend of kind **Bundle** | A static bundle served by Flightroom from your bucket, as described in [Deployments](../deployments/overview.md) |

A service or a Docker frontend is deployed once it has an **Image repository** and a version
registered by its CI pipeline. One without either is left out of the deploy. The first version the
pipeline registers also fills the **Image repository** when it is still blank. See
[Services](./services.md#image-versions).

The same **Deploy** moves both worlds at once: the frontends are snapshotted and activated as
before, and the containers are committed to Git. The deployments page shows each deployment with its
**Frontends**, **Backends**, **Config maps** and **Secrets**.

title: Deploy to Kubernetes — What each app gets in each environment
text:
| Object | Comes from |
| --- | --- |
| A **Namespace** per environment | The **Kubernetes namespace** field of the environment, or its slug in lowercase when left empty |
| A **Deployment** and a ClusterIP **Service** | The Helm chart in the applications repository, with the image and version of the service |
| **Liveness and readiness probes** | The **Liveness probe path** and **Readiness probe path** of the service |
| **ConfigMaps and Secrets** as environment variables | The [config maps and secrets](./config-maps-and-secrets.md) attached to the service |
| An **HTTPRoute** on the environment's Gateway, with TLS | The **Exposure path** of the service and the project's [exposure](./exposure.md) settings |

The values file sets one replica and the container port of the service, `8080` unless you change
**Port**. The chart passes that port to the container as `HTTP_PORT`.

### Health checks from the templates

The backend templates preset the probe paths, so Kubernetes knows when the app is up from its first
deploy:

| Template | Liveness | Readiness |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Node.js & Fastify | `/health/live` | `/health/ready` |
| Python & FastAPI | `/health/live` | `/health/ready` |
| Spring Boot | `/actuator/health/liveness` | `/actuator/health/readiness` |
| Quarkus | `/q/health/live` | `/q/health/ready` |

A service created without a template starts from `/health/live` and `/health/ready`. Change them
under **Runtime and image** in the service settings. See [Templates library](../templates/templates-library.md).

title: Deploy to Kubernetes — What the cluster needs
text:
| Requirement | What for |
| --- | --- |
| A Git provider: GitHub, GitLab or Azure DevOps | The configuration and applications repositories, through a [code repository connection](../repositories/connect/github.md) of the project |
| Argo CD 2.8 or later, reachable over HTTPS | Syncing the repositories to the cluster. See [Argo CD](./argo-cd.md) |
| The ApplicationSet policy override in Argo CD | Keeping applications from being deleted when a values file goes missing |
| Gateway API CRDs and Traefik v3 with its Gateway provider | Exposing apps on a URL. Only needed for exposure |
| cert-manager and a ClusterIssuer | TLS certificates. Without one, environments answer in plain HTTP |

title: Deploy to Kubernetes — Who can do what
text:
| Action | Who |
| --- | --- |
| Turn GitOps on, pick the repositories | An owner of the project (**Admin** in the console) or an administrator of its organization |
| Initialize or re-align Argo CD | An owner of the project or an administrator of its organization. Other members see the status |
| Deploy | Any member of the project except a **Viewer**: with GitOps on, a viewer's deploy is refused |

A member scoped to a functional domain commits the Helm values of their own domain's applications
only.

title: Deploy to Kubernetes — What Flightroom does not do
text:
Flightroom does not create clusters or databases, does not scale workloads and does not show pod
logs or events. Those stay with Kubernetes, Argo CD and the tools you already use. Watch the sync
and the health of each application in Argo CD.

title: Deploy to Kubernetes — Set it up
text:
1. Connect a [code repository](../repositories/connect/github.md) to the project, and create your
   [services](./services.md).
2. Turn on [GitOps](./gitops.md) and pick the configuration and applications repositories.
3. Set the [exposure](./exposure.md) domain and, if you want TLS, a certificate issuer.
4. Prepare and [initialize Argo CD](./argo-cd.md).
5. Create [config maps and secrets](./config-maps-and-secrets.md) and attach them to your services.
6. Press **Deploy**.

title: Deploy to Kubernetes — Where to go next
text:
- [Services](./services.md): creating a service and registering its image versions
- [GitOps repositories](./gitops.md): what each deploy commits
- [Rollback](./rollback.md): bringing a Kubernetes deploy back to a known-good state
- [Databases](./databases.md): registering the SQL databases your apps work with

title: Rolling back a Kubernetes deploy
text:
With GitOps, the cluster runs what the repositories say, and the repositories change only when
someone presses **Deploy**. A rollback of a service is therefore a new deploy that commits the earlier
state, which Argo CD then applies.

title: Rolling back a Kubernetes deploy — Redeploy does not touch the cluster
text:
**Redeploy**, on a deployment in **History**, re-activates that snapshot in Flightroom. It commits
nothing to Git, so Argo CD has nothing to apply and the containers in Kubernetes keep running what the
last **Deploy** committed. The deployments page then shows the older snapshot as active, while the
cluster still runs the newer one.

That makes **Redeploy** the right tool for frontends served by Flightroom, as described in
[Rollback and redeploy](../deployments/rollback-and-redeploy.md), and the wrong one for services and
Docker frontends.

title: Rolling back a Kubernetes deploy — Rolling back a service
text:
A deploy commits the version each service has in the console, which is the latest version its CI
pipeline registered. Rolling a service back means bringing that version back to good code, then
deploying:

1. In the repository of the service, put the last known-good code back on the branch the pipeline
   builds, for example by reverting the faulty change.
2. On the **Overview** tab of the service, press **Create version** to tag a new version. The button
   is there only when the service has a linked code repository. The dialog asks for the **Branch**,
   offered as a choice only when the repository has more than one, and the **Version**: letters,
   digits, `.`, `-` and `_`, at most 128 characters. The version becomes a Git tag, the tag starts the
   pipeline, and the pipeline builds the image and registers it, so the service moves to it. See
   [Services](./services.md#image-versions).
3. Open **Deployments**, select the environment and press **Deploy**.

The deploy commits the new version to the environment's values file, and Argo CD rolls the workload
over to it.

:::info[The version moves forward only]
A service follows the newest version its pipeline registers. A service with no version yet takes the
first one registered, whatever its tag. After that, a version is taken only when it is a newer semantic
version than the current one, and a tag that is not a semantic version, such as `latest` or a commit
SHA, never moves the service. Registering an older version again therefore does
not roll the service back. Ship the good code as a newer version instead.
:::

title: Rolling back a Kubernetes deploy — Rolling back configuration
text:
Config maps and secrets roll back the same way: set the previous values again in the console, then
press **Deploy** on the environment. The deployments page shows, for each past deployment, which
**Config maps** and **Secrets** it shipped, which helps you find what changed. Secret values are not
kept in the deployment, so you need to type them again.

title: Rolling back a Kubernetes deploy — Do not roll back in Git or in the cluster
text:
- **A revert made directly in a GitOps repository** is applied by Argo CD, but the next deploy of the
  environment overwrites it with what the console holds. Make the change in the console, so the next
  deploy keeps it.
- **A change made by hand in the cluster** is undone by Argo CD, which syncs every Application with
  self-heal.

The Git history of both repositories still tells you what each environment ran and when: every deploy
is a commit, authored by the person who pressed **Deploy**. See [GitOps repositories](./gitops.md).

title: Rolling back a Kubernetes deploy — Where to go next
text:
- [Deploy to Kubernetes](./overview.md): the whole deploy path
- [Argo CD](./argo-cd.md): what syncs the cluster

title: Services
text:
A **service** is a backend of the project that runs as a container in Kubernetes: an API, a worker,
or an agent that calls a model. The console holds its definition, the versions its CI pipeline
publishes and the configuration it receives, and the **Deploy** button ships it as described in
[Deploy to Kubernetes](./overview.md).

Services live under **Services**, in the **Backend services** section of the sidebar.

title: Services — The list of services
text:
The list opens at `/services`. Switch between a **Grid view** and a **Table view** with the buttons
next to **New service**. Search by name or slug, and narrow the list to one functional domain with
the domain filter.

The table view shows, for each service:

| Column | Content |
| --- | --- |
| **Name** | The name of the service |
| **Slug** | Its identifier in URLs and in the CI registration |
| **Runtime** | Node.js, Python, Go, .NET, Java or Other |
| **Latest version** | The version the service is at, the one the next deploy ships |
| **Repository** | The linked code repository |

![The Services page in table view, listing the Orders API and Support agent services with their latest version](../assets/services-table.png)

A project without services shows **Create from a template** instead.

title: Services — Creating a service
text:
Press **New service**. The form opens at `/service/new`.

![The New service form, with the General information card and the start of Runtime and image](../assets/service-new.png)

### General information

| Field | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| **Template** | The [service template](../templates/service-templates.md) to start from, listed as *name (framework)*. Optional |
| **Name** | 3 to 100 characters. Typing it fills the slug |
| **Slug** | 2 to 50 lowercase letters, digits or dashes, not starting with a dash. Unique in the project, and fixed once the service exists: the CI registration URL is built on it |
| **Description** | What the service does |
| **Domain** | The functional domain it belongs to. Optional |

Choosing a template fills **Port**, the probe paths, **API docs path** and **OpenAPI spec path** with
the template's values. Only the fields you have not edited by hand are replaced, so picking another
template does not overwrite what you typed.

### Runtime and image

| Field | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| **Port** | The port the container listens on. `8080` by default |
| **Liveness probe path** | Kubernetes restarts the container when this path stops answering. `/health/live` by default |
| **Readiness probe path** | Kubernetes sends traffic to the container only while this path answers. `/health/ready` by default |
| **API docs path** | Optional. The page of the public API documentation, e.g. `/docs` |
| **OpenAPI spec path** | Optional. E.g. `/openapi.json` |
| **Exposure path** | Optional. Where the service answers on the host of every environment, e.g. `/api/orders`. See [Exposure](./exposure.md) |
| **Image repository** | Optional. E.g. `ghcr.io/acme/orders-api`. Left blank, the first version the CI registers fills it |

Paths start with `/`, hold no spaces and are at most 256 characters long.

### Endpoints

One base URL per environment of the project: where the service is reachable there, for example
`https://orders-api.dev.example.com`. Each one is an absolute `http` or `https` URL, without
credentials, query (`?`) or fragment (`#`). Leave it blank where the service is not exposed.

The **API docs path** and **OpenAPI spec path** are relative to these URLs: the overview of the
service links each environment's documentation from them.

:::info[Endpoints are not exposure]
The endpoints only record where the service answers, for people and for the documentation links. They
do not create any route. What puts a service on a URL in Kubernetes is its **Exposure path**, together
with the project's [exposure](./exposure.md) settings.
:::

### Code repository

When the project has a [code repository connection](../repositories/connect/github.md), the **Code
Repository** card creates a new repository for the service at the provider, from the selected
template when there is one: code, Dockerfile and pipeline ready. A new service always gets a new
repository; it cannot be linked to an existing one from this form.

### Environment variables

The variables the container expects, each with a **Name**, a **Description**, and the **Required**
and **Secret** switches. This list documents names only, never values: the values come from the
[config maps and secrets](./config-maps-and-secrets.md) attached below.

### Config maps and secrets

Tick the config maps and secrets of the project the service receives as environment variables. No key
may be set by two of the selected maps. See
[Config maps and secrets](./config-maps-and-secrets.md#attaching-them-to-a-service).

### AI context

Markdown notes for the AI agents working on the service: architecture, conventions, useful commands.
AI agents read them before changing the service's code.

title: Services — The pages of a service
text:
A service has up to three tabs:

| Tab | Address | What it holds |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Edit with AI** | `/service/:id` | The AI workspace on the service's repository. See [Change code with AI](../build-with-ai/ai-changes.md). Shown only when the project can use at least one [AI model](../build-with-ai/ai-models.md) and the service has a linked code repository; otherwise the service opens on its overview |
| **Overview** | `/service/:id/overview` | What the service is and runs, read-only |
| **Details & settings** | `/service/:id/settings` | The same form as creation, without the template, and the danger zone |

### Overview

- **Code repository**: the linked repository, if any.
- **Versions**: the images the pipeline published on each tag, newest first, with **Version**,
  **Image**, **Digest**, **Commit** and **Date**, and a button to copy the image reference.
- **Configuration**: the port, the paths and the image repository, the endpoint of each environment
  with links to its **API docs** and **OpenAPI spec**, and the environment variables the container
  expects.
- **Config maps and secrets**: the maps the service attaches, map by map.

![The Overview tab of the Orders API service, with no linked repository, two registered versions and the configuration](../assets/service-overview.png)

With a linked code repository, the overview also offers **Create version**, which tags the repository
and starts the pipeline. See [Rolling back a Kubernetes deploy](./rollback.md#rolling-back-a-service)
for the dialog.

### Deleting a service

At the bottom of **Details & settings**, the **Danger zone** deletes the service. Confirm by typing its
name. The service goes with its registered versions and the deploys reported for it; its local working
copy and AI change requests are cleaned up too. The code repository is left untouched at the provider,
and nothing is removed from the cluster until the next deploy of each environment drops its values
file.

title: Services — Image versions
text:
A service does not build itself: its CI pipeline builds the image, pushes it to your registry, then
tells the console about it. The [service templates](../templates/service-templates.md) ship pipelines
that do this for you.

```
POST /services/by-slug/:serviceSlug/versions/:version
```

`:version` holds only letters, digits, `.`, `-` and `_`, at most 128 characters.

The call takes an [API key](../ci-cd/api-keys.md) with the `MANAGER` role, in the `api-key` header,
and a JSON body:

| Field | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| `image` | Required. The full image reference, e.g. `ghcr.io/acme/orders-api:1.2.0` |
| `digest` | Optional. The image digest |
| `commitSha` | Optional. The commit the image was built from |

```bash
curl -X POST \
  -H "api-key: $MFE_ORCHESTRATOR_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"image": "ghcr.io/acme/orders-api:1.2.0", "commitSha": "3f2c1ab"}' \
  "/services/by-slug/orders-api/versions/1.2.0"
```

- **Running the pipeline again on the same tag** replaces what was stored for that version.
- **The service moves to the new version** when it has none yet, or when the new one is a newer
  semantic version. A tag such as `latest` or a commit SHA is recorded but never moves the service.
  See [Rolling back a Kubernetes deploy](./rollback.md).
- **The first registration fills the Image repository** of a service that has none, from the image
  reference without its tag and digest.

:::info[What a deploy ships]
The Helm values file of the service uses its **Image repository** and its current version as the tag.
The `image` and `digest` you register are shown on the overview, but the deploy does not read them:
an image pushed to another repository than the one set on the service is not what Kubernetes pulls.
:::

title: Services — Reporting where a version runs
text:
A deploy pipeline of your own can tell the console which version of a service now runs in an
environment:

```
POST /services/by-slug/:serviceSlug/environments/:environmentSlug/deployments
```

With a `MANAGER` API key, and a JSON body with `version` (required: letters, digits, `.`, `-` and
`_`, at most 128 characters), and optionally `image` and `commitSha`. The version does not have to be
one the CI registered. Every report is kept, and the latest one per environment is the version shown
as running there in the [Deployed versions](../domains/overview.md#deployed-versions) matrix of a
domain.

A **Deploy** made through [GitOps](./gitops.md) does not write these reports: they come only from this
call.

title: Services — Where to go next
text:
- [Config maps and secrets](./config-maps-and-secrets.md): the configuration a service receives
- [Exposure](./exposure.md): putting a service on a URL
- [Service and agent templates](../templates/service-templates.md): what a template gives a new service

title: Managing an organization
text:
Everything at organization level starts from one button in the console header. The sidebar is
entirely about the project; the organization has a single door.

title: Managing an organization — The header menu
text:
![The console header with the organization menu open, showing settings, switch and create](../assets/organization-menu.png)

The header reads *organization › project*, and both parts are useful:

| Element | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| The organization name in the breadcrumb | Links straight to the organization page |
| **Organization settings** | The same page: details, members, AI and danger zone |
| **Switch organization** | Opens the picker |
| **Create new organization** | Opens the creation form directly, skipping the list |

title: Managing an organization — Switching organization
text:
**Switch organization** opens a dialog listing the organizations you belong to, with a search field
for accounts that belong to many.

![The switch or create organization dialog listing the organizations of the account](../assets/organization-switcher.png)

Any organization invitation still waiting for an answer is offered above the list — accepting one
adds it to the list right there.

What happens to the project you were working in is the part worth understanding: **the project does
not follow you**. It belongs to the organization you are leaving, so it is dropped and forgotten,
and the project list is refetched for the organization you arrived in. What gets selected there is
decided in one order, always the same:

1. the project already in use, if it belongs to this organization — which after a switch it never
   does, but it is what makes an ordinary refetch leave your selection alone;
2. otherwise the project this browser remembers for this organization from a previous visit;
3. otherwise, if the organization holds exactly **one** project, that one, automatically;
4. otherwise nothing is selected, and the project picker asks.

:::info[Accepting an invitation can move you]
The project switcher also lists project invitations you have not answered yet, naming the
organization a project belongs to when it is not the one you are in. Accepting such an invitation
switches you to that organization — the console works inside one at a time, so staying put would
hand you a project list that does not contain the project you just accepted.
:::

:::tip[A project shown under the wrong organization is a bug, not a mode]
The header always names the organization the current project belongs to. If you ever see a project
listed under an organization that does not own it, you are on a build older than 4.0.0 — the race
that caused it was fixed there.
:::

title: Managing an organization — Creating an organization
text:
**Create new organization**, from the header menu or from the button at the bottom of the picker,
opens the form directly.

![The create new organization form, asking for a name and a description](../assets/organization-create.png)

| Field | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| **Name** | Required, at least 2 characters |
| **Description** | Optional |

Whoever creates an organization becomes its **owner** — an organization with no owner could never be
administered. The console switches into the new organization as soon as it is created, which means
no project is selected yet and the project wizard opens.

title: Managing an organization — The organization page
text:
`/organization` is the organization's own page, titled **Organization settings** with the subtitle
*Details, members and AI of …* and the organization's name. It is split into three tabs, and the tab
in use is part of the address (`?tab=general`, `?tab=members`, `?tab=ai`), so a link can point
straight to one of them:

| Tab | What it holds |
| --- | --- |
| **General** | The [details](#details) of the organization and, for owners only, the [danger zone](#danger-zone) |
| **Members** | The member count, the [members](#members) and [pending invitations](#inviting-a-member) tables, and **Invite user** |
| **AI** | The [AIs](#ai) the projects of the organization use, and which project may use which |

:::info[The old address still works]
Until 4.0.0 the members lived in the sidebar at `/organization-users`. That path now redirects to
`/organization?tab=members`, so existing links and bookmarks keep working.
:::

### Details

The **General** tab opens on the **Organization details** card.

![The General tab, with the Organization details card and the danger zone refusing to delete an organization that still holds a project](../assets/organization-settings-general.png)

| Field | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| **Name** | Editable by owners and admins. Renaming updates the header and the switcher immediately |
| **Description** | Optional; clearing the field removes it |
| **ID** | Read-only, with a copy button. This is the stable identifier — it survives renaming |

A plain member sees the name and the description as text, with no form and no save button.

### Members

The **Members** tab shows the number of members on its label, and opens on the members table.

![The Members tab, with Invite user and the members table, the owner shown as a badge because they are the last one, and the projects column reading All projects](../assets/organization-settings-members.png)

The table has one row per accepted member:

| Column | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **User** | Name and email, or the email alone for an account that has not filled in a name |
| **Role** | A selector for owners and admins, a badge for everybody else |
| **Projects** | *All projects* for owners and admins, the number of projects reached for a member |
| **Actions** | Remove the member from the organization |

Changing a role commits as soon as you pick it — there is no save button on that selector. The
**last owner** is shown as a badge instead of a selector, and their remove button is rendered but
disabled: they cannot be demoted or removed until somebody else is made an owner.

Removing a member asks for confirmation and, as the dialog says, takes their access to **every
project of the organization** with it.

### Inviting a member

**Invite user**, at the top right of the **Members** tab, is available to owners and admins.

![The invite a user to the organization dialog, with an email field and a role selector](../assets/organization-invite.png)

Enter an email address, choose a role, and **Send invitation**. If the address has no account yet,
one is created in an invited state and the invitation email walks them through setting a password —
[the screen they land on](../account/email-flows.md#accepting-an-invitation) asks for it.

Invitations wait for an answer in their own table:

![The pending invitations table with the expiry date and the resend and revoke actions](../assets/organization-pending-invitations.png)

| Action | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| **Send again** | Issues a fresh token and sends the email again — the classic case of it landing in spam |
| **Revoke invitation** | Drops the invitation; the link stops working and a new one can be sent |

The **Expires on** column is the deadline: invitations are valid for five days.

:::info[Email delivery is required]
Organization invitations are delivered by email, exactly like project invitations, so the
installation needs SMTP configured. On an installation with no email channel the invited user is
added to the organization straight away instead — a confirmation link that cannot be delivered would
leave them stuck. See [Environment Variables](../self-hosting/environment-variables.md).
:::

### AI

The **AI** tab lists the **Artificial intelligences** of the organization — the models its projects
use for the [console assistant](../build-with-ai/console-assistant.md) and every other AI feature.
Owners and admins add, edit and delete them with **Add AI** and the row actions; everybody else sees
the list read-only, or a note to ask an owner or an admin when there is none.

Below it, owners and admins of an organization with at least one AI find **Project access**, which
says which AIs each project may use: *All (default)*, including those added later, or only the ones
selected. A project left with no AI has the AI features turned off.
See [AI models](../build-with-ai/ai-models.md) for the providers, the credentials and the access
rules.

![The AI tab, with the system AI in the Artificial intelligences table and Project access set to All (default) for the project](../assets/organization-settings-ai.png)

### Danger zone

Only an **owner** sees this section, at the bottom of the **General** tab.

Deleting an organization is deliberately not a cascade: an organization holds every project of a
tenant, and wiping all of them behind one click is not something a confirmation dialog can make safe.

So the action is refused while the organization still holds projects, and says so before you try it.
Delete the projects first, one at a time, where
[each project's own danger zone](../project-settings/projects.md#deleting-a-project) spells out what
is being lost. Once the organization is empty, deleting it asks you to type its name to confirm and
removes the organization and its memberships.

:::caution[What deletion does not touch]
Deleting an organization removes the organization and its membership rows. The user accounts
themselves, and their membership of other organizations, are unaffected.
:::

title: Organizations overview
text:
An **organization** is the tenant that owns your projects. It sits one level above the project and
answers a question the project alone could not: *which projects does this person get to see at all?*

Two rules follow from that, and everything else in this section is a consequence of them:

- A **project belongs to exactly one organization**, decided when the project is created and never
  changed afterwards.
- A **user can belong to any number of organizations**, with a different role in each.

Organizations were introduced in **4.0.0**. Installations that predate it are migrated automatically
— see [Upgrading to organizations](./upgrading-to-organizations.md).

title: Organizations overview — Where it sits in the object model
text:
```
Organization
├── Members (Owner, Admin, Member)
└── Project
    ├── Environment (dev, uat, prod, …)
    ├── Frontend (host or remote, versioned)
    ├── Storage / Bucket, Code Repository, API Key
    └── Members (Admin, Editor, Viewer)
```

The project is still the boundary every other object belongs to — frontends, environments,
deployments, API keys are all project-scoped, and nothing about that changed. What the organization
adds is a boundary *above* the project: an authorization level that decides reachability rather than
ownership. See [Core concepts](../core-concepts.md#the-object-model).

title: Organizations overview — Why the level exists
text:
Before 4.0.0 the only way to reach a project was to be an explicit member of it. That has two
consequences an installation notices sooner or later:

- **A project could be orphaned.** When the last member of a project left, nobody could open it any
  more — not even the person who administers the platform for that customer.
- **There was nothing to name a customer.** One installation serving several customers had no object
  to keep them apart, and no place to describe who administers what.

The organization solves both. Whoever administers it reaches every project inside it, invited or
not, which means a project cannot become unreachable while its organization has an owner. And each
customer, team or client gets a tenant of its own, with its own membership list.

title: Organizations overview — One organization at a time
text:
The console works inside one organization at a time. The selected organization is what scopes the
project list underneath it: the project switcher only ever offers projects of the organization you
are in.

![The console header showing the organization name, the project name and the open organization menu](../assets/organization-menu.png)

The header reads as a breadcrumb — *organization › project* — and the organization name is a link to
the [organization page](./managing-an-organization.md#the-organization-page). The button on the
right is the single door to the organization level: settings, switching and creation all start
there. Everything in the sidebar below it is about the project.

:::info[The selection is remembered per browser]
The organization and the project you are working in are stored in the browser, not on the server.
Signing in from another browser asks again. An account that belongs to exactly one organization is
never asked at all — it is selected automatically.
:::

title: Organizations overview — Your first organization
text:
A project cannot exist outside an organization, so an account with none is asked to create one
before it reaches anything else. The first run therefore goes:

1. Register, and follow the activation link when the installation sends email — until then the
   account cannot be used. See [Registration and activation](../account/email-flows.md#registration-and-activation).
2. Sign in. An account that belongs to no organization lands on **Create your organization** —
   *"An organization holds your projects and the people who reach them."* — with two fields:
