   **Name**, required and at least 2 characters, and an optional **Description**. There is no
   cancel button on this screen: it is the only way forward. **Create organization** makes you its
   owner.

   ![The Create your organization screen, with the name and description of a new organization filled in](../assets/organization-first-create.png)

3. The [project wizard](../project-settings/projects.md#creating-a-project) opens inside it. Its last
   screen offers **Start deploying your frontends**, which opens the console on the
   **AI agent** page, [Maestro](../build-with-ai/console-assistant.md) — or on **Frontends**
   when the project can use no AI yet.

If somebody invited you instead, the pending invitation is offered on that same screen, above the
creation form: accepting it puts you into their organization rather than opening one of your own.

:::caution[A plain member cannot create the first project]
Only an owner or an admin of an organization can create a project in it. Somebody invited to an
organization as a plain member, with nothing shared with them yet, sees an empty project picker and
the organization switcher — not the project wizard, which would fail on submit. See
[Roles and project visibility](./roles-and-visibility.md).
:::

title: Organizations overview — Where to go next
text:
- [Roles and project visibility](./roles-and-visibility.md) — who reaches which project, and how
  organization roles interact with project roles
- [Managing an organization](./managing-an-organization.md) — switching, creating, members, settings
  and deletion
- [Upgrading to organizations](./upgrading-to-organizations.md) — what happens to projects created
  before 4.0.0
- [Project members and roles](../project-settings/users-and-roles.md) — the second, finer level of
  access control

title: Organization roles and project visibility
text:
Access in Flightroom is decided at two levels. The **organization role** decides which projects
you can reach at all. The **project role** decides part of what you may change inside one: the
members list, the delivery settings, the AI and everything that writes to your Git provider or your
cloud. The rest of a project's configuration is open to every member. See
[Project members and roles](../project-settings/users-and-roles.md) for the detail.

title: Organization roles and project visibility — The three organization roles
text:
| Role in the console | In the API | Reaches | Can also |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Owner** | `OWNER` | Every project of the organization | Everything an Admin can, plus granting and taking ownership, and deleting the organization |
| **Admin** | `ADMIN` | Every project of the organization | Rename the organization, invite and remove members, change roles, create projects |
| **Member** | `MEMBER` | Only the projects they were invited to | Nothing at organization level — the role grants no access on its own |

Owner and Admin administer the organization and are treated identically by every visibility check.
They differ in three places only:

- the **last owner** cannot be removed or demoted, because an organization with no owner could no
  longer be administered by anybody;
- **only an owner** can make somebody an owner, or take that role away — an admin cannot promote
  themselves;
- **only an owner** sees the [danger zone](./managing-an-organization.md#danger-zone) and can delete
  the organization.

title: Organization roles and project visibility — What a Member actually gets
text:
Belonging to an organization as a plain member grants nothing by itself. It is a seat, not an
access: a member who has been invited to no project sees an empty project list, and the members
table records that honestly.

![The organization members table and the Projects column, reading All projects on the owner row](../assets/organization-members.png)

The **Projects** column is the visibility rule made visible. Owners and admins read *All projects*,
because that is literally what they reach; a member reads the number of projects of this
organization they were actually invited to.

A member also cannot create a project. Project creation is reserved to whoever administers the
organization — otherwise adding something to a tenant you only visit would be the one thing a member
could do that an admin never approved.

title: Organization roles and project visibility — How the two levels combine
text:
For a given project, the question *can this user open it?* has exactly two ways to answer yes:

1. the user holds a **project membership** on it — an invitation they accepted, whatever the project
   role; or
2. the user **administers the organization** that owns the project.

If neither holds, the project is not returned in any listing and every endpoint touching it is
refused. The rule lives in a single gate shared by every backend service, so it applies uniformly to
frontends, environments, variables, storages, repositories, builds and deployments — there is
no endpoint where it was forgotten.

| Organization role | Project membership | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Owner or Admin | none | Reaches the project, with full project rights |
| Owner or Admin | Admin / Editor / Viewer, whole project or specific domains | Reaches the project; neither the project role nor a domain scope restricts them |
| Member | Admin | Reaches that project only, with full rights on it, members included |
| Member | Editor | Reaches that project only; cannot manage its members or change its delivery settings |
| Member | Viewer | Reaches that project only; on top of the Editor's limits, cannot write to its Git provider or its cloud |
| Member | Editor / Viewer on **Specific domains** | As above, and confined to the frontends and services of the domains they were given |
| Member | none | Does not reach the project at all |
| none | any | Does not reach the project at all |

:::caution[A project role limits writes, but not all of them]
The project role is enforced on a defined set of actions. Managing the members of a project needs a
project **Admin** of the whole project, or an organization Owner or Admin. A **Viewer** is refused
committing to the GitOps repositories, creating, editing or deleting storages and databases, and
creating a code repository — including the one created with a new frontend or service. An
organization Owner or Admin is never refused any of these, whatever their project role.

Everything outside that set is still open to whoever reaches the project, Viewers included —
renaming it, editing frontends, environments and variables among others. So a Viewer is not
read-only. The full list is in
[What the role decides](../project-settings/users-and-roles.md#what-the-role-decides); keep somebody
out of the project, or out of the organization, if they must not change it at all.
:::

title: Organization roles and project visibility — Pending invitations are not memberships
Organization roles and project visibility — Inviting to a project creates a membership in the organization
text:
A project sits inside an organization, so somebody invited to a project has to belong to that
organization too — otherwise they would accept an invitation into a tenant they are not part of.

Inviting a collaborator to a project therefore also adds them to the owning organization, as a
**plain member, already accepted**. Creating it accepted is deliberate: it avoids keeping two
invitation tokens in sync, and a plain membership grants nothing on its own — the project invitation
they still have to answer is what actually gives them something.

Two safeguards apply:

- somebody who **already holds a role** in that organization keeps it. A project invitation never
  quietly demotes an admin to member.
- **declining** the project invitation takes the implicit membership back, provided the user has no
  other project in that organization and holds no role of their own there. The same clean-up runs
  when a project invitation that was never accepted is revoked, and the account itself is deleted if
  it only ever existed to be invited.

:::info[A removed member stays in the organization]
Removing somebody from a project after they accepted does **not** remove them from the organization:
they stay as a plain member with no project, which is what the members table shows as *0 projects*.
Take them out of the organization as well if you want them gone entirely.
:::

title: Organization roles and project visibility — Removing somebody from the organization
text:
Removing a member of the organization also removes them from **every project of that organization**.
Leaving the project rows behind would keep granting access to data inside a tenant the person no
longer belongs to, so the two are done together and cannot be separated.

Their account, and their membership of projects in *other* organizations, are untouched.

title: Organization roles and project visibility — Relation to project roles
text:
The project-level roles — Admin, Editor, Viewer — are documented in
[Project members and roles](../project-settings/users-and-roles.md). Read the two levels this way:

> The organization role answers *which projects*. The project role answers part of *what, inside
> it* — see [What the role decides](../project-settings/users-and-roles.md#what-the-role-decides).

For machine access, [API keys](../ci-cd/api-keys.md) are project-scoped and unaffected by
organization membership. Their role is checked by the MCP server and when a pipeline registers the
version of a service or a Docker frontend, and an expired or revoked key is refused — see
[API keys](../ci-cd/api-keys.md).

title: Upgrading to organizations
text:
Projects created before 4.0.0 have no organization: the concept did not exist. They are given one
automatically, by a migration that runs when the backend starts. There is nothing to run by hand and
no downtime to plan, but it is worth knowing what it decided.

This page matters to [self-hosted](../self-hosting/docker-compose.md) installations upgrading from
3.x. On the hosted console the migration has already run.

title: Upgrading to organizations — What the migration does
text:
At startup, the backend looks for projects that still have no organization. If there are none — the
normal case on every boot after the first — it stops there.

For the ones it finds:

1. **It picks an owner for each project.** The project's *Admin* (`OWNER` in the API), the oldest
   membership first when there are several. A project whose owner row was lost falls back to its
   most senior accepted member of any role, and that substitution is written to the log as a
   warning: a project nobody can administer is worse than a viewer promoted to owner of their own
   organization.
2. **It creates one organization per owner**, named after the account — *`Name Surname` workspace*,
   falling back to the local part of the email address. All of that person's projects go into the
   same organization, so an installation serving several customers keeps them apart instead of
   pooling everything into one shared tenant.
3. **It carries the other members over**, converting their project role into an organization role.
4. **It stamps the organization onto the projects.**

### How roles are converted

| Project role | Becomes, in the organization |
| --- | --- |
| The picked owner | `OWNER` |
| Admin (`OWNER`) | `ADMIN` |
| Editor (`MEMBER`) | `MEMBER` |
| Viewer (`VIEWER`) | `MEMBER` |
| Any role, invitation still pending | `MEMBER` |

A second Admin of the project becomes an `ADMIN` of the organization rather than a plain member: an
organization has exactly one owner, and demoting the others would take away administration they
already had. A membership still waiting for an answer converts to `MEMBER` whatever role it was for
— an unanswered invitation must not already hand over every project of the organization.

Whoever already holds a role in the target organization keeps it. The migration never demotes.

:::caution[Editors and Viewers become plain members]
An Editor or a Viewer of one project becomes a plain `MEMBER` of the organization, which reaches
only the projects they were invited to. That is the same set of projects they could see before the
upgrade, so nothing is lost — but it also means they cannot create projects any more. Promote them
to `ADMIN` on the [organization page](./managing-an-organization.md#members) if they need to.
:::

### Projects with no members at all

A project with not a single user attached to it has nobody to name an owner after. Those are
collected into an organization called **Default organization** and the backend logs a warning saying
so. Nobody owns it: assign an owner by hand — directly in the database, or by creating a membership
through the API — otherwise the projects inside it stay unreachable from the console.

title: Upgrading to organizations — Safe to run, safe to interrupt
text:
Two properties are worth relying on:

- **Idempotent.** The migration only ever looks at projects that still have no organization, so
  running it again — which happens on every boot — costs one empty query and changes nothing.
- **Resumable.** An organization the account already owns is reused rather than duplicated, so an
  interrupted run continues filling the organization the previous pass created instead of opening a
  second one beside it.

It also reads and writes in a fixed number of round trips rather than one query per project, so its
duration does not grow with the size of the installation. That matters at boot: the database plugin
waits for the migrations before the application declares itself ready, and an overrun there means
the API answers `502` while the static files are served normally.

title: Upgrading to organizations — After the upgrade
text:
Worth checking once, on the [organization page](./managing-an-organization.md):

1. **The organization name.** It was generated from an account name; rename it to whatever your
   team actually calls itself.
2. **The startup log**, for the two warnings the migration can emit — a project with no owner, and
   the *Default organization*.
3. **The member roles.** Everyone who used to administer several projects is now an `ADMIN` of the
   organization and reaches all of them, including projects they were never invited to. That is the
   intended behaviour, but it is a wider reach than they had before — see
   [Roles and project visibility](./roles-and-visibility.md).
4. **Who can create projects.** Only owners and admins can, which is new.

title: Upgrading to organizations — Endpoints that changed
text:
Three project endpoints had no access control at all before 4.0.0 and are now behind the same gate
as everything else: inviting a collaborator to a project, listing a project's members, and resending
a project invitation. If you drive the API directly, a caller that used to reach them without
belonging to the project will now be refused.

Two more changes affect API clients on this release:

- `PUT /api/projects/:projectId` is schema-bound. It accepts `name`, `description` and `isActive`
  only — `slug` and `organizationId` are not writable, because the slug is part of the storage path
  the already-uploaded bundles live under. The response is the project itself, no longer wrapped in
  `{ success, data }`.
- Stored credentials are never returned by the API any more; a placeholder comes back in their
  place, and a field sent back identical to the placeholder counts as "not retyped".

title: Projects and access control
text:
A **project** is the container every configuration object belongs to: frontends, environments,
storages, code repositories, API keys and members all belong to exactly one project.

The project in turn belongs to exactly one **organization**, which is the tenant that owns it and
the level deciding who reaches the project at all. See
[Organizations](../organizations/overview.md).

title: Projects and access control — What belongs in one project
text:
A good rule of thumb: **one project per application**, where an application is a set of
frontends deployed together and sharing a host.

Signs you want a second project rather than a bigger one:

- The frontends are never deployed together
- Different teams should not see each other's configuration
- The release cadences are unrelated
- The environments genuinely differ (not just in values, but in which environments exist)

Signs you want one project:

- A shared host loads all of them
- They are promoted through the same stages
- The same people manage all of them

Bear in mind that frontends can only be wired into a host graph *within* a project, and API
keys are project-scoped. Splitting an application across projects means losing the relation graph
that generates your Module Federation configuration — usually not worth it.

title: Projects and access control — Creating a project
text:
Your first project is created during onboarding: after signing in for the first time you are asked to
create an [organization](../organizations/overview.md#your-first-organization), and the project wizard
opens inside it.

Additional projects are created from the project switcher in the header, with **Create new project**,
which opens the wizard at `/project-wizard`. The wizard, titled *Create a new project*, has five
steps, shown in a stepper at the top: **Name → Environments → Storage → Repositories →
Collaborators**.

### 1. Name

*Let's name your project* asks for:

| Field | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| **Project name** | Required, at least 3 characters. The slug is derived from it and never changes afterwards |
| **Description (optional)** | Free text |

**Create project** creates the project and moves to the next step.

When the organization has at least one [AI](../build-with-ai/ai-models.md), a box above the fields
offers a shortcut: **Describe the project and let the assistant draft it**. Describe what you want to
build in your own words — up to 4,000 characters — and choose **Generate a proposal**. The assistant
fills in the name and the description, proposes the environments for the next step and, where your
description suggests them, a storage provider and a Git provider. A **Proposal applied** box sums up
what it did. Nothing is created from the proposal: you review every field, and still confirm each
step yourself. If the AI fails, the box says so and you fill in the fields by hand.

![The Name step with the assistant box filled in and a Proposal applied summary listing the proposed environments](../assets/project-wizard-ai-draft.png)

### 2. Environments

*Configure environments* offers **Default Environments** — presets of two (Development, Production),
three (Development, UAT, Production) or four (Development, UAT, Test, Production) environments — and
**Your Environments**, the list that will actually be created. Click a preset to fill the list, add,
edit or remove environments, drag them to reorder, then **Save**. When the assistant drafted the
project, the list starts with the environments it proposed. See
[Environments](../environments/overview.md).

![The Environments step with the three presets and the Development, Staging and Production environments proposed by the assistant](../assets/project-wizard-environments.png)

### 3. Storage

*Where do we host your frontends?* shows the same form as a new
[storage](../buckets/overview.md), with **Save and continue**, or **Skip**.

:::note[This step is not essential]
Without a storage, the bundles of your frontends are hosted by Flightroom itself. You can
connect an external storage at any time from the project settings.
:::

### 4. Repositories

*Connect your source code* offers **Connect a repository**, which opens the same provider picker as
the [Code repositories](../repositories/connect/github.md) page — GitHub, GitLab or Azure DevOps — or
**Skip**.

### 5. Collaborators

*Invite collaborators* takes one row per person: an email address and a role, with **Add
collaborator** for more rows. The roles are the same as in the invite dialog of
[Members and roles](./users-and-roles.md#roles):

| Role in the wizard | Project role |
| --- | --- |
| **Admin** | `OWNER` |
| **Editor** | `MEMBER` |
| **Viewer** (the default) | `VIEWER` |

**Complete** sends the invitations — each person receives an email invitation, exactly as from
[Members and roles](./users-and-roles.md#inviting-a-member) — and **Skip and complete** finishes
without inviting anybody. An invalid or duplicated address, or your own, is flagged before anything
is sent.

### Project ready

The wizard ends on **Project ready!**, which offers **Go to dashboard** (the frontends of the new
project) and **Add frontend**. During onboarding it offers **Start deploying your
frontends** instead, which opens the console on the
[AI agent page](../build-with-ai/console-assistant.md), or on **Frontends** when the project can
use no AI.

![The Project ready! screen at the end of onboarding, with Start deploying your frontends](../assets/project-wizard-ready.png)

The close button (**✕**) at the top right leaves the wizard for **Frontends** at any step. It is
not shown during onboarding.

Storage, repositories and collaborators are skippable, and every step can be done later from
**Settings**.

:::caution[Leaving the wizard halfway creates a half-configured project]
The project row is created the moment you complete step 1, before any environment exists. Nothing
remembers where you were: the step you are on is component state, with no draft saved anywhere, so
closing the wizard or reloading the page starts a fresh one — and completing that fresh one creates a
**second project**, leaving the first behind with whatever it had at the time.

If it happens, delete the abandoned project from its own
[Danger Zone](#deleting-a-project) rather than trying to resume it.
:::

The project is created inside the organization you are currently working in, and it stays there:
a project cannot be moved to another organization afterwards.

:::caution[Only organization owners and admins can create a project]
A plain member of an organization reaches the projects they were invited to and nothing else, so the
wizard is not offered to them at all. See
[Roles and project visibility](../organizations/roles-and-visibility.md).
:::

title: Projects and access control — Switching projects
text:
The project selector sits in the console header, next to the
[organization selector](../organizations/managing-an-organization.md#the-header-menu). Everything
below it — frontends, deployments, settings — follows the selection.

![The project switcher, which also creates a new project](../assets/project-switcher.png)

The list only ever offers projects of the organization you are in. If a page looks empty, check the
selected project — and the selected organization — before anything else. It is the most common cause
of "my frontends disappeared".

title: Projects and access control — Project settings
text:
**Settings** in the sidebar (`/settings`) is the project's control panel. It is split into four tabs,
and the tab in use is part of the address (`?tab=general`, `?tab=access`, `?tab=resources`,
`?tab=delivery`), so a link can point straight to one of them.

### General

The **General** tab holds the project's own data, top to bottom:

- **Project Information** — the name, the description and the identifiers, described below.
- **Project AI context** — free markdown notes for AI agents (MCP clients and the console assistant)
  that apply to the whole project: domain, conventions, rules shared by the frontends. Up to
  20,000 characters. See [Build with AI](../build-with-ai/overview.md).
- **Danger Zone** — [deleting the project](#deleting-a-project).

Under **Project Information** you will find:

| Field | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| **Name** | Editable display name. Required, at least two characters |
| **Description** | Editable free text |
| **Slug** | Read-only. URL-friendly identifier, part of storage paths. Copyable |
| **ID** | Read-only. The project id used in API calls and public serve URLs. Copyable |

The **ID** is what you need for the serve API and for `project-id` headers — this is where to copy
it from.

![The General tab of Settings, with the project information form and the start of the Project AI context](../assets/project-settings-general.png)

### Access

The **Access** tab, *People and access*, has one card per way into the project, each with a count and
a link to its page:

| Card | Leads to |
| --- | --- |
| Team Members | [Members and roles](./users-and-roles.md) |
| API Keys | [API keys](../ci-cd/api-keys.md) |
| AI assistants | The MCP clients connected to the project — see [MCP server](../build-with-ai/mcp-server.md). This card shows no count, only **Manage** |

![The Access tab, with the Team Members, API Keys and AI assistants cards](../assets/project-settings-access.png)

### Resources

The **Resources** tab, *Project resources*, works the same way for what the project is built on:

| Card | Leads to |
| --- | --- |
| Environments | [Environments](../environments/overview.md) |
| Code Repositories | [Code repositories](../repositories/connect/github.md) |
| Storages | [Buckets](../buckets/overview.md) |
| Databases | [Databases](../kubernetes/databases.md) |

![The Resources tab, with the Environments, Code Repositories, Storages and Databases cards and their counts](../assets/project-settings-resources.png)

### Delivery

The **Delivery** tab configures how the project reaches your clusters, in the order the settings are
set up. Changing **GitOps**, **Argo CD** or **Pipeline templates** needs a project **Admin**, or an
organization Owner or Admin — see
[What the role decides](./users-and-roles.md#what-the-role-decides).

| Section | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| **GitOps** | Every deploy commits what it ships to a Git repository. See [GitOps](../kubernetes/gitops.md) |
| **Exposure** | The domain the environments are exposed on. See [Exposure](../kubernetes/exposure.md) |
| **Argo CD** | Argo CD deploys the environments from the GitOps repositories. See [Argo CD](../kubernetes/argo-cd.md) |
| **Pipeline templates** | Where the pipeline of a new frontend or service comes from, described below |

**Exposure** and **Argo CD** appear only once GitOps is on and saved with a repository: both work on
what GitOps commits.

![The Delivery tab of a project with GitOps off, showing only the GitOps and Pipeline templates cards](../assets/project-settings-delivery.png)

**Pipeline templates** decides the CI pipeline a repository gets when it is created for a new
frontend or service. By default it comes from the official
[`template-pipelines`](https://github.com/mfe-orchestrator/template-pipelines) repository. Turn on
**Use the pipeline templates of a repository of the project** to pick one of your own instead,
reached through one of the project's code repository connections, with a **Branch or tag** (left
empty, the default branch). Your repository needs the same `<type>/<compiler>/<provider>/` layout;
the **How it works** section of the card spells it out. Repositories already created are left as they
are. See [What gets added on top](../templates/templates-library.md#what-gets-added-on-top).

### Renaming a project

Edit the **Name**, then **Save**. The name and the description are one form and are saved together,
so an edit to either writes both.

The **Slug** does not follow the name, and cannot be edited at all. It is baked into the storage path
of every bundle already uploaded — see the caution below — so re-deriving it from a new name would
leave those files where nothing looks for them. A renamed project keeps the slug it was created
with, which is worth knowing when you audit a bucket and find a path naming a project that no longer
goes by that name.

:::caution[The slug is part of your storage paths]
Artifacts are stored under `<projectSlug>-<projectId>/…`. The id keeps paths unique regardless, but
be aware the slug appears in bucket paths when auditing storage.
:::

title: Projects and access control — Deleting a project
text:
**Settings → General → Danger Zone → Delete Project** removes the project and everything scoped to it, in one
transaction: frontends, environments, variables, deployments and their history, API keys, member
and invitation rows, **storage connections**, **code repository connections**, the record of every
built version uploaded for those frontends, and any
[canary user enrolment](../frontends/canary-releases.md) on those deployments.

You must type the project name to confirm. There is no undo and no soft delete.

What is *not* deleted:

- Files already stored in **your own buckets** — the storage connection goes away, the objects stay
- **Git repositories** created from templates — those live in your provider
- Secrets written into your Git provider — remove `MICROFRONTEND_ORCHESTRATOR_API_KEY` yourself if
  you want it gone

:::caution[Deleting a project breaks live applications]
Every public serve endpoint for that project stops answering immediately. Any application currently
loading frontends through it will fail to load them. Make sure nothing is serving from the
project before you delete it.
:::

title: Projects and access control — API access
text:
When calling the management API directly, the project is selected with a header:

```http
project-id: 68f1a2b3c4d5e6f7a8b9c0d1
```

Some endpoints also take an `environment-id` header for environment-scoped resources such as
variables. Requests authenticated with an [API key](../ci-cd/api-keys.md) derive the project from
the key and do not need the header.

title: Project members and roles
text:
A user can be a member of several projects, and a role is recorded for them in each one. The role
decides some things and not others: it guards the members list, the delivery settings, the AI and
everything that writes to your Git provider or your cloud, but most of the day-to-day configuration
is open to every member. Read [Roles](#roles) before you invite anybody.

Which projects a person can reach at all is decided one level up, by the organization that owns
them:

> The [organization role](../organizations/roles-and-visibility.md) answers *which projects*.
> The project role answers *what they may change in one*.

Two consequences are worth keeping in mind while reading the rest of this page:

- **Whoever administers the organization reaches every project in it**, invited or not, and acts
  there as an Admin. Somebody who must be read-only cannot be an organization owner or admin.
- **Inviting somebody to a project also puts them into the owning organization**, as a plain member.
  See [Inviting a member](#inviting-a-member) below.

Members live under **Settings → Access → Team Members**.

title: Project members and roles — Roles
text:
There are three roles:

| Role in the console | Stored and returned by the API as | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Admin** | `OWNER` | The last Admin of a project cannot be removed |
| **Editor** | `MEMBER` | |
| **Viewer** | `VIEWER` | The value the invite dialog starts on |

The console is not consistent about which of the two names it shows. The **invite dialog** offers
*Admin*, *Editor* and *Viewer*; the badge on the members list prints the stored value — `OWNER`,
`MEMBER` or `VIEWER` — and so does the API. Invitation emails name the role as well.

### What the role decides

| Action | Who may do it |
| --- | --- |
| Invite and remove members, change their role | Project **Admin**, or an organization Owner or Admin |
| Change the GitOps, Argo CD and pipeline-template settings | Project **Admin**, or an organization Owner or Admin |
| Ask for an AI change, apply it, open its pull request, discard it | Anyone but a **Viewer** |
| Create a code repository, for a frontend or a service | Anyone but a **Viewer** |
| Create, edit, test or delete storages and databases | Anyone but a **Viewer** |
| Deploy, when the project has GitOps on | Anyone but a **Viewer** |
| Change anything through the [console assistant](../build-with-ai/console-assistant.md) or an [MCP client](../build-with-ai/mcp-server.md) | Anyone but a **Viewer**, within what their role allows |

Organization owners and admins are never refused any of these: they act in every project of their
organization as an Admin would.

:::warning[What the role does not decide]
Everything else is open to every member who reaches the whole project, Viewers included: renaming
and deleting the project, editing frontends, services, environments and variables, and
deploying a project that does not have GitOps on. The console may still show a button to a Viewer
that the backend then refuses. Invite somebody to a project only if you are comfortable with them
changing its configuration.
:::

Keep at least two Admins, so the protection of the last one cannot strand a project whose only
Admin has left.

### Restricting who can deploy to production

There is no per-environment permission split. With [GitOps](../kubernetes/gitops.md) on, Viewers
cannot deploy at all, but every Editor can deploy every environment, `prod` included. Without
GitOps, every member can. To keep production to a smaller group, give it a **separate project**
whose membership is that group. **Redeploy** is not restricted by role at all: it re-activates a
previous snapshot in Flightroom, and does not touch the cluster — see
[Rolling back on Kubernetes](../kubernetes/rollback.md).

title: Project members and roles — Inviting a member
text:
1. Go to **Settings → Access → Team Members** and click **Invite user**.

   ![The Project Members page](../assets/team-members.png)

2. Enter their **email address**.
3. Choose a **role**.
4. Choose the **Access**: the **Whole project**, or **Specific domains** and the domains to tick.
   An Admin always has the whole project, so the choice is hidden for that role.
5. **Send invitation**.

   ![The invite dialog, with email, role and access](../assets/invite-user-dialog.png)

An email goes out with an invitation link. The invitee follows it, signs in or registers, and joins
the project with the role you chose — see
[Accepting an invitation](../account/email-flows.md#accepting-an-invitation) for the screen they land
on and how long the link lives.

:::info[The invitation reaches the organization too]
A project sits inside an organization, so inviting somebody to a project also adds them to that
organization — as a plain **member**, created already accepted. That membership grants nothing on
its own: a plain member reaches only the projects they were invited to, which is exactly the project
you just invited them to. Somebody who already holds a role in the organization keeps it; a project
invitation never demotes an admin. Declining the invitation takes the implicit membership back
again, unless they have other projects there. See
[Roles and project visibility](../organizations/roles-and-visibility.md#inviting-to-a-project-creates-a-membership-in-the-organization).
:::

:::caution[Without SMTP an invitation becomes an unverified membership]
Invitations are delivered by email, so the installation needs SMTP configured. On a self-hosted
instance without `EMAIL_SMTP_HOST` set the invitation does not fail — it degrades. No email is sent,
no link is generated, and the address you typed is added to the project as an **already active
member**, with nothing having proved that the person owns that address. Resending an invitation is
the only action that errors in that state.

That means a typo hands the role you picked to whoever owns the address you mistyped. Configure SMTP before you invite anybody — see
[Environment Variables](../self-hosting/environment-variables.md).
:::

title: Project members and roles — Managing invitations
text:
Accepted members and pending invitations are two separate sections of the page, not one list with a
status column:

| Section | Columns |
| --- | --- |
| Members — as cards, or as a table from the view switcher | User, Role, Actions |
| **N pending invitations** — the heading counts them, and appears only when there are any | Email, Role, Expires on, Actions |

An invitation expires five days after it is sent, which is the date under **Expires on**.

For a pending invitation you can:

- **Resend** — send the email again, for the classic case of it landing in spam. The only action with
  a visible label, and even that is hidden on a narrow window.
- **Revoke** — cancel it, so the link no longer works. An icon-only button: the **✕** at the end of
  the row, which names itself on hover.

title: Project members and roles — Changing a role
text:
Choose **Edit access** on the member's row. The dialog changes the role and the **Access**: the
**Whole project**, or **Specific domains** only. An Admin always has the whole project. The last
Admin cannot be given another role.

Only a project Admin, or an organization Owner or Admin, can change a role. For an invitation that
is still pending, inviting the same address again also refreshes the role and sends a new link.

title: Project members and roles — Removing a member
text:
Remove them from the row's actions — the trash icon in the table, the **Remove** button on the card.
The confirmation is a plain dialog naming the person ("Are you sure you want to remove … from this
project?"), not the type-the-name gesture that [deleting a project](./projects.md#deleting-a-project)
asks for. The button is disabled for the last Admin, and when the project would be left with no
members at all.

They lose access to this project immediately; their account and their membership of other projects
are unaffected.

:::caution[Removing them from the project does not remove them from the organization]
Somebody who accepted the invitation stays in the organization as a plain member with no project —
harmless, since that grants nothing, but they remain on the organization's members list. Take them
out from [the organization page](../organizations/managing-an-organization.md#members) if you want
them gone entirely; doing so also removes them from every other project of that organization. An
invitation that was never accepted is cleaned up on its own when you revoke it.
:::

:::tip[Removing a person is not enough]
People leaving is also the moment to audit [API keys](../ci-cd/api-keys.md). A key that person
created keeps working after they are removed — keys belong to the project, not to the user who
created one. **Delete** any key they were the only consumer of: deletion is the only thing that
stops a key authenticating, as [Machine access](#machine-access) explains.
:::

title: Project members and roles — Authentication
text:
How members sign in depends on the installation:

| Method | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| Email and password | Available when embedded login is enabled |
| Google | Available when configured |
| Microsoft Entra ID (Azure) | Available when configured |
| Auth0 | Available when configured |

The hosted console offers email/password and Google. For self-hosted installations, the enabled
providers are whichever you configure — see
[Enable SSO](../self-hosting/enable-sso/Google.md).

Whichever method a user signs in with, their memberships are the same: authentication decides who
they are, project membership decides which projects they reach.

title: Project members and roles — Machine access
text:
For CI pipelines and scripts, use [API keys](../ci-cd/api-keys.md) rather than a user account. A key
belongs to the project, so it survives any change to your own account.

The create dialog asks for two things, a **name** and an **expiration date**; the role is not among
them, and every key the console creates is stored as `MANAGER`.

:::info[Expired and revoked keys are refused]
A key past its expiration date, or revoked, is refused on the next request. Delete a key you no
longer need. See [API keys](../ci-cd/api-keys.md).
:::

Creating a "service user" with a shared password is the anti-pattern here: it cannot be rotated
without coordinating with everyone using it, and it muddies the audit trail.

title: Quick start: from a description to a live app
text:
This is the golden path: describe what your team needs, let the AI write it in your own
repositories, review what comes back, and ship it with one click. Steps 1 to 4 run on the
**free hosted console**, with nothing to install. Step 5 needs a Kubernetes cluster with Argo CD,
because that is where your apps run.

:::info[Words you will see in the console]
The site speaks of *apps* and *agents*. The console names the pieces they are made of: a web
interface is a **frontend**, a backend or an agent is a **service**, and a **functional
domain** groups the ones that serve the same business capability. An agent is a service that
calls the AI model you chose. See [Build with AI](./build-with-ai/overview.md).
:::

title: Quick start: from a description to a live app — 1. Create an account
text:
Open **[console.flightroom.dev](https://console.flightroom.dev)** and register with email or
Google. With email, follow the activation link you receive before signing in: until you do, the
account cannot be used. You are then asked to create an **organization**, the tenant that owns your
projects, and the project wizard opens inside it. When it is done, the console opens on the
**AI agent** page — or on **Frontends** until your organization has an AI, which step 2 adds.

Details: [Get started with Flightroom](./intro.mdx)

title: Quick start: from a description to a live app — 2. Set it up once: a Git provider and an AI
text:
These two steps are for whoever administers the project. After them, every member can build.

1. **Connect your Git provider.** In **Settings → Resources → Code Repositories**, connect GitHub,
   GitLab or Azure DevOps. The AI writes into repositories it creates there.
2. **Add an AI.** In **Organization settings → AI**, choose **Add AI** and enter your own
   credentials: Claude through Anthropic, Azure AI Foundry or AWS Bedrock, GPT through Azure
   OpenAI, or Gemini. Only organization owners and admins can do this.

Details: [Connect GitHub](./repositories/connect/github.md) ·
[AI models](./build-with-ai/ai-models.md)

title: Quick start: from a description to a live app — 3. Describe it
text:
1. Open **Domains** in the sidebar and create a **New domain**, for example *Expenses*.
2. On the domain's **Edit with AI** tab, write what the team needs, the way you would explain it
   to a colleague. For example: *"An agent that checks each expense claim against the travel
   policy and flags the ones over the limit before approval."*
3. Press **Generate proposal**.

Because the domain is empty, the AI first proposes the components the request needs, at most
three frontends and three services. Edit the names, slugs, repositories and templates, untick
what you do not want, and confirm. Flightroom creates each repository from its template, CI
pipeline included, and the AI writes a first version on a branch of its own.

Details: [Generate a domain with AI](./build-with-ai/generate-a-domain.md)

title: Quick start: from a description to a live app — 4. Review it
Quick start: from a description to a live app — 5. Deploy it
text:
Once the change is merged, open **Deployments**, pick the environment and press **Deploy**.
Flightroom commits the manifests and Helm values to Git, your Argo CD syncs the cluster, and the
app answers on its own URL in that environment, with TLS.

This needs a one-time setup by a project admin under **Settings → Delivery**: a GitOps
repository, your Argo CD, and the domain the environments are exposed on.

Details: [Deploy to Kubernetes](./kubernetes/overview.md)

---

title: Quick start: from a description to a live app — Where to go next
text:
- **[Core concepts](./core-concepts.md)**: organizations, projects, domains, environments and
  deployments, and how they relate.
- **[Console assistant](./build-with-ai/console-assistant.md)**: press ⌘J and ask the console
  to create environments, check versions or start a deploy.
- **[Frontend quick start](./frontends/quick-start.mdx)**: the path for a web
  interface served by Flightroom and composed with Module Federation.
- **[Self-hosting](./self-hosting/helm.md)**: run Flightroom on your own Kubernetes, with your
  single sign-on and your models.

If Flightroom is useful to you, a
[star on GitHub](https://github.com/flightroom/flightroom) helps the project get found.

title: Connect an Azure DevOps repository
text: This guide will walk you through connecting your Azure DevOps repositories to Flightroom.

title: Connect an Azure DevOps repository — Prerequisites
text:
- An active [Azure DevOps](https://dev.azure.com) account
- Access to at least one organization and project
- Admin permissions to create Personal Access Tokens

title: Connect an Azure DevOps repository — Step 1: Navigate to Code Repositories
text:
1. Go to **[Code Repositories](https://console.flightroom.dev/code-repositories)** in Flightroom
![The Code Repositories page](../../assets/code-repositories.png)
2. Click the **Add Repository** button
![The Add Repository dialog, listing the available providers](../../assets/add-repository-provider.png)
3. Select **Azure DevOps** as your provider
![The Azure DevOps connection form](../../assets/repository-form-azure.png)

title: Connect an Azure DevOps repository — Step 2: Create a Personal Access Token (PAT)
text:
A Personal Access Token is required to authenticate Flightroom with your Azure DevOps account.

### 2.1 Access Token Settings

1. Go to your Azure DevOps organization at `https://dev.azure.com/{your-organization}`
2. Click on your **User Settings** icon (top right corner)
3. Select **Personal Access Tokens**
4. Click **+ New Token**

### 2.2 Configure Token Settings

Fill in the token configuration:

- **Name**: Enter a descriptive name (e.g., "Flightroom")
- **Organization**: Select the organization(s) you want to connect
  - You can select **All accessible organizations** if you have multiple organizations
- **Expiration**: Set an expiration date
  - Recommended: 90 days or custom date
  - For security, avoid selecting "Full access" indefinitely

### 2.3 Required Token Scopes

:::warning[Critical: Select the Correct Scopes]
Make sure to select these **exact scopes** for Flightroom to function properly:
:::

In the **Scopes** section of the token creation dialog, configure the following permissions:

**1. Configure Code Scope**
   1. Find the **Code** section in the scopes list
   2. Click on the dropdown next to **Code**
   3. Select **Read, write & manage**

   > *This grants access to read source code, commits, and branches - required for fetching repository content and managing deployments*

**2. Configure Project and Team Scope**
   1. Find the **Project and Team** section in the scopes list
   2. Select **Read**

   > *This grants access to projects and team information - required for listing the projects of the organization when you connect*

**3. Configure Build Scope**
   1. Scroll down to find the **Build** section
   2. Click on the dropdown next to **Build**
   3. Select **Read, write & manage**

   > *This grants access to build pipelines and build results - required for triggering builds and monitoring build status*

**4. Configure Release Scope**
   1. Continue scrolling to find the **Release** section
   2. Click on the dropdown next to **Release**
   3. Select **Read, write & manage**

   > *This grants access to release pipelines and deployment information - required for managing releases and deployment workflows*

**5. Configure Variable Groups Scope**
   1. Find the **Variable Groups** section in the scopes list
   2. Select **Read, create, & manage**

   > *This lets Flightroom create the `MFE_ORCHESTRATOR_SECRETS` variable group where the API key its pipeline uses is stored*

:::tip[Quick Check]
After selecting all scopes, verify that you have:

- Code: Read, write & manage
- Project and Team: Read
- Build: Read, write & manage
- Release: Read, write & manage
- Variable Groups: Read, create, & manage

The connection screen lists four of them next to the form: it leaves out Project and Team, which
Flightroom still needs to list the projects of the organization.
:::

### 2.4 Generate the Token

1. After selecting all required scopes, click **Create**
2. **Important**: A dialog will appear with your token
3. **Copy the token immediately** and save it securely, you won't be able to see this token again!

title: Connect an Azure DevOps repository — Step 3: Configure Connection in Flightroom
text:
Now that you have your PAT, return to Flightroom to complete the connection.

### 3.1 Fill in Connection Details

In the **Add Repository** dialog, enter the following information:

1. **Name**: Enter a descriptive name for this connection
   - Example: `"My Azure DevOps"` or `"Company Name DevOps"`
   - This helps you identify the connection if you have multiple repository sources

2. **Organization Name**: Enter your Azure DevOps organization name
   - This is the part after `https://dev.azure.com/` in your URL
   - Example: If your URL is `https://dev.azure.com/my-company`, enter `my-company`

3. **Personal Access Token**: Paste the PAT you created in Step 2
   - Copy and paste the full token
   - Make sure there are no extra spaces

### 3.2 Test the Connection

Before saving, verify that everything is configured correctly clicking on **Test Connection** button

:::tip[Connection Test Success]
If the test is successful, you'll see a **green checkmark** and a success message. If it fails, double-check your organization name and PAT.
:::

### 3.3 Select the Project

The test does more than validate the token: it returns the projects in the organization, and a
**Select project** dropdown appears under the green checkmark listing them. Pick the Azure DevOps
project new frontend repositories should be created in.

This step is not optional. The field is required and **Connect Azure Dev Ops** stays disabled until
the test has succeeded, so the form cannot be submitted without a selection. The project is also what
Flightroom needs in order to create the `MFE_ORCHESTRATOR_SECRETS` variable group holding the
deploy key — see
[Deploy with Azure Pipelines](../../ci-cd/azure-pipelines.md#the-variable-group).

### 3.4 Save the Connection

1. With a project selected, click **Connect Azure Dev Ops**
2. Your Azure DevOps connection is now active!

title: Connect an Azure DevOps repository — Troubleshooting
text:
### Connection Test Fails

If the connection test fails, check the following:

- **Invalid Organization Name**: Verify that the organization name matches exactly what appears in your Azure DevOps URL
- **Insufficient Permissions**: Ensure you selected all five required scopes — Code, Build and
  Release with "Read, write & manage", Project and Team with "Read", and Variable Groups with
  "Read, create, & manage"
- **Expired Token**: Check if your PAT has expired and create a new one if needed
- **Network Issues**: Verify that you have internet connectivity and can access Azure DevOps

### Token Permissions Error

If you see a permissions error after connecting:

1. Go back to Azure DevOps - Personal Access Tokens
2. Find your Flightroom token
3. Click **Edit** or **Revoke** and create a new token
4. Ensure all required scopes are selected
5. Update the token in Flightroom settings

### Cannot See My Project

If your project doesn't appear in the dropdown:

- Verify that you have access to the project in Azure DevOps
- Make sure the PAT has access to "All accessible organizations" or the specific organization
- Check that the project is not archived or deleted

title: Connect an Azure DevOps repository — Security Best Practices
text:
:::warning[Token Security]
Follow these best practices to keep your account secure:
:::

- **Never share** your Personal Access Token with anyone
- **Use specific scopes** - only grant the permissions that are needed
- **Set expiration dates** - tokens should expire after 90 days or less
- **Rotate tokens regularly** - create new tokens periodically
- **Revoke immediately** if compromised - if you suspect a token has been exposed, revoke it right away and create a new one
- **Use separate tokens** for different services - don't reuse the same PAT across multiple integrations

title: Connect an Azure DevOps repository — Need Help?
text:
If you encounter any issues or need assistance:

- Check the [Azure DevOps documentation](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/)
- Review the [PAT documentation](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/organizations/accounts/use-personal-access-tokens-to-authenticate)
- Contact Flightroom support

title: Connect a GitHub repository
text: This guide will walk you through connecting your GitHub repositories to Flightroom.

title: Connect a GitHub repository — Prerequisites
text:
- An active [GitHub](https://github.com) account
- Access to at least one organization or personal repository
- Permission to authorize OAuth applications — on an organization, an owner may have to approve it

:::info[GitHub uses OAuth, not a token]
Unlike [GitLab](./gitlab.md) and [Azure DevOps](./azure.dev-ops.md), GitHub does not ask you for a
Personal Access Token. You authorize Flightroom on GitHub instead, and it holds the
resulting credential for you.
:::

title: Connect a GitHub repository — Step 1: Navigate to Code Repositories
text:
1. Go to **[Code Repositories](https://console.flightroom.dev/code-repositories)** in Flightroom
![The Code Repositories page](../../assets/code-repositories.png)
2. Click the **Add Repository** button
![The Add Repository dialog, listing the available providers](../../assets/add-repository-provider.png)
3. Select **GitHub** as your provider

title: Connect a GitHub repository — Step 2: Authorize on GitHub
text:
Selecting GitHub sends you to GitHub's own authorization page. Sign in if you are not already, then
review the access being requested and confirm. GitHub asks for the scopes Flightroom needs to
read your repositories, create one from a template, and store the deploy secret its pipeline uses:
`repo`, `public_repo`, `read:user`, `read:org`, `workflow` and `admin:org`.

If the repositories you want belong to an organization, grant access to that organization on the
same page. Without it, only your personal repositories appear later.

:::caution[Organization approval]
Some organizations require an owner to approve third-party OAuth applications. If your organization
does, the authorization stays *pending* until an owner approves it, and the organization's
repositories will not be listed in the meantime.
:::

Once you confirm, GitHub returns you to the console and the connection appears in the repository
list. From there you can [create a frontend from a template](../../frontends/create-a-frontend.md),
which scaffolds the repository and its pipeline for you.

title: Connect a GitHub repository — Troubleshooting
text:
**GitHub is not offered in the Add Repository dialog** — the installation has no GitHub OAuth
application configured. On a self-hosted instance, set `CODE_REPOSITORY_GITHUB_CLIENT_ID` and
`CODE_REPOSITORY_GITHUB_CLIENT_SECRET`; see
[Environment Variables](../../self-hosting/environment-variables.md).

**Your organization's repositories are missing** — either organization access was not granted
during authorization, or an owner has not yet approved the application. Re-run the authorization
from **Code Repositories → Add Repository → GitHub** and grant the organization explicitly.

title: Connect a GitLab repository
text: This guide will walk you through connecting your GitLab repositories to Flightroom.

title: Connect a GitLab repository — Prerequisites
text:
- An active [GitLab](https://gitlab.com) account (or access to a self-hosted GitLab instance)
- Access to at least one project or group
- Permissions to create Personal Access Tokens

title: Connect a GitLab repository — Step 1: Navigate to Code Repositories
text:
1. Go to **[Code Repositories](https://console.flightroom.dev/code-repositories)** in Flightroom
![The Code Repositories page](../../assets/code-repositories.png)
2. Click the **Add Repository** button
![The Add Repository dialog, listing the available providers](../../assets/add-repository-provider.png)
3. Select **GitLab** as your provider
![The GitLab connection form](../../assets/repository-form-gitlab.png)

title: Connect a GitLab repository — Step 2: Create a Personal Access Token (PAT)
text:
A Personal Access Token is required to authenticate Flightroom with your GitLab account.

### 2.1 Access Token Settings

1. Go to GitLab and click on your **avatar** (top right corner)
2. Select **Edit profile** or **Preferences**
3. In the left sidebar, click on **Access Tokens**
4. Click **Add new token**

:::tip[GitLab.com vs Self-Hosted]
- For GitLab.com, go to: `https://gitlab.com/-/profile/personal_access_tokens`
- For self-hosted GitLab, use your instance URL: `https://your-gitlab-instance.com/-/profile/personal_access_tokens`
:::

### 2.2 Configure Token Settings

Fill in the token configuration:

- **Token name**: Enter a descriptive name (e.g., "Flightroom")
- **Expiration date**: Set an expiration date
  - Recommended: 90 days or custom date
  - For security, avoid tokens without expiration dates

### 2.3 Required Token Scopes

:::warning[Critical: Select the Correct Scopes]
Make sure to select these **exact scopes** for Flightroom to function properly:
:::

In the **Scopes** section of the token creation dialog, configure the following permissions:

**1. Configure API Scope**
   1. Find the **api** checkbox in the scopes list
   2. Check the **api** checkbox

   > *This grants complete read/write access to the API, including all groups and projects, the container registry, and the package registry - required for full integration with Flightroom*

**2. Configure Read User Scope**
   1. Find the **read_user** checkbox in the scopes list
   2. Check the **read_user** checkbox

   > *This grants read access to your user information - used to identify the account the connection belongs to*

**3. Configure Read Repository Scope**
   1. Scroll down to find the **read_repository** checkbox
   2. Check the **read_repository** checkbox

   > *This grants read-only access to repositories - required for fetching repository content*

:::tip[Quick Check]
After selecting all scopes, verify that you have checked:

- `api`
- `read_user`
- `read_repository`

These are the three scopes the connection screen lists next to the form. Writes — pushing a
template into a new repository, committing a generated configuration — go through the API, which
the `api` scope already covers.
:::

### 2.4 Generate the Token

1. After selecting all required scopes, click **Create personal access token**
2. **Important**: A dialog will appear with your token at the top of the page
3. **Copy the token immediately** and save it securely, you won't be able to see this token again!

title: Connect a GitLab repository — Step 3: Configure Connection in Flightroom
text:
Now that you have your PAT, return to Flightroom to complete the connection.

### 3.1 Fill in Connection Details

In the **Add Repository** dialog, enter the following information:

1. **Name**: Enter a descriptive name for this connection
   - Example: `"My GitLab"` or `"Company GitLab"`
   - This helps you identify the connection if you have multiple repository sources

2. **GitLab URL**: Enter your GitLab instance URL
   - For GitLab.com, use: `https://gitlab.com`
   - For self-hosted GitLab, use your instance URL: `https://your-gitlab-instance.com`

3. **Personal Access Token**: Paste the PAT you created in Step 2
   - Copy and paste the full token
   - Make sure there are no extra spaces

### 3.2 Test the Connection

Before saving, verify that everything is configured correctly clicking on **Test Connection** button

:::tip[Connection Test Success]
If the test is successful, you'll see a **green checkmark** and a success message. If it fails, double-check your GitLab URL and PAT.
:::

### 3.3 Select the Group

The test does more than validate the token: it returns the groups the token can see, and a **Select
Project** dropdown appears under the green checkmark listing them. Pick the group new frontend
repositories should be created in.

This step is not optional. The field is required and **Connect GitLab** stays disabled until the test
has succeeded, so the form cannot be submitted without a selection. The group is also what
Flightroom needs in order to create the group-level CI/CD variable holding the deploy key — see
[Deploy with GitLab CI](../../ci-cd/gitlab-ci.md#the-cicd-variable).

### 3.4 Save the Connection

1. With a group selected, click **Connect GitLab**
2. Your GitLab connection is now active!

title: Connect a GitLab repository — Troubleshooting
text:
### Connection Test Fails

If the connection test fails, check the following:

- **Invalid GitLab URL**: Verify that the GitLab URL is correct (e.g., `https://gitlab.com` for GitLab.com or your self-hosted instance URL)
- **Insufficient Permissions**: Ensure you selected all three required scopes (`api`, `read_user`, `read_repository`)
- **Expired Token**: Check if your PAT has expired and create a new one if needed
- **Network Issues**: Verify that you have internet connectivity and can access GitLab
- **Self-Hosted GitLab**: If using a self-hosted instance, make sure Flightroom can reach your GitLab server (check firewall rules)

### Token Permissions Error

If you see a permissions error after connecting:

1. Go back to GitLab - User Settings - Access Tokens
2. Find your Flightroom token
3. Click **Revoke** and create a new token
4. Ensure all required scopes are selected (`api`, `read_user`, `read_repository`)
5. Update the token in Flightroom settings

### Cannot Access My Repositories

If your repositories don't appear or you can't access them:

- Verify that you have at least **Developer** role in the project/group
- Make sure the token has the correct scopes selected
- Check that the repositories are not archived or deleted
- If using group/organization name, verify it matches exactly the GitLab group path

### Self-Hosted GitLab Issues

For self-hosted GitLab installations:

- **SSL Certificate Errors**: Ensure your GitLab instance has a valid SSL certificate
- **Firewall**: Make sure Flightroom can access your GitLab instance (port 443 for HTTPS)
- **Version Compatibility**: Check that your GitLab version supports Personal Access Tokens (GitLab 8.8+)

title: Connect a GitLab repository — Security Best Practices
text:
:::warning[Token Security]
Follow these best practices to keep your account secure:
:::

- **Never share** your Personal Access Token with anyone
- **Use specific scopes** - only grant the permissions that are needed
- **Set expiration dates** - tokens should expire after 90 days or less
- **Rotate tokens regularly** - create new tokens periodically
- **Revoke immediately** if compromised - if you suspect a token has been exposed, revoke it right away and create a new one
- **Use separate tokens** for different services - don't reuse the same PAT across multiple integrations

title: Connect a GitLab repository — Need Help?
text:
If you encounter any issues or need assistance:

- Check the [GitLab documentation](https://docs.gitlab.com/)
- Review the [Personal Access Tokens documentation](https://docs.gitlab.com/ee/user/profile/personal_access_tokens.html)
- Contact Flightroom support

title: Dependency analysis and peer dependency alignment
text:
Every frontend of a project lives in its own repository, so nothing stops two of them
from pinning a different version of React, of the design system, or of any other shared
library. This feature walks those repositories, reports what each one declares, flags what is
behind the npm registry, and can rewrite the misaligned `peerDependencies` for you.

title: Dependency analysis and peer dependency alignment — In the console
text:
Open **Dependencies** in the sidebar (`/dependencies`). The page scans the project when it opens and
shows, top to bottom:

- **Branches to compare**: one row per frontend with a connected repository, on its default
  branch. Pick another branch for any of them; a row on a non-default branch reads *Different from
  the default branch*, and **Rescan** becomes **Apply the selected branches** until you press it.
- Four counters: **Scanned frontends**, **Distinct packages**, **Outdated packages** and
  **Misaligned peer dependencies**.
- **Peer dependencies to align**, then **Shared dependencies with different versions** (reported
  for visibility only), each with the **Suggested range**. Hovering a declaration tells whether it is
  *Already aligned* or *Will be aligned to* the suggested range.
- **Dependencies by frontend**: every declared package with its **Type**, **Declared range**,
  **Latest version** and **Status**. **Show outdated only** hides what is up to date, and a package
  marked deprecated on the registry carries a **Deprecated** badge.

![The Dependencies page of a project with no frontend connected to a repository: zero counters, nothing to align and Align peer dependencies disabled](../assets/dependencies.png)

The header has three actions:

| Action | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| **Analyze the conflicts** | Asks [Maestro](../build-with-ai/console-assistant.md) to explain the conflicts between shared dependencies. Shown when the project can use an AI |
| **Rescan** | Runs the scan again, on the branches selected above |
| **Align peer dependencies** | Opens the alignment dialog. Disabled when nothing is misaligned, or while a branch change has not been applied with a rescan |

The **Align peer dependencies** dialog lists, repository by repository, the compared branch and each
package with its current and target range. Set the **Target branch**
(`chore/align-peer-dependencies` by default, created from the compared branch of each repository if
it does not exist yet) and press **Create the commits**. The dialog then shows the outcome per
repository: the branch committed to, *Already aligned*, or *Failed* with the reason. See [Applying the alignment](#applying-the-alignment) for what happens underneath.

title: Dependency analysis and peer dependency alignment — What the scan does
text:
1. Lists the frontends of the current project that have a
   [code repository connected](./connect/github.md).
2. Reads the `package.json` at the root of each repository, on the branch chosen for that
   frontend, through the provider API (GitHub, GitLab or Azure DevOps — no clone involved).
3. Resolves every distinct package name against the npm registry and compares the declared
   range with the version published as `latest`.
4. Groups the declarations across frontends to find the ones that disagree.

The scan is read-only and is never cached in the database: it always reflects the current state
of the repositories. Registry answers are cached in memory for one hour.

### Choosing the branch

Each frontend is compared on its own branch, picked independently of the others. The
default is the **default branch of its repository**, so the scan works out of the box; the UI
lists the available branches per frontend and lets you point one at `develop`, a release
branch, or anything else before rescanning.

`GET /api/dependencies/targets` returns what the scan would walk — one entry per frontend
with its `defaultBranch` and the `branches` available — and the three `POST` endpoints accept a
`branches` map keyed by frontend id. Frontends left out of the map — and every request
to the two `GET` report endpoints, which take no body — fall back to the default branch.

### Update status

The status of a dependency compares the **floor of the declared range** (`^18.2.0` → `18.2.0`)
with the registry `latest`:

| Status         | Meaning                                              |
| -------------- | ---------------------------------------------------- |
| `UP_TO_DATE`   | The floor is greater than or equal to `latest`       |
| `PATCH_BEHIND` | Same major and minor, older patch                    |
| `MINOR_BEHIND` | Same major, older minor                              |
| `MAJOR_BEHIND` | Older major                                          |
| `UNKNOWN`      | The range does not point to a registry version (`*`, `file:`, git urls, …) or the package is not published on the registry |

### Alignment issues

A package is reported as misaligned when at least two frontends declare it and the
declared ranges are not all identical. The **suggested range** is the highest range already in
use inside the project — never a version nobody has validated yet — with ties broken by the
most frequently declared range, so that the alignment touches as few repositories as possible.

Mismatches are computed both for `peerDependencies` and for `dependencies`. The ones on
`dependencies` are reported for visibility only: the alignment action never rewrites them.

title: Dependency analysis and peer dependency alignment — Applying the alignment
text:
The alignment commits the updated `package.json` on a dedicated branch of every repository —
`chore/align-peer-dependencies` by default — created from the branch that was compared.

:::warning[The base branch is never modified]
If the target branch resolves to the branch being compared, that repository is skipped with an
error. Existing branches are reused, and the manifest is re-read from the target branch before
the change is applied, so re-running the alignment is idempotent.
:::

Pass the same `branches` map used for the scan, otherwise the alignment is computed — and
branched — from the default branches instead of the ones you compared.

Only the `peerDependencies` section is rewritten. The indentation and the key order of the
original file are preserved.

Every repository is processed independently: a failure on one of them (revoked token, missing
`package.json`, protected branch) is reported in the response and does not stop the others.

title: Dependency analysis and peer dependency alignment — API
text:
All the endpoints below are served under `/api` and are scoped to the project carried by the
`Project-Id` header, except `/api/projects/:projectId/dependencies`, which takes the project from
the path.

| Method | Path                                    | Description                                                       |
| ------ | --------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `GET`  | `/api/dependencies/targets`             | Frontends the scan would walk, with default and available branches |
| `GET`  | `/api/dependencies`                     | Full report on the default branches                                |
| `GET`  | `/api/projects/:projectId/dependencies` | Same report, with the project in the path                          |
| `POST` | `/api/dependencies/report`              | Full report on the branches given in the body                      |
| `POST` | `/api/dependencies/peer/alignment-plan` | Dry run: what would change, repository by repository               |
| `POST` | `/api/dependencies/peer/align`          | Applies the alignment and returns the outcome per repository       |

The body of the `POST` endpoints is optional. `/api/dependencies/report` accepts `branches` only,
the two alignment endpoints accept every field:

```jsonc
{
  "branches": { "<frontendId>": "develop" }, // branch to compare, defaults to the repository default
  "frontendIds": ["..."], // restrict to these frontends, defaults to all
  "packages": ["react"],       // restrict to these packages, defaults to every misaligned one
  "branchName": "chore/align-peer-dependencies",
  "commitMessage": "chore(deps): align peer dependencies"
}
```

title: Dependency analysis and peer dependency alignment — Configuration
text:
| Variable           | Default                      | Description                                              |
| ------------------ | ---------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------- |
| `NPM_REGISTRY_URL` | `https://registry.npmjs.org` | Registry queried for the latest published versions        |

On a self-hosted instance this is set like every other
[environment variable](../self-hosting/environment-variables.md).

When the registry cannot be reached the report is still produced: the update status of every
dependency falls back to `UNKNOWN`, `registryAvailable` is `false`, and the cross-frontend
comparison — including the peer dependency alignment — keeps working.

title: Dependency analysis and peer dependency alignment — Limitations
text:
- Only the `package.json` at the **root** of the repository is analysed; monorepo workspaces
  inside a frontend repository are not walked.
- Ranges are compared through a minimal semver implementation: the floor of the range is used,
  complex unions (`1.x || 2.x`) are reduced to their first version token.
- Private packages that are not published on the configured registry are reported as `UNKNOWN`,
  never as outdated.

title: Import repositories as frontends
text:
A project that already exists does not start from an empty frontend list: its
frontends are repositories that have been around for months, one per team. Declaring them
one by one in the console is the boring part of adopting the orchestrator, so the frontends
dashboard can read the repositories reachable through a code repository connection and create
one frontend per repository, in a single pass.

The import only creates and links the frontends. It does not clone, build or deploy
anything: [uploading a version](../frontends/versions-and-builds.md) and assigning it to an
environment stays a separate, explicit step.

title: Import repositories as frontends — Before you start
text:
The import needs a **code repository connection on the project** — a
[GitHub](./connect/github.md) account or organization, a [GitLab](./connect/gitlab.md) group, or
an [Azure DevOps](./connect/azure.dev-ops.md) project — configured under **Settings → Resources → Code
Repositories**. Until at least one connection exists the action is not shown at all, because
there would be nothing to list.

title: Import repositories as frontends — Where the action is
text:
On the **Frontends** dashboard, **Import from repository** sits next to
**Add New Frontend** in the page header, and again in the empty state of a project that has no
frontend yet.

On the **Structure** of a [functional domain](../domains/overview.md), the **Add frontend** and
**Add service** menus also offer **Import from repository**. From there every imported repository
lands in that domain, and from **Add service** it becomes a **service** instead of a frontend
(see [Importing as services](#importing-as-services)). It is the only place in the console to import
services.

![The Import from repository action in the frontends dashboard header](../assets/repository-import-action.png)

title: Import repositories as frontends — Choosing what to import
text:
The dialog lists every repository the connection exposes, sorted by name, and shows for each one
the **slug** the frontend would get.

![The import dialog listing the repositories of a connection, with slugs and already imported badges](../assets/repository-import-dialog.png)

- **Connection selector** — shown only when the project has more than one connection. The
  default connection of the project is preselected. Switching connection clears the selection.
- **Search** — filters the list by repository name.
- **Select all** — selects the repositories currently visible, so it composes with the search:
  filter by prefix, select all, refine, import.
- **Already imported** — repositories already linked to a frontend or a service of this
  project carry an *Already imported* badge in place of the slug and cannot be selected. The API still reports the
  slug they were imported with, in `slug` and in `importedAs`.

A repository counts as already imported when its provider id matches the one stored on a
frontend of the project linked to the same connection. Frontends
[created by hand](../frontends/create-a-frontend.md) do not always carry that id — it
is only known once the repository exists — so a case-insensitive match on the repository **name**
is used as a fallback.

title: Import repositories as frontends — What each import creates
text:
One frontend per selected repository, with:

| Field           | Value                                                                                                   |
| --------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Name            | The repository name                                                                                      |
| Slug            | The name slugified (lowercase, non-alphanumeric runs collapsed to `-`), with a numeric suffix on collision |
| Description     | The repository description, when the provider exposes one                                                |
| Version         | `1.0.0`, or the `version` sent to the API                                                                |
| Host            | The [default storage](../buckets/overview.md) of the project when there is one, the Flightroom Hub otherwise, with entry point `assets/remoteEntry.js` |
| Code repository | Linked and enabled, with the provider id, the HTTPS and SSH clone urls and — on GitLab — the group and path |

Those are the same defaults the
[add frontend form](../frontends/create-a-frontend.md) applies, so an imported
frontend is not a second-class one: continue from its detail page exactly as you would with
a hand-created frontend.

Slugs are unique per project. When the slugified name is taken, the next free numeric suffix is
used (`header`, `header-2`, `header-3`), and the suffix is allocated across the batch too, so
importing two repositories that slugify identically produces two frontends rather than a
failure.

title: Import repositories as frontends — Importing as services
text:
Imported as services, each repository creates a service with the same name, slug, description and
code repository link, and no version: the first one is registered by its CI, as for a service made
from a template. Services have a slug space of their own, separate from the frontends'.

A service slug takes **2 to 50** lowercase letters, digits or dashes, because it names the CI
registration URL of the service. A repository whose slug would be longer lands in **failed**: create
that service by hand with a shorter slug.

title: Import repositories as frontends — Partial results are the normal case
text:
Repositories are imported **independently**: one that fails does not abort the batch and does
not roll back what has already been created. The result splits into three lists:

- **imported** — the created frontends or services, with the slug and the id each one got
  (`frontendId` or `serviceId`).
- **skipped** — repositories that were not touched, with the reason: `ALREADY_IMPORTED` for one
  already linked to a frontend or a service, `NOT_FOUND` for an explicitly requested id the connection
  does not expose (a repository deleted or made private since the list was loaded).
- **failed** — repositories whose creation raised an error, with the error message.

The console reports each list on its own: a success notification with the number of
frontends created, an error notification naming the repositories that failed. When
something failed the dialog stays open, reloads the list and clears the selection: the
repositories that were imported come back flagged as already imported, and the failed ones can be
